POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 20:38:52 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 ‘The only way to get this done’: Why the US wants Europe at Ukraine talks next time https://www.politico.eu/article/why-the-us-wants-europe-at-ukraine-talks-next-time/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 11 Nov 2026 19:53:57 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9310596 ABU DHABI — When Jared Kushner walked into the briefing room to announce the results of two days of peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, he didn’t try to conceal how hard it had been. 

“The reality is there’s no trust right now between the sides,” Donald Trump’s son-in-law and trusted envoy told POLITICO during a post-talks briefing. “There were some pretty tough discussions.” 

The two sides, one led by a Kremlin aide and the other by Ukraine’s spy chief, discussed all the most difficult topics including the toughest — what happens to disputed territory — and fought hard for their own objectives, according to those in the room. 

The mood cooled from the first day to the second. On Tuesday, with negotiations lasting four and a half hours, officials on the ground in Abu Dhabi who were familiar with the talks described them as “constructive.” The best they could muster on Wednesday, when the session broke up after just two hours, was that the exchange had been “neutral.” 

In truth, few on the Ukrainian side ever believed this week’s resumption of face-to-face negotiations would deliver a breakthrough. The biggest announcement concerned the non-trivial matter of a planned prisoner exchange — which Kushner said would be the biggest in the war so far, but on even this they failed to announce the final agreed numbers. 

Yet despite the muted rhetoric, the meeting in the air-conditioned environs of a secure government guest house — where staff were constantly on hand to provide coffee, sandwiches and even pizza — was nevertheless a significant moment in the stop-start journey toward peace after nearly five years of war. 

Here’s what you need to know about where things stand.

What did they discuss?  

Everything. According to Kushner, there was no significant topic that was not raised over the two days. The question of territory, he said, would clearly be “the hardest” to resolve. According to Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Kyiv’s negotiators scored a major win on day one by convincing the Americans to accept their analysis of where the front line stands, and just how much less Ukrainian territory Russia has conquered than Moscow claims. 

It’s hard to see a quick resolution on that issue, although privately U.S. officials say both sides have shown some flexibility on how to settle territorial claims. Zelenskyy still insists, and it seems the American mediators agree, that matters relating to the fate of Ukrainian land can only be discussed at the level of leaders. That kind of meeting is still very far away. “Clearly, there’s not great trust or love between the leaders,” Kushner said. 

What did they agree? 

A big prisoner exchange — potentially the largest since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022. But even this isn’t yet final: Kushner made it clear that it would depend on approval from Vladimir Putin, and that he’d try to obtain that on Thursday on a visit to Moscow . 

“One of the positives was that we agreed that we’re going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners — we’re gonna finalize the numbers tomorrow,” Kushner said. He said he would be traveling with Steve Witkoff, Trump’s other envoy, “to Moscow tomorrow to meet with President Putin, to go over what was discussed today, and try to make more progress on some of the issues.” 

Ukraine’s negotiators said “strict directives” from Moscow had limited the scope of their Russian counterparts to reach agreements this week, making the talks harder. 

What happens next? 

The Moscow trip is key. Kushner said his other big goal in speaking to Putin would be to get him to allow Europeans to join the next round of negotiations. “I believe that hopefully tomorrow in Moscow, Steve and I will be successful and President Putin will give the blessing for that to occur. I think that if he agrees to that we will be able to make a lot more progress,” Kushner said in response to a question from POLITICO. 

Then the Americans plan to head to Dublin to meet Zelenskyy in person and try to push the agenda forward. The Ukrainians want to get the next date in their diary for more talks because they hope to have a deal before the end of the year, with Russia ramping up strikes on Ukraine’s power grids and energy facilities and another winter looming. 

The big shift 

Arguably, the biggest change in recent days has been in America’s attitude. This was never simply a negotiation between Russia and Ukraine, after all; ever since Trump returned to power nearly two years ago, Kyiv and Brussels have been trying to persuade Washington to take their arguments more seriously. For Ukraine’s European allies, that lobbying has paid off. 

Kushner and Witkoff now want European officials to join the next round of negotiations — so they can move on to discussing one of Putin’s most totemic obsessions: Relations with NATO, and the future system of European security. 

“We need to have the Europeans at the table,” Kushner said, answering a question from POLITICO at the briefing. “We have relayed to President Putin directly several times and to his team that the only way to get this done is to have them by our side, and I think they are receptive to it.”

Ukrainian negotiators said Russian attitudes only started to soften — and open to dialogue — once the U.S. moved to discuss postwar settlements for both sides.

On Ukraine, too, American attitudes have changed. Only a few weeks ago Trump was angrily demanding that Zelenskyy be replaced amid a bust-up over Ukraine’s criticism of the U.S. president’s diesel deal with Putin. Russia, Trump said, had been “fine” on Ukraine. 

Now, however, Kushner is careful to praise the Ukrainian negotiating team and “the great efforts” they made in Abu Dhabi. “I think they fought very, very hard for their issues, were very constructive, and I think it was a very productive session.” The Ukrainians also expressed gratitude to the U.S. side. 

Europe’s big question 

It’s one thing to be invited to take part in real talks with Russia and Ukraine — and Europeans have yet to be given even this chance. But it’s another to participate and then influence the conversation when it finally happens. For that, Europe needs to choose its representatives wisely. 

Zelenskyy says he wants to be consulted on who should get the role of speaking for Europe — and that it should be a single person. He also wants Europe to decide by the end of this month. 

So far, however, Europe’s approach has been anything but streamlined. Attending the talks on the sidelines in Abu Dhabi were representatives of the European Commission, the European Council, NATO, the U.K., France, Germany and Italy. 

Wearing his diplomatic hat, Kushner described this arrangement as “strong” — but added that “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation.”

Europe’s danger moment 

If the latest negotiations have achieved nothing else, after months of worrying about being left on the sidelines, Europe now finds itself — subject to Putin’s approval, of course — in the thick of the most perilous negotiations in the continent’s recent history. 

One critical question is how far talks about changing the continental security framework, which is underpinned by NATO, will be tied to the peace negotiations regarding Ukraine. Europeans have long campaigned for Ukraine to get the strongest possible security guarantees to prevent Russia from attacking again when the war ends. And U.S. officials want to explore the idea of providing a NATO-like collective defense agreement with Ukraine that could even involve NATO itself as a guarantor. 

Officials in European capitals say the sequencing of these talks will be critical. The European side has signaled its willingness to explore the continent’s wider security system to allay Russia’s concerns — in parallel with the Ukraine peace process. But they don’t want to sign up to any wider reforms until peace has been achieved. 

‘Trying to survive’

Kushner said the aim was to discuss all the issues and then “find a pathway to settle them all at the same time.” 

“I think that having these discussions is very important,” he said. “But the implementation of postwar security will not occur until there’s an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues.” 

If that position holds, it could work for Europe. But in the end, anything agreed among officials in the negotiating room is always provisional. All it would take is a phone call from Putin to Trump. 

Some Europeans are wary. German officials involved in the Abu Dhabi talks see very little potential upside and view the process as a “Russian trap” to give a false impression that Moscow is willing to make peace, said one German official with knowledge of talks, who was granted anonymity to speak frankly. 

“The Europeans are only trying to survive this,” the official said.

James Angelos and Veronika Melkozerova contributed reporting.

]]> en Lagarde would equal any other centrist in Elysée run, poll shows https://www.politico.eu/article/lagarde-would-equal-any-other-centrist-in-elysee-run-poll-shows/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 11 Nov 2026 16:45:41 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9310155 Christine Lagarde, the departing president of the European Central Bank, would fare as well as center-right candidate Edouard Philippe were she to run in next year’s French presidential election, according to new polling commissioned by POLITICO.

Lagarde, who served as French economy minister almost two decades ago under former President Nicolas Sarkozy, would get 14% of the vote were she to run instead of Philippe, who would receive 13.5% against a similar slate of candidates, according to polling from Cluster17.

While Lagarde has previously ruled out running, her early departure from the ECB next February has renewed speculation she could take part in a contest where centrist and right-wing candidates have struggled to break through.

In a highly unlikely scenario in which Lagarde runs next to Philippe and multiple recently declared candidates, including Olympic judo champion Teddy Riner and columnist Natasha Polony, she would also rival President Emmanuel Macron’s former prime minister with 8% support.

In both cases, far-right candidate Marine Le Pen and leftist hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon are projected to finish first and second, respectively, which would qualify them for next May’s runoff round.

Cluster17’s survey, the first public poll to test a Lagarde candidacy, shows the centrist vote is “very fluid,” according to the institute’s president, Jean-Yves Dormagen. “At this stage there is a patent lack of leadership in the moderate and centrist space.”

The centrist camp is grappling with an internal conflict between Philippe and Gabriel Attal, another former prime minister. Philippe, who was once a favorite to face Le Pen in the second round, has struggled to gain traction despite months of campaigning, POLITICO’s Poll of Polls show.

Conservative Bruno Retailleau, who served as interior minister under Macron, is also a candidate along with right-wing Cannes Mayor David Lisnard and center-left MEP Raphaël Glucksmann. All hope to defy the increasing odds of a Le Pen-Mélenchon runoff.

Lagarde previously dismissed her candidacy as “not a good idea at all,” but since announcing her early exit from the ECB on Oct. 29 she has avoided answering the question directly.

Asked by POLITICO whether she was still ruling out running during a panel at the Paris Peace Forum on Wednesday, Lagarde stuck to her guns: “I said I want to recover my freedom to speak, my freedom to engage in matters that are not monetary policy, and that’s what I want to do.”

Lagarde will leave her ECB post on Feb. 7 next year, about a month before presidential hopefuls must formally apply to run.

L’institut Cluster 17 a testé* l’hypothèse d’une candidature de l’ancienne ministre de Nicolas Sarkozy. *Sondage réalisé par questionnaire auto-administré en ligne entre les 9 et 10 novembre 2026 auprès d’un échantillon de 1164 personnes inscrites sur les listes électorales issu d’un échantillon de 1242 personnes représentatives de la population française, selon la méthode des quotas (sexe, âge, catégorie socioprofessionnelle et régions de résidence).

There are also restrictions on “loot boxes,” which contain surprise virtual items that players can buy with real money. The law also stipulates that in-app virtual currencies must be turned off by default for under-18s.

The Commission says these practices encourage overspending, which is especially dangerous for vulnerable consumers like kids. Violating the rules can lead to fines of up to 6% of global revenue in cases that affect more than two-thirds of the EU population.

“We want the European gaming industry to continue to thrive,” said Michael McGrath, the commissioner for consumer protection, announcing the measures. But competition, McGrath added, should be based “on creativity, innovation, and quality, and not on practices that exploit consumers.”

In a joint statement, the European Game Developer Federation, an association representing EU firms, and Video Games Europe, which includes global juggernauts like Sony and Epic Games, say that the proposed definition of pay-to-win is “fundamentally flawed, lacks clear definitions and would create huge confusion for players and developers alike” since it could cover “any purchase.”

Angry Birds & friends

Video game spending in the bloc topped €27 billion, accounting for 17% of the global market, last year, according to the European Audiovisual Observatory.

The gaming groups argue that the industry already does a good job regulating itself with parental controls and the content rating system PEGI, which the DFA doesn’t take into account.

“Effectively, the DFA moves all decisions from parents and children to the Commission,” they wrote.

The DFA aims to regulate a slew of other industries, cracking down on manipulative practices in online commerce such as addictive design, dynamic pricing and making it difficult to unsubscribe from a digital subscription.

]]> en ‘Systemic’ sexual misconduct in German armed forces, study finds https://www.politico.eu/article/study-finds-widespread-bundeswehr-sexual-misconduct/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Wed, 11 Nov 2026 13:45:35 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9308541 BERLIN — Most cases of sexual misconduct in Germany’s armed forces go unreported, according to a major study presented Wednesday, as Defense Minister Boris Pistorius acknowledged a “systemic problem” in how the military handles complaints.

The report found that sexual misconduct was three to six times more common than official figures suggest. The findings come as Germany tries to recruit more soldiers, including more women, as part of efforts to rebuild its military.

Four in 10 female soldiers and roughly one in five male soldiers said they had experienced at least one form of sexual misconduct in the previous year.

That includes unwanted sexual comments, sexual images, unwanted touching and sexual violence. Over the same period, 2% of both women and men reported experiencing sexual violence.

More than 8,100 soldiers completed the July 13 to Aug. 27 anonymous survey, about 18% of those contacted. The researchers said they had adjusted the results to reflect the makeup of the military.

The study found that only one-sixth to one-third of sexual incidents were reported, depending on the type of misconduct, with many victims saying they didn’t want to draw attention to themselves. Others feared consequences or doubted that reporting an incident would lead to action.

Pistorius presented the findings to the defense committee in the country’s parliament alongside Germany’s top military officer, Carsten Breuer. Speaking afterward, he promised “zero tolerance” for sexual misconduct.

Pistorius called the handling of complaints a “systemic problem.” He said military structures and the traditional responses of some commanders to complaints were partly to blame.

He announced a 34-point plan to improve protection for victims and make it easier to report incidents, including a new advice service outside the usual military chain of command. The service is currently available daily but is expected to become available around the clock.

Commanders will also be assessed on how they respond to complaints, and victims will receive more information about investigations. Commanders who tolerate misconduct or fail to deal with it properly “will no longer hold a leadership position,” Pistorius said.

The study also found that women had reported less misconduct in units where they made up more than 15% of personnel.

Asked what he would tell a mother worried about her daughter joining the military, Pistorius insisted the Bundeswehr remained a “safe employer” because it was taking action.

In a move designed to build confidence between the warring nations, Kushner announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to what is likely to be “the biggest” exchange of prisoners since the start of the war. The numbers will be confirmed Thursday, he added. Russian state-controlled news agency Tass confirmed that a “large-scale” prisoner exchange had been agreed. 

Kushner said that, overall, the two-day talks were “substantive” and “pretty tough” but “a good first step” to get the two sides talking again after a nine-month break. 

He said that when U.S. officials met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo three weeks ago, it was not clear that Moscow and Kyiv would be able to resume negotiations. 

“It’s been a long way to get everyone back to the table,” Kushner said. “But I think this was a very good first meeting. It was a tough meeting, but a productive one.” He said all relevant issues were discussed between the two sides and that the question of territory “will be the hardest” to resolve. 

The Ukrainian negotiators blamed “very strict directives” from the Kremlin for limiting their room to negotiate in Abu Dhabi, making it impossible to achieve more progress in the talks. 

Kushner and Witkoff will aim to persuade Putin to unlock progress on some issues when they meet him Thursday and, according to officials who took part in the talks, to agree on the date of the next round of negotiations. They will then travel to meet Zelenskyy and potentially European leaders in Dublin later. 

Ukraine wants an agreement on a ceasefire by the New Year, as it fears Russia is preparing another winter of bombardments and targeting energy networks to freeze the country into submission. 

One critical question, especially for Europe, is how far the talks about changing the continental security framework underpinned by NATO will be tied to the specific negotiations over peace in Ukraine.

Europeans have long campaigned for Ukraine to get the strongest possible security guarantees to prevent Russia attacking again when this war ends. U.S. officials want to explore the idea of providing a NATO-like collective defense agreement with Ukraine, which could even see the alliance itself act as a guarantor. 

But Russia is insisting on widening the talks to include a review of the whole security architecture for Europe — something the U.S. mediators have agreed to.

European officials say the sequencing of these talks will be critical. The European side has signaled its willingness to explore overhauling the continent’s wider security system to allay Russia’s concerns — in parallel with the Ukraine peace process. But they do not want to sign up to any broader reforms until peace has been achieved. 

Kushner said the aim was to discuss all the issues and then “find a pathway to settle them all at the same time.” 

“I think that having these discussions is very important,” he said. “But the implementation of postwar security will not occur until there’s an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues.”

The U.S. desire to have Europe join the negotiations throws the spotlight back on the European Union and others such as the United Kingdom to decide who will represent them in talks. EU leaders will consider this now urgent question in Dublin at an informal summit Friday.

Zelenskyy has said he wants to be consulted over who gets to represent Europe, but has urged his allies to hurry up and ideally pick one person to take the lead in future talks.

Kushner said the current arrangement, which includes NATO, the EU institutions, and representatives from France, Germany, the U.K. and Italy, was “a really strong way to organize,” adding, “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation.”

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:43:15 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 The olive branch is a universal symbol of peace – but the West Bank’s autumn olive harvest is open season for Israeli settlers to pillage and kill https://euobserver.com/248241/the-olive-branch-is-a-universal-symbol-of-peace-but-the-west-banks-autumn-olive-harvest-is-open-season-for-israeli-settlers-to-pillage-and-kill/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248241 The olive has become much more than a household staple. In Palestine, the annual autumn harvest requires courage, protection by activists and an often deadly struggle. The contrast to Europe's olive tradition has never been so stark.]]> Autumn in Italy is always a special time.

South of the grey, industrial northern cities, from the rolling hills of Tuscany down to the rocky heel if the Ionian sea, one is never too far from the scent trailing behind the world’s most sought after harvests: the grape, and the olive. 

I was visiting my family in the fields of Rome, where this year’s crop alleviated concern brought on by last year’s meagre yield. My uncle’s generous green bounty was turned to liquid gold, one that tastes of legacy and belonging.

On the eastern seaboard of the Mediterranean, it has also come to smell like blood.

The ancient tradition, and the historic land that binds it to its sturdy tree roots, has been turned into the battleground of Israeli colonisation of the occupied West Bank. Exacerbated since 2023, the olive harvest has become the season synonymous with the most attacks by Israeli defence forces-backed illegal settlers hoping to intimidate Palestinian families out of their homes. 

Read more

From West Bank to EU supermarkets: How much longer will Israeli settler imports go on?

It’s the time where residents, forced indoors in fear of the swelling conflict increasingly taking place beyond just Gaza, dare to set foot out to reap the fruits of the land that provides a living for some 100,000 families across the Palestinian territories.

Beyond the major source of income many depend upon, depriving Palestine of its olive harvest denies some 5.6 million people with the social fabric that makes up the part of their national identity. 

According to UN data, the 2025 olive harvest brought 178 settler attacks to the occupied West Bank, in 88 Palestinian towns and villages. Over 6,000 trees and saplings were vandalised.

]]> War of propaganda: Russia calls Ukraine a ‘burden’ and uses Moldova as a ‘testing ground’ to sabotage EU enlargement https://euobserver.com/247967/war-of-propaganda-russia-calls-ukraine-a-burden-and-uses-moldova-as-a-testing-ground-to-sabotage-eu-enlargement/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:32:04 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247967 From fake celebrity sex scandals to ominous warnings about land seizures and soaring bills, Kremlin-linked campaigns are working to turn ordinary voters against EU accession long before any referendum is held.]]> As the saying goes, the first casualty of war is the truth. But in the case of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it seems the truth had been under attack for a while. 

As recently as this summer, claims that Russia had actually made significant battlefield gains were debunked after analysis found that interpretation was based on misuse of a report which actually found Ukraine had made the greater advances.

It chimes with the continuing battle for control of the narrative over Ukraine, not least when it comes to the prospect of that country, and possibly its neighbour, Moldova, ultimately joining the EU.

Media organisations in those countries have become acutely aware of what they say is Russian disinformation about EU enlargement, often circulated via the Telegram app and other online platforms such as Facebook.

They have heard various narratives against EU membership, such as a purported loss of state sovereignty, of the EU wishing to prolong a ‘proxy war’ with Russia through Ukraine, and even of Ukraine being divided up between EU member states.

As Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine approaches its sixth year, the likelihood of it joining the EU is still being actively debated. Neighbouring Moldova is also driving towards EU membership, even though it is aware that Russia is actively opposed. 

It means both countries, and others in the region where people have expressed a desire to join the EU, such as Georgia, find themselves the subject of online campaigns which, critics say, are aimed at undermining those efforts.

Read more

Moldova seen as ‘best performer’ on EU-accession reforms, despite onslaught of Russian sabotage

Disinformation is not new

It is also hard to argue that this is a new phenomenon. Over 10 years ago, the EU set up a task force in order to challenge “Russia’s ongoing disinformation campaigns”. 

A number of months after the war began in 2022, the OECD think-tank in Paris published a policy paper on ‘Disinformation and Russia’s War of Aggression against Ukraine’, in which it said: “The Russian disinformation narratives are often false, or obscure facts with half-truths and ‘whataboutisms’.” 

And just last year the delegation of the European Union to Ukraine looked at information manipulation and disinformation that summer targeting Ukraine-EU relations.

It was a topic of discussion when the deputy prime minister for European integration of Moldova, Cristina Gherasimov, visited Ireland earlier this year. 

Speaking to The Journal in Dublin last February, Gherasimov said that disinformation “continues constantly”.

Read more

How EU hopes to ‘shield’ elections against Moscow’s propaganda

“This is one of the most powerful tools of Moscow: disinformation, not necessarily about our own country or process in our own country, but a narrative that targets the EU as such. It targets the EU credibility for candidate countries or aspiring countries, for EU membership.

“Some of the narratives are usually around the future of candidate countries in the EU, saying that we are not ready,” she said.

This argument, she added, also centred on the idea of the EU as weak and unable to stand up for its own citizens.

Another line is that new entrant countries would be seen as a ‘poor relation’ and would not be as competitive when it comes to agriculture and other areas once they joined the EU.

“What we’ve learned from our own elections is that disinformation does not stop after the elections, it continues constantly, and it adapts very quickly in terms of the narratives that it promotes, depending on the vulnerabilities that exist in each society that is targeted,” she added.

“One very usual narrative targeting the EU is that all the land will be expropriated once Moldova joins the European Union, and that is meant to draw equal lines with how it used to be during the Soviet Union period for us, and that is meant to inflict fear that the EU is not there to support and protect its citizens, but it’s there to actually prey on them,” said Gherasimov.

Ukrainian accession efforts labelled ‘futile’?

Moldova knows about disinformation: a report in the New York Times last September said the Stimson Center – a research organisation in Washington – called the country “a testing ground for hybrid warfare operations” that “are likely to shape similar efforts” across Europe. 

The same New York Times article referred to how, ahead of Moldova’s parliamentary election, social media platforms were flooded with fabricated posts, videos and websites, sometimes created using AI. 

As outlined in this Euronews report, one post even impersonated the celebrity magazine OK! with a false story declaring “Moldovan president in celebrity sperm scandal!”. The concocted story, which incorrectly claimed that president Maia Sandu was buying sperm from gay celebrity donors to have a child, falsely used the name of a real reporter. 

This demonstrates how disinformation frequently attempts to erode political reputations and steer voters towards particular political agendas. 

Read more

EU accession of Moldova and Ukraine is alternative to Nato, as Russia draws new Iron Curtain in Europe

As with other forms of political disinformation, this takes many forms when it comes to EU accession, according to Vladyslav Lesyk, a journalist at Ukrainian media outlet Rubryka.

“One of the primary Russian narratives regarding Ukraine’s EU accession is the claim that Ukraine’s efforts to join the Union are futile,” he said. 

“For instance, Russian sources have spread fakes asserting that granting candidate status is a merely formal decision that offers no actual benefits. The functions of this narrative are to demoralise Ukrainian society and create the impression that the reforms required for EU membership are pointless,” he added.

“Another Russian narrative suggests that joining the EU would mean Ukraine losing its sovereignty. This builds upon a broader Russian narrative, maintained since the start of the Russo-Ukrainian war in 2014, which portrays Ukraine as a state with an illegitimate government controlled by the West, specifically the EU and the US,” said Lesyk.

Read more

Wave of Russian sabotage attacks exposes counter-intelligence gaps on Nato’s eastern flank

Disinformation is not new: EUvsDisinfo documents numerous past examples, including the infamous false story from 2014 of a boy allegedly being crucified by Ukrainian nationals in Slovyansk. This was cited to be part of a Kremlin-orchestrated campaign targeted at inciting hatred against Ukrainians.

Ukraine has long articulated a desire to join the EU and the process is well underway. Since June 2022, Ukraine has official EU candidate status, with accession negotiations having formally started. Last September Ukraine successfully completed its screening process.

Billions of euros in financial assistance have already been provided, while the EU has repeatedly affirmed its support for Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.

The ‘burden’ narrative

On the flip side, Lesyk said narratives spread in European countries lean into the idea of Ukraine becoming a “burden” on EU member states. 

“In this context, Ukraine is presented as a poor and corrupt state whose accession would supposedly drain the European budget. A specific sub-narrative focuses on the negative impact of Ukrainian grain on European farming. Russians have been spreading the narrative of ‘harmful’ Ukrainian grain for several years to sow discord,” he said.

Yet as this analysis from the European Policy Centre points out, Ukraine joining the EU would have very obvious benefits – including opening up the country’s energy potential to the EU, boosting EU food security, and providing ready trade in critical minerals.

Lesyk said Telegram is the primary hub for disseminating these Russian narratives in Ukraine, as it allows for the use of anonymous channels and is one of the most popular sources of information in the country. 

Regarding Moldova, media and fact-checking organisations have tracked a number of lines of attack regarding proposed EU membership, ranging from farms there closing due to Moldovan agricultural products not being in demand, to higher utility bills, and same-sex marriage. 

These were analysed in depth by the website NewsMaker.md. Romanian fact-checking website Veridica has tracked numerous disinformation campaigns, including that Moldova could become a destination for migrants, could lose its statehood, or even be annexed by Romania.

Read more

[Interview] ‘Whenever we take pro-European political decisions, Russia cut or reduced gas supplies’. Moldova energy minister Dorin Junghietu on why Chișinău is betting on diversification

Homegrown issues

In Georgia, another country seemingly at a crossroads when it comes to possible EU membership, websites such as OC Media have tracked what they believe are coordinated Russian information operations in recent years.

Salome Khvedelidze of OC Media said some of this runs on Facebook and other platforms. The International Society for Fair Elections and Democracy detailed material it described as “the dissemination of anti-Western, particularly anti-EU narratives”.

Common themes include the EU being a threat to Georgian values, such as EU support for LGBTQ+ rights, the potential for EU interference in Georgian domestic affairs, and the idea of the EU and the US more broadly wanting to spark conflict.

Read more

Zelensky stalls on his EU promises to protect gay rights, even as Ukraine rushes through minority-languages law

Since Russia’s war against Ukraine in 2022, Georgia has turned increasingly authoritarian, suspending EU accession talks and deepening its ties with Moscow.

Recently, the ruling Georgian Dream party sought to ban the five main opposition parties – a move which is currently being fought in court. The European Parliament warned that this puts the country’s path towards EU membership at risk.

According to Khvedelidze: “What makes Georgia different from Ukraine and Moldova, however, is where the main source of anti-EU propaganda actually comes from.”

“In Ukraine and Moldova, disinformation about EU membership is driven by Russian proxies, Russia-backed/funded media, and certain political figures, while the governments themselves are pro-European,” she said.

Arguably, it gives the impression of a message that is always changing but always the same. According to Cristina Gherasimov: “It adapts very quickly in terms of the narratives that it promotes, depending on the vulnerabilities that exist in each society that is targeted,” she added.

It is not always straightforward to verify which narratives come directly from Russia and which originate elsewhere, but there is little doubt about Russia’s attitude towards the EU, and its history of spreading disinformation abroad.

]]> [Interview] ‘I cannot be optimistic,’ says climatologist Jean Jouzel https://euobserver.com/246223/interview-i-cannot-be-optimistic-says-climatologist-jean-jouzel/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:31:15 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246223 Jean Jouzel, a renowned French climatologist, is not optimistic about the changing climate and the level of mitigation efforts. But he says people should should not give up on the fight against global warming.]]> First published in Respekt.

Jean Jouzel, a renowned French climatologist, is not optimistic about the changing climate and the level of mitigation efforts. But the scientist says people should should not give up on the fight against global warming. He explains the green deal, carbon markets, temperature rises and where the fight for a better environment stands now.

You previously said you hope that once Covid-19 passes, society would become more friendly to the environment.

Jean Jouzel: Unfortunately, this is not happening. Globally, carbon dioxide emissions continue to rise. They should stabilise over time, but that has not happened. Changes are taking place, but they are insufficient. Europe used to champion the ambitious Green Deal, but that ambition at a European level has faded.

So your optimism has gone?

When the Paris Climate Agreement was made in 2015, I was optimistic. But real progress is not being made. It is not that nothing at all has been done, but compared with the gravity of the problem, progress has been very slow. Many politicians focus only on how to adapt to climate change, which is important, but not enough.

Unless we have a good strategy and do something big by around 2040, it will be difficult to achieve carbon neutrality by the end of the century, essential to stabilising the climate.

Read more

EU states back one-year methane delay, but leave door open for more

What will this mean?

The people who are young today will live on a continuously warming planet. It is difficult to grasp that what we do over the next 15 years will have effects after such a long delay in the second half of this century.

Politicians say we have time; they argue that young people are so proficient in working with artificial intelligence that they will somehow solve the problem. But sea level rise cannot be stopped. By doing nothing, we are taking an enormous risk.

We live in a highly unstable, warring world. Does it make sense to pursue climate change mitigation now?

At an international level, I genuinely do not see solidarity between states. Clearly, the world is turning away from climate policies. And without mutual solidarity, we cannot stop global warming. So I cannot be optimistic.

Read more

Climate inaction could cost Europe €5.6 trillion by 2050, study finds

Even those who recognise the gravity of the problem say: let us not push the climate agenda now, because we are only playing into the hands of extremist political forces such as the Alternative for Germany (AfD) or the National Rally in France. Let us not talk about the climate, because we are endangering the future of democracy itself. What do you think?

We must stress the benefits of climate change mitigation, like human health through cleaner air, and economic growth.

Over the next decade, the economy should be built around a transition to a different way of operating: economic systems based on carbon and fossil fuels will shift towards systems based on achieving carbon neutrality.

Take the electric car: it is an interesting technology. There is no reason to continue relying on transport based on the internal combustion engine. China is doing a great deal in this respect and is moving in the right direction. Europe is not.

We should have been the ones setting the pace. Economic growth can be built on the shift to electric cars. Or take the retrofitting and thermal insulation of buildings, which will have positive effects both on the economy and on human health. During the summer, 8,000 died in France because of the heat, and 17,000 in Germany. When heat waves are so severe, it is very difficult to live in cities. The issue of climate change cannot be separated from everyday life. It is not only about the environment, but also about the economy.

But how can people be persuaded? There is an enormous amount of disinformation surrounding the climate.

The spread of misinformation is made easier by social media, which are so popular among young people. Climate change scepticism also arises from this. It is difficult to fight. A false message is easy to spread, but defending against it and putting forward counterarguments is difficult. At a certain point, I gave up on the idea that we could convince 100 percent of the population. It is enough to win over a majority — and that should not be impossible.

Read more

What is ‘coordinated inauthentic behaviour’ – and how is it distorting Europe’s online democracy?

People can see that something is happening to the climate. We must continue presenting our arguments to them, explaining how greenhouse-gas emissions are affected by everyday activities. If we do nothing, we will face very serious consequences in the second half of the century. It will be difficult, because climate sceptics have one huge advantage: they claim that we can continue our way of life and not worry about the climate – a very appealing idea. But if you believe there is a problem, it makes you concerned.

So how should we deal with this?

As I said, we should stress that the transition to a more sustainable way of life will bring us many benefits. Energy is at the heart of this transition. Transport and the thermal insulation of buildings are also important, but energy is where we need to start.

In your native France, do emissions taxes under the ETS2 system provoke concerns over fuel prices?

The increase in fuel prices was enormous in France, but one public response has been increased purchases of electric cars. In September, electric vehicles accounted for 40 percent of new sales. At the beginning of the year, it was only 28 percent. That is a major change. People are not buying electric cars because of the climate, but because of high petrol and diesel prices. I am afraid, however, that once prices fall, people will start returning to internal combustion engines. Prices influence their behaviour more than concern for the climate.

Read more

Compromise over chaos? How MEPs gutted Europe’s new carbon price before it even began

But the electricity for cars must be generated without emissions. Which technology is most promising? Renewables? Nuclear power?

In France, we generate most of our electricity from nuclear power, around 70 percent, but renewables are developing rapidly. If we want to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050, we must develop both: build new nuclear power plants while expanding renewables as quickly as possible.

Once you have a nuclear power plant that has been built, the electricity it produces is very cheap. But if you are only planning to build one, it is very expensive. Isn’t solar and wind power better?

High costs are indeed the biggest obstacle to the expansion of nuclear energy. By contrast, the costs of renewables are continually falling. On the other hand, they require strengthening the electricity grid in order to balance out the fluctuations in their electricity generation. That also costs money. This is why I believe we need a mix of both technologies.

Although the climate measures adopted have slowed global warming, the world is still heading towards warming of almost three degrees Celsius by 2100. What will that world look like?

    ]]>         Consumers pay the price for online manipulation, and the EU Digital Fairness Act can put a stop to it https://euobserver.com/247929/consumers-pay-the-price-for-online-manipulation-and-the-eu-digital-fairness-act-can-put-a-stop-to-it/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 12:35:02 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247929 The EU's Digital Fairness Act (DFA) is one of the few initiatives of this legislative term through which Europe can improve people's lives by strengthening their consumer rights and helping them save money, write the Socialists & Democrats.]]> Think about the last thing you did before going to sleep, and the first thing you did when you woke up. Look around you on the bus or the metro. We are hooked on our devices and the online services behind them.

    That is not a personal failing. It is by design, part of a business model.

    Digital products that we use daily – whether apps, social media platforms or online marketplaces – make their profits by exploiting our attention, our mental health and our vulnerabilities.

    Feeds that never end, subscriptions that are near impossible to cancel, and fake countdowns that push us to click and buy on impulse are no accident. They are deliberate design features with a direct impact on our wellbeing and our wallets.

    Today, the European Commission is presenting the Digital Fairness Act (DFA) as a proposal to fight these and other unfair online practices.

    It is one of the few initiatives of this legislative term through which Europe can improve people’s lives by strengthening their consumer rights and helping them save money.

    Unfair commercial practices are estimated to cost European consumers close to €8bn a year. Whether or not the DFA will become a game changer in the fight against addictive and manipulative design will depend on the ambition the EU shows.

    Read more

    Digital Fairness Act: EU cracks down on influencer ads and manipulative app design

    Despite the clear need for digital fairness, new rules will face opposition from some quarters, notably US Big Tech.

    It runs against their push to deregulate under the guise of “simplification”, and it could risk triggering transatlantic retaliation from the US administration.

    Some may also argue that we already have rules: the Digital Services Act (DSA), they will say, already tackles dark patterns and addictive design. It does not, at least not fully, not for all consumers and not across all digital spaces.

    We need to remember that 97 percent of the most popular apps and websites still use them, so the rules currently in place have not put an end to this online manipulation.

    Concrete demands

    As Socialists & Democrats, we have a clear vision of what a strong DFA can deliver for consumers. Our concrete demands are:

    Ban dark patterns. Things like subscription traps, long click paths to cancel, free trials that turn into paid plans without warning, forced registration, fake other people are viewing this alerts, and items that appear in your basket at checkout should all be prohibited outright.

    Restrict addictive design for all consumers. Features such as endless scrolling should be restricted for everyone, not only children. The bill recently proposed in the Netherlands can serve as an inspiration for Europe.

    Make influencers and the money behind them accountable. Influencers who promote illegal or fraudulent products should be held personally responsible. Commercial deals must be disclosed clearly, not hidden as “#ad” at the end of a hundred hashtags. Those paying influencers also need to be held to account. The products they promote can damage people’s health as well as their finances.

    Put an end to manipulative pricing. Imagine queuing for an ice cream on a sunny Saturday, only to find that it now costs €6 instead of the €3.50 you paid last week – just because it’s hotter and busier. This is unfair pricing, and we want it to be banned in transport, live entertainment, culture and sport. Concerts and matches should not only be for the rich. A car ride should cost the same regardless of your background, your data or your phone’s battery level. People want transparency, but they also want limits, especially in emergency situations, when they are most vulnerable and have no control over the circumstances. 

    Stop gambling-like features in games. Most gamers are adults, not children. Loot boxes and pay-to-win mechanisms should be prohibited so that everyone can play without being manipulated or trapped. This is also a matter of affordability: consumers should not feel forced to buy more than they want to.

    The principle is simple: fairness and safety, by design and by default, should be the rule for every company, whether it runs an app, a social network or an online marketplace. This would also protect the many honest businesses that are undercut today by competitors willing to manipulate their customers.

    At the end of the day, this is also about who holds power online.

    Holding Big Tech companies accountable for how their services shape our behaviour, through surveillance-based ads, harmful content and addictive design, is part of regaining Europe’s digital sovereignty.

    The EU Commission has the evidence, the mandate and our backing. The EU Kids Act, was an important step forward in protecting minors online. Let’s see if Ursula von der Leyen’s executive now shows the same determination to ensure a safer online space for everyone, children and adults alike.

    We will assess the DFA by one test: will it make people’s lives online safer, fairer and more affordable? Consumers should not have to wait any longer to be protected online.

    Reining in Big Tech is a top priority for us, and we’ll be fighting to make sure this legislation protects us all online.

    ]]>         Best way to halt migration is to sabotage Europe’s economy – but nobody wants that, so what are the alternatives? https://euobserver.com/248074/best-way-to-stop-migration-is-to-destroy-europes-economy/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248074 Keeping people impoverished abroad and destroying its economy are Europe's best tools to stop migration. Not even the most anti-migrant politician would seriously push for such a proposal.]]> European policy and law makers have a dilemma. They want to stop irregular migration and deport as many as people as possible.

    But people arriving in Europe irregularly are also lured by work. Spain needs people to pick vegetables and fruit. So does Italy.

    I remember meeting a young man from Bangladesh on the Ocean Viking, freshly rescued after a harrowing night at sea, asking when he would start working in Italy.

    Hein de Haas, a sociologist and university professor in Amsterdam and Maastricht, argues that European labour demand is the ultimate migration driver.

    “By far the best way to stop migration is to destroy your economy,” he recently told Deutsche Welle, a German broadcaster.

    Not even the most anti-migrant politician would seriously push for such a proposal.

    They are instead shoring up controls and restrictions. Some are more obvious than others.

    Bangladesh seems to be a pretty good example. Let me explain.

Calls on customs authorities and the European Commission to do a better job.]]> When Moscow launched its war against Ukraine in early the 2022, the EU quickly announced sanctions to cripple Russia’s economy.

    Twenty-one sanction packages have since been imposed, designed to punish Russia for its war. In 2021, EU trade with Russia stood at €253bn. Last year, it was €58bn.

    Yet despite EU restrictions, sanctioned trade goods, both imports and exports, still manage to slip into Russia as member states grapple with weak monitoring, spotty enforcement and legal ambiguities.

    This includes everything from dual-use and advanced-technology items found in Russian weapons to industrial goods vital for Russia’s economic and industrial base.

    Of some 202 identified parts in Russian missiles and drones, eight came directly from the EU. Even mundane products like Birch plywood from Russia and Belarus, which get relabelled in a foreign state, end up in the EU market.

    Read more

    In theory it’s from China, in reality it’s from Moscow – how sanctioned Russian timber keeps flowing into Czech Republic

    The findings were part of a larger report on EU sanctions on Russia, by the Luxembourg-based EU watchdog, the European Court of Auditors.

    The court looked at Bulgaria, Germany, Latvia, the Netherlands, and Poland. The differences between the five, in terms of compliance, appears striking.

    The report found Bulgaria recorded no violations of the sanctions. Latvia recorded 2,100. Both share borders with non-EU countries.

EUobserver talks to Patricia Llombart Cussac, the managing director for Africa for the European External Action Service, the EU’s diplomatic corps.]]> “Security in Africa and security in Europe are very much linked.     Security cooperation with Kenya is “a dynamic area of our cooperation,” adds EU ambassador to Kenya, Andreas Peschke.

    The Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) aims to use public contracts and subsidies to create steady demand for cleaner, European-made industrial products.

    ]]>         Digital Fairness Act: EU cracks down on influencer ads and manipulative app design https://euobserver.com/248072/digital-fairness-act-eu-cracks-down-on-stealth-influencer-ads-and-manipulative-app-design/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 15:31:08 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248072 The Digital Fairness Act aims to impose stricter protections for people online. While the leaked draft proposes to ban overly-complicated choices to refuse data-sharing, it does not ban addictive design practises outright, warns rights watchdog EDRi. Meanwhile, online retailer Omio have complained that compliance will be costly to businesses.]]> The European Commission is set to unveil new rules on Wednesday (11 November) to prevent people from being manipulated by companies and influencers – but digital rights experts have said the legislation doesn’t go far enough.

    According to a leak of the draft legislation, seen by EUobserver, the Digital Fairness Act (DFA) imposes more controls on how social media influencers can market products, while combatting dark patterns designed to manipulate consumers online.

    In 2022, an EU Commission study found that 97 percent of the most popular websites and apps used by consumers employed dark patterns – intentional design choices to manipulate users towards choices that are more profitable for companies.

    The DFA proposal aims to require that social media influencers state sponsorship deals by prominently labelling advertisements using terms such as “advertisement” or “commercial collaboration”, where influencers cannot misrepresent such adverts as a personal endorsement.

    “People expect that influencers provide genuine advice or tips, not to be quietly sold the latest anti-wrinkle cream or fashionable outfit,” said Agustín Reyna, director general of consumer rights body BEUC. “If someone is promoting products on social media, it should be clearly stated.”

    The draft also proposes a complete ban on misrepresenting information about products, or sending fake message notifications suggesting someone has been in touch when really, nobody messaged.

    “Digital markets have for too long left consumers feeling disempowered and frustrated in a maze of complex cancellation processes for subscriptions they do not want, untransparent ticket pricing, or ‘low stock’ warnings that pressure them,” Reyna added.

    The draft legislation forbids misleading choices about data-sharing or cookies which present refusal as the wrong choice or use deliberately confusing phrases. And the wording of the leaked act also says that cancelling an online subscription should be easy.

    Opt-out for addictive features

    The DFA proposal would only ban personalised advertising and pricing if likely to cause harm and if the consumer is vulnerable.

    And it does not set out to ban addictive features like autoplay or infinite scrolling unless users actively switch off these features.

    “That leaves significant uncertainty and potentially lengthy case-by-case assessments,” said Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, senior policy advisor at rights watchdog EDRi. “Why recognise the problem of addictive design so explicitly without introducing stronger obligations to prevent it?”

    “Offering an opt-out should not automatically be considered sufficient,” she said. 

    Read more

    What is ‘coordinated inauthentic behaviour’ – and how is it distorting Europe’s online democracy?

    However, Domínguez de Olazábal called it a “significant step” that “the commission’s proposal creates binding rules against manipulative design, banning fake message notifications, repeated pressure to reverse choices and deliberately complicated refusal mechanisms.”

    • Since the start of the invasion of Ukraine, more Russian soldiers have been killed than in all other Soviet and Russian wars since the Second World War combined. This already exceeds the number of US soldiers killed in the Second World War.

    This follows from data on the number of Russian soldiers killed, published over the weekend by two hacking groups. The Belarusian pro-opposition group Cyber Partisans and Ukrainian hackers Silent Crow wrote that they had hacked Russia’s statistics agency, Rosstat, and obtained 23 terabytes of data.

    These included records of deaths in Russia in recent years. The data can be used to reconstruct the number of Russian soldiers killed since the beginning of the invasion.

    “In terms of Russian losses, this is the biggest information leak,” German economist Janis Kluge, who researches Russia’s wartime economy and military recruitment, told The Guardian newspaper.

    ]]>         EU Commission to host security talks after week of bomb hoaxes that hit 20 airports and dozens of European flights https://euobserver.com/248019/eu-commission-to-host-security-talks-after-week-of-bomb-hoaxes-that-hit-20-airports-and-dozens-of-european-flights/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:47:21 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248019 Experts from EU member states will meet on Wednesday to discuss last week’s bomb hoaxes affecting dozens of flights across Europe and causing millions in losses.]]> Experts from EU member states will meet on Wednesday (11 November) to discuss last week’s spate of bomb hoaxes which affected dozens of flights across Europe and causing millions in losses.

    The meeting, chaired by the European Commission and also including security experts from non-EU Norway, Switzerland, and Iceland, will serve to review the situation and discuss the need for extra measures.

    At least 35 planes between various airports across Europe faced bomb threats last week, according to Eurocontrol, an organisation for safe air navigation. A Finnair flight between Helsinki and Rome was escorted by Italian fighter jets while another plane, from Dublin to Rome, was diverted to a French air base.

    The scare affected a total of 20 airports in 16 countries, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Serbia, Spain, and the UK.

    The bomb hoaxes affected in total less than 0.5 percent of European flights on any of the three days when alarms were sent, Eurocontrol told EUobserver, and so they “have not had an impact on the delay in the air traffic network.”

    “We remain at full operational readiness,” said EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas last week. “Our priority is clear: the safety of passengers and the smooth functioning of European aviation”.

    Though none of the threats turned out to be real, each alarm consumed resources, time, energy, money, and personnel involved, costing €55,000 on average according to Eurocontrol data, but sometimes reaching even €220,000 per flight affected, according to aviation expert Philippe Baum of Coventry University. This means millions of euros lost across the continent.

    ]]>         The Kraków shooting: A Polish tragedy, a Russian opportunity https://euobserver.com/248113/the-krakow-shooting-a-polish-tragedy-a-russian-opportunity/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:41:57 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248113 As soon as a few images of the perpetrator and the contents of the boot of his car appeared in the media, the Russian propaganda machine was set to work.]]> This may be a hazard of the profession of analysing Russian information warfare, but it is sometimes dazzling to observe how Moscow’s propaganda campaigns are compelled to navigate resonant current affairs and to interpret them – whatever the actual facts – in a light favourable to the Kremlin’s foreign-policy interests.

    This obviously requires a high degree of creativity on the part of Russian propagandists, or suggests to us a boundless space of imagination in which they operate.

    The most tragic events in Poland, where 24-year-old Michał Oksiński killed both of his parents and his sister at home in the town of Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski and then drove to central Kraków and shot dead six people (four Polish nationals, a Briton, and an Austrian), wounding 16 more, offer a case in point.

    As soon as a few images of the perpetrator and the contents of the boot of his car appeared in the media, the Russian propaganda machine was set to work.

    One image showed the perpetrator’s bullet-resistant vest with a patch depicting a modern version of the flag of the early-18th-century pirate Edward Teach, known as “Blackbeard” – a morale patch widely used across the West today.

    Russian propagandists immediately – but wrongly – interpreted the patch as the symbol of the US military lifestyle brand “Forward Observations Group”, whose representatives travelled to Ukraine during the Russian-Ukrainian war.

    ]]>         [Interview] Italy’s Meloni is EU’s best hope of charming Putin at Ukraine peace talks, former Russian spy says https://euobserver.com/248018/interview-italys-meloni-is-eus-best-hope-of-charming-putin-in-ukraine-peace-talks-former-russian-spy-says/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:19:42 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248018 Any EU envoy for peace talks with Russia should meet four criteria, the Russian ex-spy said: no border with Russia, no conflicts of interest, no fear of Donald Trump, and willingness to "bloody" Vladimir Putin's nose. ]]> Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni is Europe’s best hope of charming Russian president Vladimir Putin into a viable peace deal, a former Russian spy believes, but there is no sign yet that Putin wants to stop the Ukraine war.

    “Meloni has charisma. She’s decisive and unpredictable,” said Sergei (full name withheld), who is a retired officer from Russia’s SVR foreign intelligence service.

    “She can be reckless and Putin can relate to that … Yes. Meloni definitely interests him,” he told EUobserver.

    The 27 EU leaders will discuss the creation of a high-level Russia envoy at a summit in Dublin on Friday (13 November), after Meloni complained to EU Council president António Costa that European diplomacy on Ukraine was a mess.

    For the time being, at least seven officials (from France, Germany, Italy, the UK, the European Commission, the EU Council, and Nato) are representing Europe at US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine, taking place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday (10-11 November).

    But the EU aims to anoint a more senior Russia negotiator or group of negotiators at its next formal summit on 17 December, amid US president Donald Trump’s new promise of an imminent peace deal.

      <title>Democrats’ US election sweep brings the price of their promised social contract into focus</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/11/democrats-election-medicaid-costs</link>
      <description><p>‘The post-election wish list is about to run into harsh fiscal reality: there is no money’</p><p>Is this an opportunity for a new America? As the Reagan revolution four decades ago launched US society down the path to low taxes and meager solidarity, perhaps the Republican bloodbath last week could turn US politics toward building a new social contract anchored on an aspiration to equitable prosperity.</p><p>One can sense the ambition of the bumper new crop of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/democrats">Democrats</a> ushered to power last week, calling for support for programs for children and their parents; emphatically endorsing the long-held dream of Medicare for All. The project includes rolling back <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, and restoring subsidies for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act that Republicans allowed to expire. And that’s just the start.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/11/democrats-election-medicaid-costs">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Federal judge allows Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against BBC to proceed</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/10/trump-10bn-defamation-lawsuit-bbc-allowed</link>
      <description><p>Trump-appointed judge Jeffrey T Kuntz partially denies British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss over edit</p><p>Federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz ruled on Tuesday that Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the BBC can proceed, denying in part the British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss the case. The president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit stems from the BBC’s splicing together of disparate comments he made before the 6 January US Capitol insurrection, as rendered in a Panorama documentary called Trump: A Second Chance.</p><p>“Accepting the allegations in the complaint as true, the Court finds Trump plausibly pled damages where Trump alleges a defamatory documentary released toward the election caused reputational harm,” the Trump-appointed Florida district court judge wrote. “It would be difficult for the Court to accept a different framing without completely negating the significance and fragility of political elections.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/10/trump-10bn-defamation-lawsuit-bbc-allowed">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>New data comes after Republicans’ midterms losses – which were largely seen as a rebuke of the party over high prices</p><p>US inflation rose 0.4% from September to October, slightly above expectations but still a cooldown in price increases as the cost of gas dipped during the month.</p><p>The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not release the usual year-over-year inflation figure as part of the consumer price index (CPI), which measures the price of a basket of goods and services, as data was not collected in October 2025 during the government shutdown.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/10/october-inflation-report">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Farewell to Elon Musk’s Cybertruck. Has any car ever been more repellent? | Arwa Mahdawi</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent</link>
      <description><p>Safety campaigners have condemned it and owners have complained about it. Goodbye to a steel monstrosity seemingly designed by a five-year-old</p><p>Elon Musk is having a rough go of it, isn’t he? The world’s richest man spent almost half a billion dollars on the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/04/elon-musk-midterm-spending-analysis">midterms</a> in a failed attempt to defend Republican control of government. Now the tech mogul, who moved from California to Texas to escape Democrats and regulations, finds himself in a newly blue state. He also finds himself the subject of an unflattering <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/08/musk-review-epic-study-worlds-richest-most-banal-man-elon-film">documentary</a> and, if the Democrats follow through on threats to investigate him, could potentially be in a spot of legal bother.</p><p>And to top it all off? Musk’s beloved Cybertruck, the steel monstrosity that looks as if it were designed by a five-year-old, is <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/06/tesla-to-wind-down-cybertruck-production-as-elon-musk-focuses-on-robotics-and-ai">winding down production</a>. According to Musk, this isn’t because it’s an abject failure, but because he is channelling his energy into other things. “This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media,” Musk <a href="https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2119691615774146614?a=pN3ISFVZZ-aU4_-TlJw&amp;s=20">tweeted</a> on Monday. “But rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.” (The Cybercab is a two-passenger robotaxi.)</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comThu, 12 Nov 2026 02:39:09 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[European shares hit record as AI optimism returns]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/11/european-shares-hit-record-as-ai-optimism-returns/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/11/european-shares-hit-record-as-ai-optimism-returns/Wed, 11 Nov 2026 19:49:30 +0000European stocks set a fresh record on Wednesday, buoyed by rebounding energy and tech shares.

The performance came following upbeat forecasts from Siemens Energy, while investor confidence in artificial intelligence showed signs of returning after positive results at US-based AI cloud computing firm CoreWeave.

The neocloud company saw its shares rally by more than 25 per cent in early trading, which left it on track for its best day of trading since June.

Dublin

The Iseq All-Share Index rose marginally by 0.6 per cent to close at 15,035.08 on Wednesday.

Kingspan, which forecast a spike in 2026 trading profit earlier this week, saw its share price rise to €99 on Tuesday before it fell back to a low of around €92 per share. On Wednesday, it was one of the biggest gainers of the day, as its stock rose to €98.70, up 1.44 per cent since open.

Greencoat Renewables, which last week reported a €11.9 million profit for the first half of the year, was the biggest riser of the day as it added 2.1 per cent to close at €0.82. Kerry Group also registered a gain of near 2 per cent, as its price rose to €99.25.

Iseq-heavyweight Ryanair traded down nearly 2.5 per cent to €26 per share. Last week, the firm reported higher revenues, but profits were lower during the first half of its financial year to the end of September.

Insurance company FBD Holdings fell 2 per cent, while home builder Cairn Homes’ share price was down 3 per cent since open to €2.75.

London

The London stock market closed higher, with the FTSE 100 Index up almost 0.8 per cent at 10,835. The performance on Wednesday means the index is rising towards its record high.

Computer services company Computacenter, up by close to 3.9 per cent, was one of the top risers of the day, followed by investment group Polar Capital, which gained 4.7 per cent.

Rising oil and metals prices also contributed to the gains of the day in London, with BP’s share price up 2.7 per cent, while Shell rose 1.3 per cent.

Mining firms were also among the strong performers, as Antofagasta and Glencore were each up by more than 2 per cent.

British media company ITV slipped 3.6 per cent after warning that fourth-quarter advertising revenue could decline by up to 10 per cent.

Government wants to use pay deal to drive digital transformation

Europe

The Stoxx Europe 600 Index rose 0.7 per cent to close at 663.05 on Wednesday, surpassing its previous record closing high set in August.

Siemens Energy AG rose as much as 10 per cent after the company said profit margins will swell to as much as 22 per cent by 2030. It said the rise would be driven by booming demand for gas turbines and power-grid equipment.

Shares of its peers Schneider Electric and Legrand gained 3 per cent and 2.2 per cent, respectively.

Elsewhere, Czech defence group CSG NV fell 21 per cent to an all-time low after the firm reported revenue that missed estimates and lowered its full-year profit margin outlook.

New York

In the past week, the tech-heavy Nasdaq was hit heavily as investors showed concern over what a Democratic sweep of Congress would mean for the AI sector.

On Wednesday, US stocks extended gains as the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100 briefly erased losses suffered in the aftermath of the US midterm elections.

In early afternoon trading in New York, the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.3 per cent, the S&P 500 was 1.5 per cent higher and the Nasdaq rose 2 per cent.

The gains on Wednesday have come following better-than-expected results from CoreWeave, excitement over Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) and a blockbuster quarter for OpenAI.

CoreWeave’s rise came after the cloud infrastructure firm announced better-than-anticipated revenue and a full-year outlook that came in stronger than Wall Street expected after the market closed on Tuesday.

Shares in Nvidia rose by almost 4 per cent after shedding about $430 billion (€387 billion) in the previous two sessions.

On Wednesday, the Financial Times reported the company’s board has hired former New York federal prosecutor Joon H Kim to conduct its internal probe into chief executive Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with a woman the US intelligence believe was working as a spy for China.

Oil rebounded following two consecutive days of losses, with Brent rising back above $93 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate trading near $88 a barrel.

A recent report by the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) noted that the public sector wage bill would account for €31.2 billion (or 27 per cent) of gross spending this year.

On the basis of a public sector pay deal similar to the last one, which was slightly less than the 10.5 per cent currently on the table, the PBO estimated the cost to the exchequer would be between €3.6 billion and €4.7 billion by 2029. This includes projected increases in the public sector headcount (adding new teachers, nurses and gardaí to the payroll).

How will it affect the Government’s fiscal position?

The rule of thumb is that each 1 per cent hike in the public sector pay and pensions bill costs the exchequer roughly €370 million.

On that basis, in 2027 the Government’s proposed deal would cost about €1.3 billion on a recurring basis but about €2 billion in cash terms. The €700 million gap reflects the back pay carried over from the previous deal.

So the Government’s fiscal position would be €800 million worse than forecast in 2027. The additional pay bumps for 2028 and 2029 are also not factored in. That additional money will have to come out of tax resources and will reduce the Government’s budget surpluses over the period.

On the other side of the ledger, the State’s financial position is expected to be boosted by corporate tax receipts, which are predicted to rise to €45 billion by 2030.

How does the Government offer compare with what private sector workers are getting?

The Government’s recent economic and fiscal outlook, published alongside last month’s budget, forecast that wages across the economy – which is mainly private sector – would rise by 4.1 per cent in 2027 and by 3.7 per cent in 2028 and 2029.

Private sector wages have outpaced those in the public sector since 2008. According to the official data, private sector wages are up by between 52-56 per cent over that period versus 25 per cent in the public sector.

Private sector wage growth data is skewed by multinationals that pay their workers significantly more than the average. That said, tech companies in Ireland have been pruning their wage bill.

What is the likelihood of unions accepting the deal?

Workers are in the midst of a nasty cost-of-living shock, compounded by an energy price surge. Meanwhile, the Government is attempting to rein in spending that has been something of a runaway train since the pandemic. Hence the fraught atmosphere around these negotiations.

Minister for Finance Simon Harris said the Coalition’s ability to offer income tax cuts in the recent budget and increases in public sector wages was in stark contrast to many other European governments, which were short on money and facing “extraordinarily difficult” economic decisions.

Trade unions insist, however, that the surge in inflation has severely degraded the purchasing power of their members, particularly those earning €50,000 or less, and must be addressed. They also insist there are acute labour shortages in education and healthcare and argue that a lacklustre deal will worsen the exodus of young nurses and teachers.

With more industrial action looming, a breakthrough needs to come quickly.
