Europeans are afraid – very afraid – of their dependence on foreign digital technology.

A recent poll by the Bertelsmann Foundation finds almost three-quarters of European Union (EU) citizens worry that critical digital services “could be remotely disabled by actors outside Europe”. The same overwhelming majority think it important Europe should have “control over key digital technologies”.

As in other cases (such as Europeans’ negative reactions to the EU trade “deal” with Donald Trump last year), the bloc’s citizens are clear about what they want – and it’s not what they are getting at the moment. So how are European governments, and the EU in particular, going about delivering the “control” that voters demand?

Europe depends on other economies for much of the digital technology “stack”: the US for software, Taiwan for microchips, China for swathes of hardware. A first question, then, is how much of the stack needs to be home-grown inside the EU.

When I ask this of Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission vice-president in charge of tech sovereignty, she lists AI (artificial intelligence) models, semiconductors, quantum technology, satellites and the cloud as areas where Europe needs its own productive capacity. She does not go as far as self-sufficiency; the objective is “that we shouldn’t have risky dependencies [or be] dependent on one company or one third country”.

That is an ambitious list of sectors nonetheless, given how far behind Europe is. It is certainly sufficiently demanding that we must ask whether pursuing it would come at the cost of falling further behind and of giving up foreign frontier technology for the sake of inferior home-made versions. What does Brussels think about that trade-off?

US voters have rejected data centres and AI. What happens now?

It may not be that dramatic, Virkkunen suggests. “Sometimes we know that some companies ... want to give the impression that they always have the best services and the competitors don’t ... and it’s not always true,” she tells me.

She argues that the home-grown alternatives are sometimes just smaller and lesser known, rather than uncompetitive on quality or price. But that means the public sector can catalyse domestic substitutes by playing its role as a customer right.

Is the European public sector doing that, though? Many smaller EU-based digital companies feel they have a good product but government customers prefer to stick with the big providers they are used to. The commissioner accepts there is a degree of inertia. There is also a need to be “creative”, she says, to facilitate smaller companies coming together in consortiums to provide the scale of supply needed.

The biggest challenge, though, is access to funding for EU tech companies – not because of a lack of savings but thanks to Europe’s failure to channel financing to risky ventures. EU institutions as well as member states are starting to remedy this: a new scale-up fund is now operational and Brussels aims for more public-sector strategic “anchor” equity to crowd in private investors.

But so far the amounts being mobilised seem far too small compared to the hundreds of billions put into US tech investments every year. And by all accounts, talks over the EU’s next multiyear budget are whittling down further the amounts Brussels had originally proposed for new priorities including digital industrial policy.

On legislative reforms, too, from “EU Inc” (a pan-EU corporate entity) to localisation rules for sensitive digital services, member states are delaying or watering down proposals where Brussels already seemed to have been cautious not to ask for too much.

Virkkunen naturally avoids criticising national capitals. But she agrees that in the budget talks, “it’s very important that the member states keep the ambition there” for funding new technologies and defence. And not just to build domestic capacity, but because “the idea is that they should be able to compete globally”.

Ultimately, Brussels, while ambitious, seems to be aiming somewhere in between how far voters want to go and how far national governments are ready to move.

That means there are political rewards to be had for leaders bold enough to go further and faster. In the Bertelsmann poll, less than half of those asked think foreign providers are successfully held to European rules and expectations. It’s now up to politicians to convince them otherwise. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

The average premium is up a whopping 18 per cent since 2022, according to Central Bank figures.

The average car insurance premium last year was €655, an increase of €144 in just three years. But you don’t have to accept another expensive renewal.

Actuaries know exactly what insurers look for when calculating a premium. Understanding their secrets could help you get a cheaper quote. Here are 10 tips to save on your next policy.

1. Check your mileage

Which drivers present the highest risk? Those who spend the most time on the road. One of the best predictors of a car crash is how much time you spend driving, says actuary Noel Garvey, who is chairman of the Society of Actuaries’ general insurance committee.

That’s why insurers ask your estimated annual mileage when quoting for your policy.

“The more you drive, the higher the chance of an accident,” says Garvey. More mileage means more risk, so insurers will charge you more.

Close to one million people reported working from home at least sometimes in the second quarter of 2026, according to Central Statistics Office (CSO) figures. If you are one of them, tell your insurer.

The average private car in Ireland covered 15,196km in 2023, according to the CSO. Many people drive less.

To check your mileage, divide the odometer reading by the car’s age in years, says Motorcheck.ie. Or check the readings between NCT certificates, work out the difference in mileage and compare it to the national average.

Overestimating your mileage when seeking a quote means paying more than you need to. But you need to play fair. Underestimating to save money could cause problems if you need to claim.

Why is motor insurance so expensive in Ireland?

2. Excess

You don’t have to be an actuary to get a better price on car insurance but it pays to know more about how your quote is designed, says Garvey.

Ask your insurer how the price changes if you increase the excess, he says. This is the amount you agree to pay towards a claim. It’s often set at a default of €250 to €300.

If there’s a crash and you submit a claim for €4,000 and your policy excess is €200, for example, you’ll pay the first €200 and the insurance company will pay €3,800.

Agreeing to a higher excess could mean a cheaper quote.

“If you back yourself to be more careful than most, it might be well worth taking on that risk,” says Garvey.

A telematics driving policy, also called “black box” insurance, can knock thousands off the insurance policy premium for first-time drivers or those new to Ireland.

What are telematics policies, and how can they knock thousands off motor insurance costs?

Price comparison website bonkers.ie sought quotes from a range of providers, including AIG, Aviva and Zurich, under a number of conditions and found that a 20-year-old driver with a full licence could get a quote of just €570 for fully comprehensive telematics cover.

When there was no telematics cover, the price of the standard policy jumped to almost €3,900.

If you have built up several years of no claims, paying extra for no-claims discount protection can be worth considering. A single claim without protection could reset your discount to zero, significantly increasing your premium at renewal.

How common are car fires?

6. Drop to one car

If your household has two cars and one spends most of its time sitting in the drive, dropping to one car will save you thousands.

Typically, in a two-car household both members have “main driver” status on their respective policies, with individual no-claims bonus records. You probably have “named driver” cover on each other’s policies too.

EV public charging costs now exceeding those for petrol and diesel

Polestar’s future-gazing new concept is far more rational than it appears

8. Pay annually

Paying for your car insurance in instalments can ease the blow to your monthly budget, but this can mean extra charges.

“The total paid over the year may be higher than the headline annual premium,” says Garvey. “Look at the overall cost, not just the monthly instalment when comparing quotes.”

Pay the yearly amount upfront if you can, even if that means dipping into your savings, or start to put a little bit of money away each month now so that you can pay in full next year, says Mabs.

9. Don’t modify

Thinking of buying a modified car or modifying your own? Engine modifications, changes to the wheels, suspension or bodywork can all drive up your quote.

“Modifications can affect an insurer’s assessment of the vehicle’s risk, value or likely repair cost, so you should disclose them and check the potential insurance impact before making changes,” says Garvey.

Boy racers take note.

10. Shop around

Automatically renew your policy with your existing insurer and you will pay more. Too many of us do this: maybe that’s why net profit among Irish motor insurers hit €89 million last year.

Put half an hour into shopping around and you could save around €100.

You’ll need details of any claims in the past five years too. You’ll find those in your current policy documents.

If you are shopping around by phone, ask if it’s cheaper for you to complete the transaction online. Many insurers provide an online discount.

And if there is more than one car in your household, ask your insurer for a multipolicy discount.

Yet just a fifth of those in firms that have never done so think the same.

It means that the maximum credit will increase from €600 for 2024 to €800 in 2025 – and €1,000 for 2026 and 2027.

“These figures compare price changes relative to income changes over time; as such, they do not rank countries by how expensive homes are in relation to income levels in absolute terms,” Eurostat said.

Public service pensions in general make provision for a 50 per cent survivor’s pension for a spouse if the retired public servant predeceases them. It is a valuable safety net for families .

But you appear to have lost out which I certainly agree sounds very unfair.

Following an enquiry from you, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage sent you what appear to be disembodied section from various bits of legislation that are as impenetrable as this stuff usually is.

The issue here is that there are two schemes - an original one that dates back to 1956 legislation and a more recent one operating under legislation passed in the 1980s. What rights you do and do not have depend on which one covers your husband’s employment.

I am indebted to Irish Congress of Trade Unions head of social policy and employment affairs, Laura Bambrick, and a number of her colleagues in Ictu’s public service unions for guiding me through the relevant detail.

Essentially, under the original 1956 Local Government (Superannuation) Act, there was no provision for a survivor’s pension under the widow’s and orphan pension scheme in a case like yours - where you got married after your husband had retired from his public sector role.

That scheme was specifically designed to cover family relationships established during pensionable employment. Once the person was no longer contributing to the scheme - as they would not in retirement - they were not covered for any marriage that took place during their working lives, nor any child born.

However, that changed in the 1980s.

People working in the Civil Service who were appointed after September 1st, 1984 became members of a revised spouses’ and children’s pension scheme. And this scheme made specific provision that even where a marriage took place after retirement, the spouse would be entitled to a survivors’ pension.

Those pension rights were extended to local authority staff under the Local Government Officers (Spouses and Children’s Contributory Pension) Scheme, 1986, with the rights backdated to September 1st, 1984.

This is interesting because it shows that as far back as 1984, there was an understanding that there was a reasonable case for extending pension protection to spouses who, simply by accident of timing, got married after a person’s retirement.

So, if your husband started working with the local authority any time after the end of August 1984, you are entitled to a pension on the back of his employment in the event of his death.

Even if he started working with them before that date, there was an option at that time for existing employees to transfer to the new scheme. He and you would certainly need to check through his records to see if he availed of that opportunity or chose to stay with the original scheme.

The response you have got from the department does not seem to clarify that one way or the other. And one of the trade union sources notes that Article 120 of the 1998 Local Government Superannuation (Consolidation) Scheme, which was quoted to you by the Department of Housing, relates to the older Widows’ and Orphans’ arrangements.

If he was covered under the newer arrangements, it would be irrelevant.

So, first up, track down the dates when your husband started work with the local authority and when he retired. If he was employed with them before 1984, you also need to check whether he opted in to the revised arrangements that came into force at that time, or not.

I am told that the pensions section in the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation may be able to help.

And what about the fairness issue? It does seem harsh that, having accepted the argument as far back as 1984 that marriages after retirement should be recognised, you could find yourself left with no survivor’s pension more than 40 years later.

That doesn’t necessarily mean that it breaches current legislation of equality but it does suggest that a rethink in Government might be timely. There cannot be that many people in your position so the financial impact on the exchequer is hardly an issue.

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3447947/">
   <title>Demokrat erobert Senatssitz in Mississippi</title>
   <description>Die republikanische US-Senatorin Cindy Hyde-Smith hat laut US-Medien das Senatsrennen im traditionell konservativen US-Bundesstaat Mississippi gegen den Demokraten Scott Colom verloren. Kurz nach dem Sender CNN erklärten am Mittwoch auch andere Medien – darunter der Sender NBC und die Nachrichtenagentur AP – Colom  zum Sieger. Er wird demnach der erste demokratische Senator in über 40 Jahren sowie der erste schwarze Senator in dem Südstaat seit den 1880er Jahren. Das Rennen war bis zuletzt extrem eng.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3447888/">
   <title>Generalstreik in Zeiten politischer Spannung</title>
   <description>In Spanien hat am Mittwoch ein Generalstreik gegen die Wohnungskrise das öffentliche Leben und die Wirtschaft zum Teil lahmgelegt. Es war der erste ganztägige Generalstreik im Land seit 14 Jahren. Die beiden großen Gewerkschaften sahen einen Erfolg, Arbeitgebervertreter übten Kritik. Der Streik fand in Zeiten politischer Spannungen statt, schließlich steht Spanien unmittelbar vor der heißen Phase des Wahlkampfs.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3447880/">
   <title>Schärfere EU-Regeln gegen Onlinetricks</title>
   <description>Die EU-Kommission will das Internet konsumentenfreundlicher machen. Manipulative, irreführende Werbung und intransparentes Influencermarketing sollen mit dem am Mittwoch präsentierten „Digital Fairness Act“ künftig nicht mehr erlaubt sein. Auch dynamischen Preismodellen bei Ticketverkäufen und der automatisierten Verlängerung von Probeabos ohne Hinweis soll ein Riegel vorgeschoben werden. Die Kommission will auch den Verkauf virtueller Währung in Videospielen einschränken.</description>

   <title>Fossilen-Lobby „tötet den Planeten“</title>
   <description>In seiner Rede zur Eröffnung des Gipfeltreffens der Staatschefs und Regierungsspitzen im Rahmen der 31. UNO-Weltklimakonferenz (COP31) in Antalya hat UNO-Generalsekretär Antonio Guterres am Mittwoch eindringlich zur Abkehr von fossilen Energieträgern aufgerufen. „Fossile Brennstoffe müssen den Weg der Dinosaurier gehen“, die vor Millionen Jahren ausstarben, sagte Guterres. Auch Österreichs Bundespräsident Alexander Van der Bellen sprach in seiner Rede die Zerstörung durch diese Energieträger an.</description>

    <item>

Notes From Poland https://notesfrompoland.com regular summaries of news from Poland Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:06:54 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9 https://notesfrompoland.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/cropped-2019-10-29_1838-32x32.png Notes From Poland https://notesfrompoland.com 32 32 Annual Polish Independence March passes through Warsaw https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/11/annual-polish-independence-march-passes-through-warsaw/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 15:34:34 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106667

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The annual march held in Warsaw to mark Poland’s Independence Day has passed through the city without major incident. This year’s event took place amid heightened security following the deadly terrorist attack in Kraków just four days earlier.

Hundreds of thousands of people, including President Karol Nawrocki, marched through the city amid a sea of white-and-red flags. The event, which is organised by nationalist groups, also acted as a display of unity among the right-wing and far-right opposition ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections.

Figures from the more liberal government, as always, avoided the march. Prime Minister Donald Tusk celebrated Independence Day hundreds of kilometres away in the city of Szczecin, where he issued an invitation to the opposition-aligned Nawrocki to visit his home for talks.

Zapełnia się rondo im. Romana Dmowskiego. Cała transmisja z #marszuniepodległości w @TV_Trwam pic.twitter.com/TvMHypx8gn

— Michał Rybka (@_MRybka) November 11, 2026

This year’s Independence March was held under the slogan “Polak w Polsce gospodarzem”, which translates roughly as “Poles are in charge in their own country”.

The slogan was chosen to “emphasise our opposition to foreign influences on Poland and underscore that Poland should be a nation-state without mass immigration”, said Rafał Buca, the march’s spokesman. “In Poland, Poles should rule – not some foreigners, not the European Union, not big corporations.”

On the morning of the march, the organisers shared an image showing Tusk as a puppet of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. “Time to cut the strings of foreign influence,” they declared.

Czas odciąć sznurki obcych wpływów i marionetkowych decyzji!

W naszym własnym kraju to my – polscy obywatele – jesteśmy jedynym suwerenem i to my ustalamy reguły!

🇵🇱 POLAK W POLSCE GOSPODARZEM! pic.twitter.com/8Htr8s0klx

— Marsz Niepodległości (@StowMarszN) November 11, 2026

The main organisers of the march are associated with Confederation (Konfederacja), a far-right group that sits among the opposition in parliament. But it is attended by a wide range of people, from the mainstream right through to the radical right.

Leading figures from other opposition parties, including the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), centre-right Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) and radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), were present, as well as Nawrocki, who last year became the first Polish president to attend the march.

A member of the march’s organising committee, Marcin Osowski, told broadcaster WNET that around half a million people were at today’s event. The municipal authorities, which are under the control of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, later put the figure at around 250,000.

That would make today’s Independence March the largest ever other than the one in 2018, when a broader event was organised to mark the centenary of Poland regaining its independence after World War One.

 

The opposition was aiming to show a united front amid their ongoing protests against the recent takeover of the constitutional court by a group of government-backed judges and ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections, at which they hope to unseat Tusk’s government.

“It’s about showing our strength and, at the same time, for this march to be a springboard for the election campaign,” said Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of PIS, during the march, quoted by the Niezależna news website. “Unity is important.”

Meanwhile, one of the leaders of Confederation, Krzysztof Bosak, told the crowd in a speech that, “while we have different experiences and views, under the white-and-red flag we form one community”.

“Next year, we must turn this community into an election victory…We must remove the current clique from power and form a pro-Polish government,” he declared. “We do not accept the violent takeover of state institutions. We demand respect for the law.”

Na Marszu Niepodległości jesteśmy u siebie! Przyjeżdżamy z różnych stron, mamy różne doświadczenia i poglądy, ale pod biało-czerwoną flagą tworzymy jedną wspólnotę. Każdy jest w niej potrzebny. Także ten, kto dziś czuje się samotny, odrzucony i traci poczucie sensu.

Ta wspólnota… pic.twitter.com/L5pYU1RVv0

— Krzysztof Bosak 🇵🇱 (@krzysztofbosak) November 11, 2026

However, Confederation’s other main leader, Sławomir Mentzen, shared a picture of himself at the march in front of a banner showing images of both Tusk and Kaczyński crossed out, alongside the word “Reset”.

While Bosak’s nationalist faction of Confederation is seen as more amenable to the idea of working with PiS to form a potential future coalition government, Mentzen’s libertarian faction is less enthusiastic about the idea.

Nadchodzi, nadchodzi Marsz Niepodległości! 🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/o8Tkf8673G

— Sławomir Mentzen (@SlawomirMentzen) November 11, 2026

In the past, the march has sometimes seen violence, with participants clashing with police. However, in recent years it has generally passed peacefully, and that was again the case today.

The city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaszkowski, who is a deputy leader of KO, said on Wednesday afternoon that, other than the illegal use of pyrotechnics (such as a flare held up by Mentzen), the march was proceeding without incident.

Local authorities in Warsaw had put in place additional security measures following Saturday’s terrorist attack in Kraków, in which a 24-year-old Polish man, Michał Oksiński, killed six people and injured over a dozen more by shooting an AR-15 rifle from his car.

Oksiński’s rampage was quickly brought to a halt in a shootout with armed police, and he died from his injuries on Monday. On Tuesday, the justice minister revealed that evidence uncovered so far shows “strong traces of right-wing extremism” in Oksiński’s activity.

There are "strong traces of right-wing extremism" in the activity of the man who carried out the mass shooting in Kraków, says Poland's justice minister.

His search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist https://t.co/UhVbkWSaCq

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026

Tusk, meanwhile, celebrated Independence Day in the city of Szczecin in northwest Poland.

“All of us, without exception, are responsible for ensuring that Poland remains strong, secure, free and independent forever,” said the prime minister. “Everyone who holds Poland in their hearts must understand that independence, freedom and a secure republic are a common good.”

Tusk noted that, since the recent crisis around the constitutional court broke out, Nawrocki has refused his offer to meet and discuss how to find a solution to a crisis that has pitted judges appointed under the former PiS government against those chosen by the current ruling coalition.

The prime minister today renewed that offer, inviting Nawrocki and his family to visit Tusk’s home in the build-up to Christmas. “We must be able to discuss things together, without bitterness, without hatred,” said the prime minister.

Note: This article has been updated to include the official estimate of attendance at the march.

]]> Poland and US sign statement of intent on strengthening defence industry cooperation https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/11/poland-and-us-sign-statement-of-intent-on-strengthening-defence-industry-cooperation/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 11:20:52 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106650

Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, have signed a statement of intent on strengthening cooperation between their defence industries.

“Today, we are taking the next steps in our alliance,” declared Hegseth, while Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the move signalled that Poland is now “not only a model ally…but has become a strategic partner of the United States”.

The Polish defence minister added that he would also push for equipment jointly manufactured by Poland and the US to be eligible for EU defence funding. “Poland is the US ambassador in the EU,” he declared.

Wicepremier W. @KosiniakKamysz z #Waszyngton: to chyba moja najważniejsza i przełomowa wizyta w USA. To moment, w którym mogę powiedzieć, że Polska jest nie tylko modelowym sojusznikiem, ale stała się strategicznym partnerem USA. pic.twitter.com/75xdgzIaG0

— Ministerstwo Obrony Narodowej 🇵🇱 (@MON_GOV_PL) November 10, 2026

Kosiniak-Kamysz was welcomed by Hegseth in Washington to discuss a range of issues relating to security cooperation. A major item on the agenda was Poland’s desire for a new permanent US military base on its territory.

After the meeting, Kosiniak-Kamysz told reporters that there was a “green light from the Pentagon” for the base, with the final decision now resting with the White House. He said that was expected to be made in early December.

Hegseth, meanwhile, praised Poland for embracing the “NATO 3.0” concept, under which the US wants Europe to take on more responsibility for its own defence.

“Poland is building one of the most formidable armies in Europe, ready to secure and defend its territory,” said the Secretary of War, who noted that Warsaw is “leading by example” with its high levels of defence spending.

 

Hegseth also welcomed the fact that Poland is investing significantly in US equipment, including Abrams tanks, F-35 fighter jets, Apache helicopters and Patriot air-defence systems.

“You are building a fully modernised, interoperable force, and our two nations are…giving military cooperation industrial depth as well,” said the secretary of war.

Hegseth also reaffirmed Washington’s desire for a peace deal in Ukraine and “encouraged Kosiniak-Kamysz to continue Poland’s steadfast support of Ukraine”, said Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell.

American defense technology is driving innovation and creating new opportunities for transatlantic industrial cooperation.@USAmbNATO Matthew Whitaker, Assistant Secretary of Commerce David Fogel @CommerceGov and @USAmbPoland Tom Rose met with Deputy Minister of Defence… pic.twitter.com/5etw1L3X5A

— US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) November 10, 2026

Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the statement of intent he had signed with Hegseth was aimed at ensuring more US equipment was manufactured and maintained in Poland itself, including technology transfers.

He also said that he wants to secure European funds for jointly produced US equipment. The EU’s SAFE programme of defence loans, for example, largely excludes US manufacturers.

“We want American equipment manufactured by Polish-American companies to benefit from European funding. I will present such a position next Tuesday at the meeting of EU defence ministers,” said Kosiniak-Kamysz. “Poland is the US ambassador to the EU.”

The meeting between the two defence secretaries also coincided with the Transatlantic Defence Industry Access Forum, which brought together 70 Polish and 80 American firms, with the aim of strengthening ties between the two countries’ defence industries.

W ostatnich dniach dobra decyzja o utworzeniu w Polsce centrum serwisowego rakiet Patriot, a dziś podpisaliśmy kolejne porozumienie z USA, które przyspieszy współpracę naszych przemysłów zbrojeniowych.

Chcemy, by więcej uzbrojenia powstawało i było naprawiane w Polsce. To nowe… pic.twitter.com/j24E2xON66

— Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 10, 2026

Last month, the United States chose Poland as the location for a planned facility for servicing and maintaining Patriot missiles – the first to be located outside the US itself.

In July, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles. In May, an agreement was signed to establish a centre in Poland for servicing the engines of Abrams tanks.

That same month, President Donald Trump announced that his country would station an additional 5,000 troops in Poland, prompting Warsaw to formally request the establishment of a new US military base, which President Karol Nawrocki has suggested should be called “Fort Trump”.

]]> Two Ukrainians charged with spying and sabotage for Russia in Poland https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/10/two-ukrainians-charged-with-spying-and-sabotage-for-russia-in-poland/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 12:56:58 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106617

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Poland has detained and charged two Ukrainian citizens accused of carrying out espionage and acts of sabotage on behalf of Russia.

The men, aged 24 and 25, were allegedly paid to conduct reconnaissance of critical infrastructure and military facilities across Poland. They are also accused of setting fire to several vehicles with the aim of stoking anti-Ukrainian sentiment.

Funkcjonariusze Agencji Bezpieczeństwa Wewnętrznego zatrzymali w Mińsku Mazowieckim dwóch obywateli Ukrainy w wieku 24 i 25 lat podejrzanych o szpiegostwo i prowadzenie działań dywersyjnych na zlecenie rosyjskich służb specjalnych.
▶️ Mężczyźni rozpoznawali i robili zdjęcia… pic.twitter.com/G3i8hEsBHT

— Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 10, 2026

The suspects were detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) on 3 November in Mińsk Mazowiecki, a town just outside Warsaw, the capital. ABW officers also searched their residences and other locations connected to the investigation, seizing data storage devices and narcotics.

According to investigators, the suspects were tasked with setting vehicles on fire after changing their licence plates to ones used by Ukrainian military vehicles. This was “aimed at fueling anti-Ukrainian sentiment”, says the National Prosecutor’s Office.

Prosecutors have charged the men under Poland’s espionage law with working against Poland on behalf of a foreign intelligence service – a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of five years – and sabotage on behalf of foreign intelligence, which is punishable by 10 years to life.

At the prosecutor’s request, a court ordered both suspects to be placed in pretrial detention for three months.

 

In recent years, Poland has seen a huge rise in cases of espionage and sabotage carried out on behalf of Russia.

The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined.

Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe.

Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026

Last month, a Polish man was jailed for five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of an airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland.

Shortly afterwards, the trial began of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders.

In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage.

]]> “Strong traces of right-wing extremism” in activity of Kraków terrorist, says justice minister https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/10/strong-traces-of-right-wing-extremism-in-activity-of-krakow-terrorist-says-justice-minister/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 11:17:52 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106614

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

Poland’s justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, says that investigators have so far found “very strong traces of right-wing extremism” in the activity of Michał Oksiński, the man who carried out Saturday’s mass terrorist shooting in Kraków that left six people dead.

The perpetrator’s search history included websites relating to Anders Breivik, the Norwegian far-right terrorist who killed 77 people during two attacks in 2011.

Żurek’s comments come amid intense debate and dispute in Poland over the beliefs and motives of Oksiński, who on Monday died from the injuries he sustained during a shootout with police that brought his rampage to an end.

W. Żurek ujawnia nowe ustalenia po zamachu w Krakowie. Tłumik w samochodzie sprawcy i ślady zainteresowania Breivikiemhttps://t.co/nd1XPBlmrI

— Radio Kraków (@RadioKrakow) November 10, 2026

On Tuesday, Żurek, who also serves as prosecutor general, spoke to local broadcaster Radio Kraków about the progress of the investigation into Oksiński. He confirmed that the perpetrator had not left behind any letter or other kind of message revealing his motives.

“Those motives are being investigated,” said the minister. “There are very strong traces of right-wing extremism. I can already confirm some information because the services have access to the perpetrator’s computer. Indeed, visits to websites related to Anders Breivik are visible.”

Żurek also pointed to the fact that, as prosecutors announced on Sunday, a so-called Gadsden flag (showing a snake above the words “Don’t tread on me”) had been found in Oksiński’s home.

Prosecutors say a "Don't Tread on Me" flag was found hanging at the home of the perpetrator of the attack in Kraków

They emphasise that the flag is not associated with any one ideology or organisation and that they are still trying to determine the shooter's motives and beliefs pic.twitter.com/yoNfh7cHwU

— Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) November 9, 2026

Although the National Prosecutor’s Office emphasised that the flag is not associated with any one ideology or organisation, Żurek noted that it was displayed during the attack on the United States Capitol by supporters of Donald Trump in 2021.

“We know well that during the attack on the Capitol, there were quite a few of these flags among far-right groups in the United States,” said the minister. “This flag [in Oksiński’s home] also sends a signal to the security services and the prosecutor’s office.”

Żurek added that a search of the perpetrator’s workplace had also identified “symbolism there that could point to this thread [of right-wing extremism]”, but provided no further details.

The minister noted, however, that investigators are also taking into account the potential for “mental disorders” playing a role in the actions of Oksiński, whose parents and sister were found shot dead in his home.

 

Żurek’s remarks come following controversy in Poland over a statement by interior minister Marcin Kierwiński on Saturday, in the immediate aftermath of the attack, when he said that early indications suggest that Oksiński had held “very radical views”, including a “fascination with far-right ideologies”.

Over the following two days, Kierwiński refused to provide evidence supporting those claims, and in a TV interview on Sunday evening said that he had simply been sharing “first hypotheses”.

That led some right-wing opposition politicians and commentators to accuse Kierwiński of spreading false claims, either through incompetence or as a deliberate attempt to associate the attack with the right.

However, speaking to Radio Kraków on Tuesday, Żurek said that “it seems that what Minister Kierwiński communicated in those first hours is confirmed by the evidence”.

Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, is facing growing pressure to present evidence to back his claim that the Kraków shooter was driven by far-right ideologies, amid criticism from opposition parties that he is seeking to exploit the tragedy for political reasons.

— Jakub Krupa (@JakubKrupa) November 9, 2026

On social media, many people have also been sharing alleged images of Oksiński’s past activities, both online and in real life, claiming that they show he held left-wing views.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Poland’s escalating Constitutional Tribunal (TK) dispute is no longer simply a legal argument about contested appointments but a struggle over who defines constitutional legitimacy.

As the liberal-centrist government and right-wing opposition and president advance rival rule-of-law claims, the conflict risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent.

The roots of the crisis

Poland’s 15-member TK is a powerful body that rules on the constitutionality of the country’s laws. The roots of the current dispute trace back to late 2015 and began immediately prior to the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party taking office following its October parliamentary election victory.

In its final weeks in power, the outgoing government, led by the liberal-centrist Civic Platform (PO, now Civic Coalition: KO), fast-tracked the appointment of five tribunal members who were replacing those whose terms were set to expire in November and December.

Upon winning an outright parliamentary majority, the incoming PiS-led government refused to recognise these appointments, elected a slate of five new tribunal members, and party-backed President Andrzej Duda swore them in.

Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025

The tribunal (still largely composed of pre-2015 judges) ruled that three of the outgoing parliament’s appointments were lawful, so only two of the new ones could stand. PiS refused to accept this, creating the so-called “understudy” judges (dublerzy) controversy.

As further vacancies arose, the new parliament gradually installed its nominees, culminating in the appointment at the end of 2016 of one of them, Julia Przyłębska, as tribunal president. Przyłębska’s leadership was contested on procedural grounds, as was that of her 2024 successor Bogdan Święczkowski, a former senior prosecutor closely aligned with the 2015-23 PiS administration.

All of this led to the then-opposition parties and much of the Polish legal and the EU political establishments denouncing the tribunal as legally compromised and politically captured.

Total non-cooperation

Following the autumn 2023 parliamentary election, a new coalition government headed up by KO leader Donald Tusk embraced a policy of total non-cooperation with the tribunal, refusing to publish its rulings.

The battle for control took a new turn when, after initially not filling any tribunal vacancies, from March 2026 onwards the new parliament elected successive waves of new members, reaching eight by September.

However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki (who succeeded Duda in August 2025) refused to swear in five of these nominees, including former minister and close Tusk ally Maciej Berek. In response, the government took the unprecedented step of swearing in the contested nominees directly in parliament, a move that both Nawrocki and Święczkowski rejected as illegal.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

The conflict escalated sharply at the end of last month, when, backed by the government and tribunal members elected by the current parliamentary majority, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the five contested nominees but having the longest judicial tenure, asserted her seniority to order a one-month suspension of Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański in their official duties and assumed temporary control.

Justice minister Waldemar Żurek submitted requests to lift Święczkowski and Sochański’s immunity as the newly appointed members, and the new nominees entered the tribunal building under State Protection Service (UOP) escort.

This triggered protests by right-wing opposition supporters at the building’s gates, prompting a heavy police presence and tense stand-off. The severity of this was underscored when Nawrocki cut short an official visit to Senegal mid-flight, returned to Warsaw and entered the tribunal building in the early hours, condemning what he described as a violation of the constitutional order.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court.

The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

Korwin-Piotrowska then convened a tribunal general assembly which critics argued lacked the legally required two-thirds quorum because only eight of its 15 nominal members (the newly elected ones, including the five who had not taken the presidential oath) attended.

Her supporters maintained that the quorum was met because the suspension of Święczkowski and Sochański, and exclusion of the last remaining “understudy” judge, reduced the pool of eligible members to 12.

The government’s “transitional justice” logic

For the Tusk government and its legal defenders, these exceptional executive and parliamentary countermeasures were framed through the logic of “transitional justice”: as painful and extraordinary but necessary to restore the rule of law after PiS had violated the constitution and European standards, systematically packing the tribunal with political loyalists.

Justifying its non-recognition of tribunal rulings, the government argued that the presence of three defectively elected “understudy” members and their successors, together with Przyłębska’s and Święczkowski’s procedurally flawed presidential appointments, fundamentally “contaminated” the entire body, thereby invalidating its rulings.

In its efforts to restore democracy, the government may sometimes take actions that are “not fully compliant with the law”, admits @donaldtusk.

But he says this is because of the legal chaos deliberately created by the former PiS government https://t.co/AWlM6hRLie

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 11, 2024

To provide what it argued was authoritative external confirmation of this defect, the government relied heavily on landmark European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) and EU Court of Justice (CJEU) rulings which determined that, thus constituted, the tribunal could no longer be considered a legitimate body established by legal standards.

From this perspective, refusing to recognise the tribunal’s allegedly unlawful rulings was framed as the only available mechanism to neutralise a partisan weapon that PiS had left behind to block the government’s legislative agenda.

Alternative parliamentary swearing-in procedures were justified on the grounds that the president’s role in receiving oaths was purely ceremonial, not a constitutionally mandated requirement.

 

Despite his recent political role, Berek’s appointment was defended on the basis that he played more of a technocratic-expert role within the government, and was highly qualified to undertake the extraordinary transitional measures required to repair a damaged institution.

Defenders of the tribunal leadership’s suspension and occupation of its headquarters argued that by blocking the new nominees from taking up their roles, Święczkowski had paralysed the institution and decisive measures were necessary to restore its proper functioning.

A “coup d’état”?

PiS and Nawrocki, on the other hand, maintained that the Tusk government’s actions amounted to an authoritarian attempt to operate completely outside of constitutional powers, treating legality as an option when it conflicted with its political agenda.

They insisted that all of its 2015 appointments were in full accordance with the law, correcting an improper attempt by the outgoing PO-dominated parliament to entrench its influence after electoral defeat, and that the tribunal’s ruling on the legality of these three “understudy” judges went beyond its jurisdiction.

Successive tribunal general assemblies, they argued, validly and legally selected Przyłębska and then Święczkowski as presidents, and the Tusk government had no constitutional right to pick and choose which tribunal rulings it would recognise. They said that, by delaying the election of some new members when vacancies arose, the government violated existing procedures.

The constitution, they said, explicitly required these new nominees to take their oaths directly “before the president” and that by conducting improper parliamentary swearing-in ceremonies they had effectively renounced their offices.

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”

But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026

The candidacy of Berek, a recently active politician with doubtful professional qualifications, they said represented its own form of institutional capture and selective legality.

The suspension of the tribunal leadership and occupation of its headquarters amounted to an unlawful power grab or “coup d’état” that completely disregarded established constitutional procedures.

PiS rejected the “contamination” thesis and argued vigorously that Poland had never transferred jurisdiction over the organisation of the national judiciary to EU institutions and European courts, who had no authority to evaluate the legality of tribunal appointments.

They accused the EU political establishment of double standards, weaponising “rule-of-law” arguments to help a politically aligned government while ignoring the Tusk administration’s own executive overreach.

PiS also argued that by delegitimising a tribunal which had in the past ruled that the Polish Constitution superseded EU law, the Tusk government was paving the way for controversial social and economic policies to be pushed through without any domestic judicial oversight.

Tusk’s liberal critics

On the other hand, more ideologically supportive liberal critics of the Tusk government’s approach acknowledged the original 2015 irregularities but warned that selective non-recognition of an entire institution, combined with attempts to install a new tribunal without presidential participation, risked creating the same dual legitimacy problem that they accused PiS of having started.

They stressed that lasting repair required broad political consensus and careful adherence to formal procedures so that future majorities did not simply invert the non-recognition tactic. They noted the tension with earlier condemnations of PiS for elevating politically aligned figures or recently active politicians.

While sympathetic to the goal of reforming what they believed was a deeply compromised tribunal, these critics argued that, by employing legally questionable shortcuts and executive force, the Tusk government risked setting dangerous precedents and deepening the very disorder that it was claiming to correct.

Interestingly, the government’s broader “transitional justice” justificatory logic – that ordinary procedures would not adequately address a systemic capture and the priority had to be functional restoration rather than abstract purity – mirrored the arguments PiS itself advanced for its own judicial reforms after 2015.

The right-wing party argued that the post-1989 judiciary remained dominated by a post-communist elite that required deep structural overhaul rather than incremental change.

A high-risk escalation

The latest escalation is likely to entrench and intensify the profound systemic polarisation that characterises the Polish political scene, for a long-time embodied in the KO-PiS duopoly, with the conflict framed in existential terms of either “restoring the rule of law” or “defending the constitutional order”.

This fierce dispute lies at the heart of the Tusk government’s broader political “reckoning” (rozliczenie) agenda involving visibly removing PiS’s influence from key institutions.

For the ruling coalition, this was a central 2023 election campaign message, and being seen to deliver on it is an absolute political necessity to satisfy and mobilise its electoral base. A confrontational approach thus serves to consolidate the government’s support among these core voters, who have grown increasingly impatient and want to see decisive action.

However, the government’s strategy is fraught with political risk. High-stakes tactics risk uniting its right-wing opponents and alienating moderate voters increasingly exhausted by endless, hyper-partisan institutional confrontation, legal brinkmanship and the optics of police deployments around a key state body.

They provide the president and right-wing opposition with a powerful counternarrative of constitutional vandalism ahead of the next parliamentary election.

Escalation is also straining relations within the ruling coalition, especially among more conservative or legalistic coalition partners who believe that a more fundamental constitutional “reset” based on a cross-party settlement is required to break the impasse in the longer term.

The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has proposed a “constitutional reset” to resolve the crisis around the country’s top court.

It would involve removing all current judges and choosing new ones in a more consensual process https://t.co/xDwpRUVHxG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 6, 2026

Internationally, although the EU political establishment remains supportive of the Tusk government’s actions, they invite uneasy scrutiny of the stability of Poland’s legal system and have drawn explicit criticism from the US embassy.

The reliance on a “transitional justice” framing that echoes PiS’s earlier justifications for systemic change, combined with the appointment to the tribunal of a recent minister despite prior criticisms of politicised nominations, also undercuts government claims of consistent principle and provides the right with a powerful narrative of hypocrisy.

Legal dualism

Ultimately, this bitter dispute has paved the way for a protracted and deeply destabilising “legal dualism” that could plague the Polish state for years to come, with a tribunal simultaneously legitimate and illegitimate depending on who holds power.

By treating the tribunal as an illegitimate entity when its nominees did not control it, the current government has established a precedent.

Even if it now appears to have secured a clear majority for its own nominees, a future right-wing government and sympathetic president will have every incentive to use the exact same playbook: treating the reconstituted tribunal as a captured instrument of the liberal establishment, and regarding it as no more legitimate than the Tusk government did the PiS-era one.

Consequently, the tribunal’s authority, and legal certainty in Poland more generally, have been further eroded, leaving the country without a widely accepted arbiter to resolve constitutional disputes. There are no immediate prospects for a durable resolution of this conflict.

Thousands of soldiers from 11 countries began military exercises in Poland today. They are the first organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing, with the aim of preparing for a role in supporting Ukraine following a potential future peace deal with Russia.

The manoeuvres, which are being jointly led by France and the UK, are taking place in Nowa Dęba, around 100 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, and will last until 22 November.

The development has been condemned by Russia, which says it shows that Western countries are ignoring Moscow’s “legitimate security concerns” and “fueling the spiral of escalation”.​

The exercises, taking place on land, in the air, and at sea, are being conducted by the Multinational Force Ukraine (MNF-U), which serves as the military component of the coalition.

“This exercise will show that the Multinational Force-Ukraine is a real, capable, readily deployable force that represents a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine’s long-term stability and security,” said Tom Bateman, the British lieutenant-general commanding MNF-U.

The British Ministry of Defence says that the exercise, which has been named “Koalicja” (meaning “Coalition” in Polish), “will test Allies’ readiness to support Ukraine and rebuild their Armed Forces once the conflict ends”.

France’s armed forces ministry, meanwhile, says that the aim is to ensure that MNF-U is “ready to deploy at the request of the Ukrainian government” in order to help “guarantee a robust and lasting peace in Ukraine”.

In addition, just under 2,000 Polish troops will take part, bringing the total to almost 5,000 personnel, reports Polska Zbrojna, a publication linked to the Polish defence ministry. Other countries taking part are Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Turkey.

Poland’s defence ministry says the exercises will “demonstrate how quickly participating nations can mobilise and establish forces capable of supporting Ukraine after the end of the war”.

However, although Poland is hosting the manoeuvres, the defence ministry reiterated the country’s position that “it would not send its own soldiers to Ukrainian territory” as part of any postwar settlement. Poland has made clear it intends instead to help provide logistical support.

In the wake of Saturday’s deadly terrorist shooting in Kraków, a deputy defence minister has called for debate on limiting the number and types of weapons people can own. Meanwhile, a deputy interior minister says the tragedy provides an “incentive” to revisit proposals to better register certain guns.

Poland has among the lowest levels of gun ownership in Europe, though the number of firearms licences being issued has risen in recent years and some politicians have called for expanded access to guns. Saturday’s attack was carried out by a man who legally owned firearms.

On Saturday, 24-year-old Michał Oksiński drove through the historic city centre of Kraków, which was packed with tourists and locals, firing at random from his car.

He killed six people and injured over a dozen more. Later in the day, the bodies of the perpetrator’s parents and sister were found in his home, where they had been shot dead.

Oksiński’s rampage was brought to an end in a shootout with two police officers, which left all three with serious injuries. On Monday morning, the police announced that Oksiński had died in hospital. One of the police officers remains in what is described as “serious but stable” condition.

From 2015 to 2023, Ziobro served as justice minister in a PiS-led government, overseeing judicial reforms that are widely seen as having undermined the rule of law.

After a new, more liberal ruling coalition led by the current prime minister, Donald Tusk, took power in December 2023, it launched a number of investigations into the actions of senior PiS officials.

That led, last year, to prosecutors announcing that they want to charge Ziobro with 26 crimes, including leading a criminal group and approving the unlawful purchase of Pegasus spyware, which was used to surveil some of PiS’s political opponents.

 

However, although parliament approved the lifting of Ziobro’s immunity from prosecution, he had by then already travelled to Hungary, which was at the time ruled by conservative PiS ally Viktor Orbán. In December 2025, the Hungarian government granted Ziobro political asylum.

At this year’s Hungarian parliamentary elections in April, Orbán’s Fidesz party was removed from power and his successor, Péter Magyar, pledged to extradite Ziobro to Poland.

But, just as Magyar was being sworn in in May, Ziobro left Hungary and flew to the United States, reportedly with the help of a senior US State Department official.

In July, Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office announced that it was sending a request to the US authorities to detain and extradite Ziobro. In late October, the National Prosecutor’s Office told newspaper Fakt that “we have so far not received any response from the US”.

Credit rating agency S&P has revised Poland’s outlook to negative, saying that the country has seen “one of the most significant fiscal deteriorations globally” and that “political polarisation hinders fiscal consolidation”. It also lowered the country’s long- and short-term local currency ratings.

S&P’s decision follows similar ones by the other members of the big three rating agencies. Fitch has had Poland on negative outlook since last year, while Moody’s cut the country’s credit rating in September this year to its lowest level since 2002.

In a statement issued on Friday evening, S&P said that its “negative outlook reflects the risk that elevated budgetary deficits and rising government debt could constrain policy flexibility in the face of future shocks”.

“This could expose Poland to shifts in investor sentiment or necessitate a sharp fiscal adjustment that would weigh on economic growth,” they added.

Last year’s deficit, at 7.3% of GDP, was the second-highest in the European Union. This year it is forecast to drop slightly, to 6.7%, according to recent finance ministry projections. But next year’s budget foresees a deficit of 7.1%.

Those figures are much higher than those the government pledged to reach when, in 2024, Poland was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. For example, the deficit was supposed to fall to 3.7% of GDP in 2027.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Wed, 11 Nov 2026 21:36:27 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Poundland set for crunch decision on survival after owner grilled by MPs https://www.cityam.com/poundland-set-for-crunch-decision-on-survival-after-owner-grilled-by-mps/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:30:37 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2476673

Poundland is approaching a crunch decision to stave off its collapse after its owner was accused by MPs of jeopardising “thousands of jobs on Britain’s high streets”. The retailer’s directors, Barry Williams and Shaun Wills, are set to hold an emergency board meeting on Wednesday night over whether to trigger an extension to a moratorium [...]]]>

Poundland is approaching a crunch decision to stave off its collapse after its owner was accused by MPs of jeopardising “thousands of jobs on Britain’s high streets”.

The retailer’s directors, Barry Williams and Shaun Wills, are set to hold an emergency board meeting on Wednesday night over whether to trigger an extension to a moratorium which is holding off its creditors from calling in their debts, sources told City AM. 

Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators last month, but the 10-day freeze on creditors expires in a matter of hours. 

The crucial decision comes after Gordon Brothers, the Boston-based investment firm which owns Poundland, was grilled by MPs at a closed-doors hearing of Parliament’s business select committee on Wednesday afternoon.

Liam Byrne MP, chair of the committee, said on Wednesday night: “After extensive cross examination this afternoon, I’m deeply concerned that Gordon Brothers behaviour may have jeopardised  thousands of jobs on Britain’s high streets. 

“Gordon Brothers refused to say it will prioritise saving jobs over and above its own financial returns.”

The investment firm has faced political backlash in recent weeks after refusing a number of solvent offers to buy Poundland, insisting it is repaid for a £22.5m loan it inherited when it bought the retailer for just £1 last year.

‘Strangled of access to its own funds’

During the two-hour grilling, Newton-Jones told MPs he would support a move to hold off administrators, though this decision rests with Williams and Wills. Sources said the retailer’s directors were likely to agree to an extension.

Newton-Jones denied that Gordon Brothers had restricted Poundland’s access to funding during the sale process, a claim made by Steve Smith, the retailer’s founder. 

The Gordon Brothers executive also defended its commitment to protecting the retailer’s 12,000 jobs, though one MP questioned why he had not mentioned the company’s staff until late in the session.

Poundland managing director Barry Williams and finance chief Shaun Wills also appeared in front of the committee on Wednesday, telling MPs that the investment firm had made it harder for the retailer to access funds with which they could pay suppliers, which Gordon Brothers denies.

The investment firm appeared to offer a vastly different account of Poundland’s health to that offered by Poundland’s management, sources said, who suggested the business had turned a corner, pointing to its expected £18m profit.

Gordon Brothers released £10m of funding to Poundland earlier this week but  Byrne said “there’s concerning signs [Poundland has] been strangled of access to its own funds in what should be its busiest trading period in the run up to Christmas”. Gordon Brother claims it has made all funds available when requested.

‘Exasperated at the media coverage’

The investment firm has faced significant scrutiny over recent weeks after refusing a number of solvent offers to buy Poundland. Newton-Jones appeared “exasperated at the media coverage” of the sale process and “tried to paint Gordon Brothers as the savior of the situation,” one person with knowledge of the session said.

They said they have “very little confidence” that the investment firm wants to keep Poundland intact.

Gordon Brothers is in talks with NCP-owner Martin Property Group, little-known investor Xyra Group and Irish investment firm Innovest Holdings over a solvent takeover of the discount retailer, sources told City AM. 

Retailers including Tesco, B&M, Lidl, Iceland, The Range and Poundstretcher are waiting in the wings to snap up Poundland’s stores and stock if it falls into administration. 

Political pressure

A collapse of Poundland would be the most significant to hit the retail sector in years and would strike a blow to Andy Burnham’s pledge to revive the high street.

The Prime Minister and Chancellor have made supporting Britain’s retail sector a key pillar of their government since taking power in July.

“The truth is that too many high streets have been left to hollow out, leaving town centres a shell of what they once were,” Burnham said in September. “That must change.”

He has previously called on Gordon Brothers to protect as many jobs as possible. He said last month: “If there was a potential owner to avoid [collapse] that hasn’t been accepted, then the business secretary and I want to know why that is the case.”

]]> 2476673 Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong Hire a lawyer, don’t ask AI: Taxpayers warned as HMRC set to snoop on chat logs https://www.cityam.com/hire-a-lawyer-dont-ask-ai-taxpayers-warned-as-hmrc-set-to-snoop-on-chat-logs/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 18:23:21 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2476566

HMRC’s powers to probe digital records are set to increase under newly proposed rules, as the tax authority will soon be able to view the chat histories of AI chatbots taxpayers use for tax questions. The tax authority currently has powers to request and obtain copies of digital “records” if it has a legitimate reason [...]]]>

HMRC’s powers to probe digital records are set to increase under newly proposed rules, as the tax authority will soon be able to view the chat histories of AI chatbots taxpayers use for tax questions.

The tax authority currently has powers to request and obtain copies of digital “records” if it has a legitimate reason to do so to determine whether a taxpayer has paid the correct amount of tax.

However, under the government’s newly proposed rules in the Finance Bill, expected to receive Royal Assent next March, the definition of digital information will be expanded to allow access to “relevant” digital records.

The move will also require third parties, including software providers, to give HMRC people’s tax information if they hold it.

HMRC can demand access to personal information under a so-called Schedule 36 notice. However, those who fail to respond to information requests could face an initial fine of £300, and taxpayers who do not report inaccuracies may face a fine of up to £3,000.

Matthew Holman, partner at Cripps, told City AM there is a “clear risk” arising from taxpayers using AI to discuss tax issues and the “unpredictability” of AI systems.

“The nature of the technology is fundamentally discursive and conversational; it is not challenging to imagine that a discussion with a sophisticated large language model about an individual’s tax affairs could easily (and unintentionally) contain content later used to allege intention to evade tax,” he said.

He added that an AI model “may suggest certain tax arrangements which could amount to evasion or generate responses with the user which indicate an intention to evade tax, all of which would be useful to an HMRC investigation.”

Holman said that while the Bill does not explicitly reference AI, the revised definition of ‘digital information’ will be “significantly broader” than it is now.

Holman said that while the Finance Bill is not “explicitly enabling access to AI history”, it is instead “expanding its operative definitions in such a way that AI could be within its new (wider) scope.”

“It is being suggested by various commentators that the rationale for broadening the definition is to encompass records created by the use of artificial intelligence by those under investigation,” he added.

Nicola Cain, chief executive and principal consultant at legal consultancy firm Handley Gill, told City AM the changes may raise data protection issues, and while the changes “will provide HMRC with a lawful basis to access additional information about taxpayers under the UK GDPR”. The tax authority will still be expected to follow legal requirements, meaning it must do so only when necessary and in a proportionate manner.

Cain added that taxpayers using AI for tax questions, which might be “better directed to a tax lawyer”, and creating a permanent digital record on a third-party platform which HMRC may be able to access “risks exposing taxpayers and their activities.”

‘Deeply intrusive overreach’ by HMRC

Anne Strickland, researcher at lobby group the Taxpayers’ Alliance, said the government’s plans to expand “sweeping powers” HMRC already has “further risks trampling over the privacy of ordinary Britons.”

“Forcing taxpayers to hand over private AI conversations would be a deeply intrusive overreach by the taxman,” Strickland said.

“Ministers must rein in the tax authority and ensure that this never becomes implemented,” she added.

When contacted for a comment, an HMRC spokesperson said: “This is about updating our existing information powers to reflect how tax information is now stored and processed digitally. It is not about going through everyone’s use of large language models. We can only request information where we already have a lawful basis to do so.”

The government has thrown its weight behind Heathrow’s third runway expansion for the first time since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister.

John Healey told the Treasury Committee that the Andy Burnham government “was behind a third runway at Heathrow” and lamented the thicket of regulation preventing it from being approved sooner.

“Successful airports are very often an engine for economic growth in the wider area – that’s true in Manchester, it’s true in London and elsewhere,” he said, adding: “I was responsible for the National Planning Act in 2008, and that was designed for the first time to deal with Britain’s deep-seated problem of delays in infrastructure projects […] but yes it still takes too long.”

The remarks represent the government’s first formal endorsement of £49bn project since Burnham took office in July. The former Manchester mayor has so far ducked several opportunities to back the plan, and instead dismissed it as a decision “for London and Londoners”.

Burnham’s comments, made in the days leading up to September’s Labour party conference, represented a striking departure from the tack of the Starmer government, which had made the mega-project a key pillar in its growth agenda.

Separately, transport secretary Heidi Alexander said the government had moved “heaven and earth” to speed up the delivery of Heathrow’s third runway.

In a speech to an aviation summit in London, she hailed its approval of Gatwick and Luton expansions as a “shot in the arm” for the South East.

She added the “same logic applies to Heathrow”, despite the Prime Minister refusing to back the £49bn scheme since entering office.

“We’ve been clear that a third runway has the potential to unlock opportunities, jobs, investment and growth across the country,” Alexander said. “That’s why we’ve moved heaven and earth to deliver a draft Heathrow [planning blueprint] faster than anyone expected.”

Heathrow expansion in limbo ahead of key vote

Earlier this year, the government concluded a public consultation into the planning framework against which ministers would judge the applications of Heathrow airport and rival bidder Heathrow West. It is now expected to publish the final draft – known as the National Policy Statement – early next year ahead of a crucial MP vote.

Alexander also launched a fresh broadside on the organisation responsible for Britain’s struggling air traffic control system, which has been struck by two major outages this year.

The transport secretary said she was “angry” at the breakdown, which left thousands of passengers stranded and triggered a wave of cancellations and delays.

“The impact on passengers was simply unacceptable, and it would have been even worse had the airlines and airports not pulled out all the stops to clear the disruption in just a few days,” she told the Airlines 2026 conference, adding that the results of a watchdog inquiry would be published soon.

“I can assure you that I will do whatever it takes to ensure that lessons are learned,” said.

City law firm Pinsent Masons is set to slash jobs in its alternative legal resourcing unit as it plans to overhaul the platform. City law firm Pinsent Masons is set to slash jobs in its alternative legal resourcing unit as it plans to overhaul the platform.

The unit, Vario, was set up in 2013 and employs full-time staff and a network of freelancers. The firm created it as a separate business to provide flexible staffing and legal services where needed, including for in-house clients. Vario lists on its LinkedIn page that it employs between 1,000 and 5,000 people.

Pisnents has launched a consultancy round on the redundancies, and the number of roles affected has not been confirmed.

This comes after the firm hired Ian Stott in August from Eversheds Sutherland to join Vario and lead the unit’s financial regulatory consulting section.

The London-headquartered law firm said in a statement shared with City AM it is “optimising how we organise and deliver our services to best meet the needs of our clients and our business. This includes making some adjustments to Vario, our alternative legal service delivery model, and to our business operations function.”   

“We have built significant expertise and capability in alternative legal service delivery through Vario. We are ambitious about capitalising on that success, moving towards a model that embeds its people and capabilities more deeply within the wider firm,” they said.

The spokesperson added the move is “an important evolution” but that it is “assessing a range of options, including making greater use of the talent and capabilities available across our international network.

“Having listened to our clients and the market, that will strengthen how expertise is deployed to make alternative legal service delivery a more integrated component of how we deliver innovative and effective solutions for our clients.

“This means that some roles will be subject to consultation. We understand that this is an unsettling period for our colleagues and we are engaging directly with them to provide transparency and support throughout this period,” the spokesperson added.

Firm’s ‘misleading’ AI letters sent to court

In May, a High Court judge criticised Pinsent Masons after a lawyer sent the court AI-generated letters containing false legal information.

The judgment found that a junior solicitor at Pinsent Masons used AI to draft two “misleading” emails containing so-called hallucinations, sent to the High Court in March and April this year during an insolvency case in which the firm was acting for the applicants.

The firm apologised to the court following the incident and referred itself to the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA), which will investigate further.

The law firm reported revenue of £703m for the 2025/26 financial year, up over three per cent from the previous year. But profit per equity partner (PEP) fell more than seven per cent to £740,000 from £797,000 the previous year, due to heavy investment in new offices, technology, and staff.

Thomas Woldbye said the west London hub’s recent reshuffle of terminal occupancy would allow 2.5m more travellers through Heathrow every year and cut the charge applied passenger air fares by one pound.

The pair of carriers have had a transatlantic joint venture since 2014 and Delta owns a stake of Virgin. Separating the two operators’ terminals will lengthen connection times for passengers and make logistics harder for the airlines.

Heathrow move ‘mindless and anti-competitive’

Koster branded the move “anti-competitive, mindless [and] irrational”, and vowed to challenge the decision wherever it could.

““Heathrow refuses to engage commercially, they will hide behind regulation,” he said at the Airlines 2026 conference. “We’re going to challenge this extremely hard together with Delta. There’s no way we will ever accept it.”

“They tried to do a trick that the media in the room will recognise – which is slide it out before the Budget, so that no-one would mention, no one would notice it,” he added. “Well clearly this move doesn’t stand up to public scrutiny, so nice try Heathrow.”

Koster’s fresh broadside comes just weeks after Heathrow Airport Limited announced plans to split Virgin Atlantic and Delta up, with flights running different terminals. 

Speaking at the same event, the boss of the aviation regulator said he “would consider” Virgin Atlantic‘s complaints should they be escalated to the watchdog.

“These are serious issues that are being raised,” Rob Bishton, chief executive of the Civil Aviation Authority said. “All I can commit to is saying that we will consider… that which is put in front of us, and we will play our role.”
