Cloud 9 | National Theatre | ★★★☆☆

First staged in 1979, Caryl Churchill’s Cloud 9 was once considered a sensational, salacious and provocative piece of theatre. Nearly 50 years later, Dominic Cooke’s National Theatre revival doesn’t pack the same punch.

It’s a play of two halves, both in structure and setting. The first act takes place in Victorian colonial Africa, opening with the cast singing an imperial anthem before patriarch Clive (Sam Troughton) introduces his family. Wife Betty, children Edward and Victoria, governess Ellen, mother-in-law Maud and servant Joshua all exist under his strict patriarchal rule. Sexual repression, gender conformity and racism are the order of the day. There isn’t much in the way of conventional plot; instead, we see the family romp through a series of interactions with one another. It’s satirical and slapstick, but disturbing, too.

The second act leaps forward to “present day” 1979, though the characters only age 25 years. Watching it in 2026, we are almost as far removed from the era of the second act as Churchill was from the first when she wrote the play. Naturally, then, many of its observations have lost their cutting edge.

What has aged badly in Caryl Churchill’s Cloud 9

Some aspects of the production have inevitably evolved; Joshua, Clive’s black servant, was originally written for a white actor but is now portrayed (brilliantly) by Eloka Ivo. But other elements feel awkwardly outdated. The play’s treatment of topics such as incest or corporal punishment of children reflects a 1970s permissive outlook that’s at odds with the rest of the progressive piece.

Whatever its inconsistencies, the production is carried by a wildly versatile cast and the whole thing serves as something of an actor’s showcase. It’s a technical feat by Rebecca Humphries in particular, who plays both the repressed governess Ellen and the liberated family friend Mrs Saunders in act one, only to return unrecognisable as the edgy Lin in act two. Likewise, having spent the first act playing nine-year-old Edward, Ellen Robertson stands out in the second act as the older, divorced Betty, delivering a particularly stirring monologue about marriage and liberation. While ironic and amusing, the cross-casting does read as a little on the nose when the patriarchal colonialist Clive later plays demanding toddler Cathy (an entertaining and crowd-pleasing switch-up by Troughton).

Miriam Buether’s stage design is a visual spectacle. So much so that any stragglers still in their seats during the interval are gently ushered out to make way for an elaborate set change. What Buether does with the second half is interesting and unnerving, not least because the audience spends it under the exposing glare of the house lights.

Cloud 9 at the National Theatre: A fascinating historical piece more than a play for today

At 88 years old, Churchill is still going strong as one of our greatest living playwrights. Her oeuvre has consistently demonstrated a great skill for responding to our time, but this revival doesn’t make the case for Cloud 9 as a play for today. That doesn’t lessen its importance – much of the intersectional gender, sexual and racial dynamics are still relevant – but overall makes it feel more like a fascinating historical piece than a work of theatre offering a fresh perspective.

In contrast, Churchill’s latest satire Triumph debuted at the Almeida earlier this year, about the blonde press secretary of an unnamed American president. Triumph had a lot more to say in its 15-minute run time than this revival does in nearly three hours. If you missed it, fear not: more of Churchill’s new short plays are to be staged at the Almeida next year as part of Dominic Cooke’s first season as artistic director (he’s evidently a fan). I expect those will be as powerful now as Cloud 9 was then.

]]> 2476796Olivia Jordan Olivia Jordan IBM sounds alarm over AI governance at British firms https://www.cityam.com/ibm-sounds-alarm-over-ai-governance-at-british-firms/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:23:59 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2476343

British businesses might be sleepwalking into future compliance issues as AI governance lags behind the rollout of advanced technologies, says tech giant IBM. Leon Butler, chief executive of IBM UK and Ireland, said businesses need to build governance into business processes from the start. “We have something called an AI operating model, which is looking [...]]]>

British businesses might be sleepwalking into future compliance issues as AI governance lags behind the rollout of advanced technologies, says tech giant IBM.

Leon Butler, chief executive of IBM UK and Ireland, said businesses need to build governance into business processes from the start. “We have something called an AI operating model, which is looking at the outcome, the process, and redefining that process, and then making sure that the right data and governance follow it…[if] you build it up, that governance will follow at an overall level,” he told City AM.

This comes as the IBM Digital Sovereignty Index showed a gap in corporate AI maturity, as 87 per cent of executives claim they have AI under control, but only 27 per cent can prove it to an auditor.

Debbie Lawrence, group head of data strategy and management at London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG), stated that having the right evidence means a business will be ready when an issue arises.

“It’s all well and good having a system in place and having all the tools, but if you haven’t started to think proactively around what the evidence is that I need… it starts to become a real issue because when you have an event, you don’t have time to scramble. It has to be all at your fingertips,” she said.

Data increasing in value

The New York-listed tech giant said most British businesses have faced at least one sovereignty challenge in the past three years. “For business leaders shaping their digital sovereignty strategies, the focus must be on stronger evidence,” said Butler.

Lawrence pointed out how important data has become for businesses and the focus on authenticated data. “If I look now across the industry, more and more companies are recognising that their data is an asset,” Lawrence said.

She added: “The concept of data as an asset is going to become a really interesting discussion because I think people are going to recognise that data is valuable [and the] crown jewels [of a business].”

Lawrence stated that historical data will increase in value. “I definitely believe that certain data sets are far more valuable today than they were five years ago. Because you can mine data and you can mine the history in a way that you weren’t able to do five years ago, so suddenly the fact that you can go back and look at historical trends and patterns in a much easier, faster way makes a lot of that data more valuable,” she explained.

]]> 2476343Maria Ward-Brennan Maria Ward-Brennan Cyber response firms ‘nearing capacity’ as attacks grow https://www.cityam.com/cyber-response-firms-nearing-capacity-as-attacks-grow/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 17:10:49 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2476658

Top cyber defence consultancies are operating at near “full capacity” after a surge of AI-enabled cyberattacks over the past year, a leading risk advisor has warned. “There’s an interesting dynamic right now in the market where the best incident response shops, […] are all almost full on capacity,” Kroll’s risk advisory president, Brent Tomlinson, told [...]]]>

Top cyber defence consultancies are operating at near “full capacity” after a surge of AI-enabled cyberattacks over the past year, a leading risk advisor has warned.

“There’s an interesting dynamic right now in the market where the best incident response shops, […] are all almost full on capacity,” Kroll’s risk advisory president, Brent Tomlinson, told City AM.

Over the last year, scores of high profile firms have been hit by cyberattacks. The retail sector has been particularly badly affected, with M&S, Co-op and Asos all facing huge disruption to their operations after hacking incidents. Last week, supermarket refrigerators at retailers across Europe, as well as France’s national blood service, were targeted in attacks that raised their temperatures.

Cyber incident response is a structured process businesses use to detect, contain, eradicate, and recover from a cyberattack or security breach.

Brits who make innocent errors on their tax returns face being treated the same way as those who deliberately evade payments, under aggressive new powers quietly introduced after the Budget.

Under rules buried in the Finance Bill, which had its first reading in Parliament on Monday, HMRC will introduce a statutory ‘Duty to Correct’ regime from April 2028. The measure legally requires taxpayers to rectify mistakes on old tax returns upon becoming aware of them.

Existing tax law allows an uncorrected mistake discovered after filing to be treated as “careless”, which carries a lower penalty cap of up to 30 per cent of the unpaid tax and a six-year assessment window where HMRC can scrutinise old returns, impose fines and demand back taxes.

But the new regime will see that taxpayers who fail to take steps to correct their mistakes will have the inaccuracy branded as “deliberate”, which is used when HMRC is knowingly and intentionally fed false figures or withheld information to pay less tax.

It is the highest penalty tier from the tax authority, carrying a fine of between 70 per cent and 100 per cent, and allows HMRC to scrutinise taxpayers’ forms going back two decades.

Blurring the line

The shake-up comes as HMRC cracks down on tax avoidance in a bid to close the £59bn tax gap. The move aims to end the culture of taxpayers who spot historical errors and choose to “let sleeping dogs lie” rather than report it.

But tax barristers and City figures have questioned the legislation blurring “the long-established distinction” between honest mistakes and intentional fraud.

“HMRC’s policy objective is easy to understand, they want to close what they perceive to be a gap in the current compliance framework,” said Fiona Fernie, partner at Blick Rothenberg.

“Since the conduct of concealing income from the outset and failing to correct an honest mistake are plainly not in the same category there is a question over the proportionality of the proposed measure given that the legislation risks producing similar outcomes for both.”

HMRC will also be granted the power to issue Customer Correction Notices, which can be sent if the department has reason to suspect that a tax return is incorrect.

Andy Wood, tax barrister at Tax Barrister UK, said: “Failure to respond properly to a Customer Correction Notice could also create a presumption of carelessness, although taxpayers would have an opportunity to challenge this.

“HMRC should distinguish between deliberate non-compliance and taxpayers who genuinely struggle to understand their obligations or reconstruct historic financial information.”

Thresholds and clashes

Tax bodies also raised the alarm over the absence of a minimum threshold, a decision Wood branded a “concern”.

“Without one, taxpayers could potentially face formal correction notices over relatively small amounts of unpaid tax,” he said. “There is a risk that taxpayers could end up spending more on professional advice and administration than the tax originally at stake.”

Wood called for a threshold in order to “protect taxpayers from unnecessary compliance costs”.

The extended 20-year window also clashes with statutory record-keeping rules for the self-employed.

They are only legally required to keep records for up to five to six years, meaning those facing a 20 year audit may be unable to produce needed receipts and bank statements.

Fernie said: “This legislation needs clearer safeguards and a finite time limit for making corrections. Otherwise, a measure intended to modernise compliance could undermine it.”

A HMRC spokesperson said: “We know most of our customers act in good faith and want to get their tax right. These changes make it quicker and easier for taxpayers to correct errors when we flag them.

“They won’t be penalised for innocent mistakes, and deliberate penalty charges only arise where taxpayers fail to take reasonable steps to correct an inaccuracy they were already aware of.”

The gains this year dwarf all but one of the UK’s six biggest listed pub chains (All Bar One owner Mitchells and Butlers is narrowly ahead), of which half remain down sharply since 2021.

For those who obsess over US tech mega-caps, you’d have been better off holding Fuller’s this year than you would Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, Netflix, Nvidia and Alphabet.

So is Fuller’s overvalued? Is the stock frothier than the head on a London Pride? There are reasons to think not. 

A quick glance at the numbers suggests the chain is doing well. Today the pub group said it grew its revenue by six per cent to £221m in the year, while its pre-tax profit jumped more than a third to £28.5m.

Boss Simon Emeny points out that because the firm’s estate is in affluent parts of London and the South East – plenty in the Square Mile, dozens across leafy West London and a good smattering in the Home Counties – its clientele is fairly insulated from wider cost-of-living pressures.

The firm’s pubs are among the nicest in the capital, and its customers are as well-heeled as the fireside armchairs are upholstered (my own favourites, not that you were asking, are the Counting House in Cornhill, the Scarsdale Tavern in Kensington and the Victoria in Paddington, where Emeny once bought me a pint).

“We spend a lot on staff training. Make sure the service is impeccable. I think if you get all of those ingredients right and you’re in the right areas, then customers will pay a little bit more,” Emeny told City AM.

Alongside this, like many in the sector, the company is less exposed to wider market forces, and energy cost pressures, because it doesn’t brew beer. Fuller’s sold off its Chiswick brewery in 2019 – meaning whether you like its classic Extra Special Bitter (ESB) or not, is really not its problem. Some rivals like Shepherd Neame – which last month said it would downsize its brewing operations – have had a rougher ride by keeping things in-house.

Lastly, the business is adapting to rapidly changing drinking habits. Sales of peach-flavoured lager Jubel, rapidly becoming one of the capital’s favourite drinks, soared by 71 per cent in the six months to September, while demand for spritzes soared by 118 per cent.

“Customers are always looking for the next thing. And the next thing at the moment is high quality premium continental lagers, fruit lagers, spritzes, and some of that is coming off Guinness,” Emeny said.

All this being said, the stock’s rally could leave some punters with a headache greater than that after my ESB marathon last Thursday. Investors have been steadily selling off big tech stocks since the start of October, from which London mid-caps such as this one have been a clear beneficiary. But last orders often creeps up on you faster than you think.

The legislation, which was introduced in Sir Keir Starmer’s King’s Speech, will allow the City to take advantage of post-Brexit regulatory freedoms and also launch an overhaul on the Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS). This will include a 10-year time limit on complaints made to the ombudsman.

It will introduce a new test where if the firm can prove it followed the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) rules, the ombudsman must assume it acted fairly, even if the customer believes they got a bad deal.  Under the system, cases must be referred to the FCA where there is ambiguity.

John Godfrey, managing director of public affairs at TheCityUK, said a “just get it done” approach was the “way to go forward”.

He added the group was “broadly supportive” of the bill, but called for greater clarity on designating the FCA as the single professional services supervisor for anti-money laundering.

Treasury committee chair Meg Hillier said the bill could be seen as “moving the pendulum more towards the financial services sector and further from regulation to support consumers”.

Healey responded that the assertion that the bill acts as though “the firm is always right is incorrect.”

UK financial services don’t want to be a ‘rule-taker’

Consumer champions such as Fairer Finance, Which? and Martin Lewis’ Money Saving Expert have warned consumers could be locked out of free, independent redress because of changes in the Bill.

A spokesperson for trade body UK Finance told City AM the bill should be “passed without delay”.

“The bill is an important step in delivering the government’s wider financial services reform agenda, helping to drive growth and competitiveness while strengthening outcomes for consumers,” they added.

The new legislation marks the latest step for the City to take advantage of Brexit’s regulatory advantages.

The split from the EU paved the way for London’s financial hub to break from restrictive Brussels-era directives and burdensome capital rules. This has included lifting the banker bonus cap, overhauling insurers’ Solvency II regime, and streamlining wholesale market regulations. 

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called for closer ties with the European Union, sparking friction over what it could mean for the City’s new regulatory framework. According to Bloomberg reports, the government is seeking to maintain the City’s independence in EU negotiations and does not want the 27-state bloc’s regulations to apply to UK financial services.

“What the industry generally tells us is they don’t want to be a rule-taker, they want the UK to be a rule-maker,” Godfrey said.

Scott Devine, TheCityUK’s associate director for Europe, told City AM the industry had “regular engagement” with officials and has “fed in practical priorities” ahead of the forthcoming UK-EU summit on 20 November.

It also scraps the old system for approving foreign financial firms, allowing the government to let overseas companies operate in the UK as long as their home rules achieve similar results, rather than forcing them to copy UK laws word-for-word.

]]> 2476414 Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong Female founders “in toxic relationships” with their businesses https://www.cityam.com/female-founders-in-toxic-relationships-with-their-businesses/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 11:19:13 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2476344

Why women entrepreneurs need to stop doing it all to have a real chance at scale.

For many women, their relationship with their business has quietly turned unhealthy. The startup they love so much is harming their mental, emotional and even physical wellbeing, but they feel trapped caring 24/7 for the thing they have created.

Ambition is rarely the limiting factor when it comes to scaling a company. More often, growth is held back by a founder who cannot let go.

Sometimes, the most strategic move a founder can make is to make herself less essential.

Ahead of the female founders’ SCALE session in Manchester on 11 November, I sat down with Julia Spencer, Accelerator Community Manager for Universities at NatWest, to talk about what really holds female founders back at the point of scale.

We were joined by Pauline Vuyelwa Muswere-Enagbonma, founder of Jessamy Care Group and creator of the Founder Intelligence programme, who will deliver the session for women and non-binary entrepreneurs at NatWest’s Spinningfields offices.

Don’t confuse busy with growth 

Pauline opens her sessions with one question: are founders building a business that is actually growing, or one that is simply becoming more demanding of them?

“Those two experiences can look remarkably similar from the outside, but they are not the same thing,” she said.

She speaks from experience. “I had a business where revenue was increasing, the team was expanding, my diary was full. My name was being mentioned in so many rooms, and my phone never stopped ringing. So to the world, that looked like success. But I was drowning as a founder, because everything was permanently urgent.”

The test, Pauline said, is whether a founder is carrying all the risk on her own shoulders, solving every problem herself and holding everyone and everything together. Or, is she building a team that can hold those things for her instead?

Women’s caring instinct keeps a business going, and keeps a founder stuck

Running a care business taught Pauline that whatever she was feeling, she had to show up calm and composed. “I’ve got to be confident, whether I feel confident inside or not,” she said, “because I’ve got carers that are caring for somebody that can’t get out of bed without them.”

Julia recognises that women operate like this at home as well. “It doesn’t matter how I’m feeling. I need to turn up consistently and create a safe space for the kids,” she said. “And we take the same exacting standards into our professional lives.” 

The problem is that women’s caring superpowers can keep a founder holding everything herself. She cares for her team, her customers and her business, and puts her own needs last, when what the business actually needs is for her to let go.

The founder does not have to be the CEO

One of the most painful discoveries a founder can make, Pauline said, is that an investor would back the business, just not with her in charge of it. Her advice is to think about that before someone else forces you to. 

“We’re not asking founders to disappear, because there is a lot of value in the founder. We’re just asking you to step back from what is not your speciality.”

Pauline is following that advice herself, building the leadership and systems needed to ensure the mission can continue without depending on her being involved in every decision.

Julia sees the same pattern among the academic founders she works with through NatWest’s university partnerships. “Being technically brilliant and having a PhD doesn’t always mean you’re a natural CEO,” she said. 

“Those founders can continue building and driving innovation and become Chief Scientific Officer, for instance.” But what the business needs is someone with a track record of scaling. 

Trying to wear every hat, or stubbornly clinging to a role that doesn’t fit you, doesn’t do you or the business any good.

There’s “good pain” in making yourself replaceable 

Pauline has a visual impairment and has epilepsy. Seizures can temporarily take her out of action. Even so, like many founders who care for everyone else first, she kept carrying everything herself, because she could.

“When I’m unable to run this business, the mission must still be protected,” she said. “So really, I must be replaceable.” Every day, she asks herself which of her functions need to be handed over in case she cannot do them tomorrow. “It was painful to learn that, but it’s good pain.”

“I always say founders have toxic relationships with their businesses,” said Pauline. Many are tied to businesses that are doing well, while their next chapter, and their next startup idea, waits in the wings.

Julia agrees. “It can definitely become a toxic relationship,” she said. “The support system is essential: people you trust who can say, ‘It’s gone too far. That’s not okay. This thing you love should not be doing that to you.’” 

The bigger question is about impact and legacy. “Do you want a business that will grow and outlive you, or do you just want a hobby?” Pauline asked.

Julia put it in investor terms: “Are you trying to create an asset of value, or is it a lifestyle business? Both are absolutely valid, but whichever you choose, do it with purpose. Do the soul searching first.”

A new approach to ‘investor-ready’ 

Most pitch preparation focuses on the deck. Pauline wants to help founders interrogate the business behind it. “All founders have brilliant ideas, but are they commercially viable? Is it investable and am I investible?”

That means separating what a founder is passionate about and what she can prove. What she needs to keep hold of, and what she needs to let go in order to unblock growth.

Join the Founder Intelligence Boardroom on 11 November

SCALE is teaming up with NatWest Accelerator to run a Founder Intelligence session for female founders preparing to pitch, on 11 November. The competition watchdog has escalated its probe into Unilever’s $65bn deal to offload its food arm to American spice giant McCormick, warning it could “substantially” weaken competition in the UK grocery market.

In an update on Wednesday, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said the mega-merger “gives rise to a realistic prospect of a substantial lessening of competition” within the condiment and spice market and called on the two companies to provide assurances over the deal.

“The CMA found that the merger will combine two of the largest brand suppliers… and the merged entity will be the largest supplier of dry ingredient mixes and dry sauces by far,” the watchdog wrote, adding it had “not seen any significant growth in the relevant product markets that would suggest new entry or expansion would be sufficient to constrain the merged entity”.

Unilever and New York-listed McCormick now have until 18 November to offer “undertakings which might be accepted” by the regulator to quash its concerns. These could include spinning off or selling brands where competition concerns are greatest.

CMA decision was ‘expected’ – Unilever

Consumer goods giant Unilever took many of its investors off-guard when it inked the $65bn (£48.8bn) deal to merge its food arm with Frank’s hot sauce owner McCormick in March. The FTSE 100 group, whose stable of brands includes Dove, Sure and Vaseline, had previously floated plans to spin off some or all of its food labels, until McCormick tabled a shock bid for the entirety of the underperforming division.

The tie-up will bring household-name brands like Unilever’s Hellman’s and McCormick’s Frank’s mustard under one roof, in what was one of the largest mergers in London Stock Exchange history.

Watchdog officials singled out the supply of dry ingredients and sauces as being especially concentrated in the newly formed entity, expected to operate under the name McCormick. The CMA found the merged company, which will combine the likes of McCormick’s Schwarz brand with Unilever’s Knorr, would be “the largest supply of dry ingredient mixes and dry sauces by far”.

“While private label and branded competitors (including Maggi in dry ingredient mixes and Bisto in dry sauces) exert some degree of competitive constraint, their products… impose only a limited constraint on the parties in dry ingredients and mixing sauces,” watchdog officials ruled.

The regulator also found “no realistic prospect of competition concerns” in the mustard market, despite the new company bringing the London-listed party’s Colman’s and Maille mustard brands together with Frank’s.

A Unilever spokesperson said the ruling was “an expected step in the regulatory process, and we are working constructively with the CMA on a suitable remedy” and that a sale process for Colman’s was already under way.

“As announced in August, a decision had already been taken to market the Colman’s brand and assets for sale to proactively address potential competition concerns,” they added. “Discussions with potential buyers are progressing well.

“We continue to make good progress on regulatory approvals globally, reinforcing our confidence in a timely closing.”

Both parties have cheered the megamerger as an important cog in their respective turnaround plans, as both battle to arrest a years-long spell of stagnating growth and languid share prices. McCormick sees it as a valuable means of adding economies of scale to its food juggernaut, which will be dual listed in London and New York, allowing it to find efficiencies.

Unilever has held it up as a flagship measure in its drive to focus on higher-margin, higher-growth divisions, like consumer healthcare and wellness.

Unilever shares traded flat on Thursday morning, while McCormick’s shares were down 2.4 per cent in out-of-hours trading.

Donald Trump’s defamation case against the BBC over a Panorama documentary is set to go to trial after the broadcaster’s bid to dismiss the case failed.

The US president filed legal action in December 2025 over the editing of a Panorama documentary which included footage of Trump’s speech at a rally before the US Capitol riots in 2021.

The documentary editors spliced two parts of his speech together into what appeared to be one quote. The documentary appeared to show the President telling supporters: “We’re gonna walk down to the Capitol… and I’ll be with you… and we fight. We fight like hell.”

The broadcaster apologised to Trump, and director general Tim Davie and news chief Deborah Turness resigned. But when his lawyer demanded compensation or threatened to file a lawsuit, the BBC refused, and Trump filed a $10bn lawsuit in the Southern District of Florida.

In July, as part of discovery, the judge ordered Trump to disclose financial details about his businesses. Last month, he was then ordered to cooperate with the discovery process mandated and to sit for sworn testimony by 11 December, or his case would be dropped.

Motion to throw out case

Earlier this month, the broadcaster filed a motion to dismiss the case, arguing the Miami court lacked jurisdiction and that “President Trump fails to state a claim”. The BBC’s main argument is that, as a British broadcaster, the programme was aimed at a UK audience, so the US court isn’t the place for this case.

However, Trump-appointed Judge Jeffrey Kuntz dismissed the BBC’s motion on Tuesday. In his ruling, the judge pointed out that “to make sure it [documentary] was seen in Florida, BBC even emailed US and Florida-based commenters with instructions on how to view the documentary.” The judge also noted that the BBC is a global organisation with an office in Florida.

On Trump’s claim, the judge ruled that his claims “extend beyond negligence and plead a claim of recklessness” and, he added, “that is more than enough to satisfy the notice-pleading standard.”

In a social media post on Truth Social, Trump said the ruling was “a huge victory against fake news BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth.”

A BBC spokesperson said: “We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage.”

“We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process,” they added.

On this day, 11 November 1999, the House of Lords Act became law, removing the automatic right of hereditary peers to sit. Eliot Wilson takes us through the day, and to this year’s action on “stage two”

In 1999, the House of Lords had 1,213 members eligible to attend: 759 hereditary peers, 545 life peers and 26 Church of England bishops. 

At that point, the House was nearly 660 years old. Some peerage titles were older still. The 27th Lord de Ros, Premier Baron of England and owner of a reproduction furniture company, traced his title back to 1264. But the 31st Countess of Mar, a farmer and former civil servant, held the oldest peerage: her Scottish title formally dated from 1115, but an unnamed holder had been recorded at the Battle of Clontarf in 1014.

Nearly all the 750 hereditary peers were excluded a little after 5.00 pm today, 11 November, in 1999. It completely changed the nature of the Lords, even more than the introduction of life peers in 1958. And it happened with four words of Norman French.

Le Reyne le veult. The Queen wishes it.

It was the day of Prorogation to end the parliamentary session, and the Queen was represented by a Royal Commission of five peers. Seven bills which had been agreed by both Houses were waiting to be given Royal Assent to make them acts of Parliament.

La Reyne le veult

The Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, Sir Hayden Phillips, would read each title; Michael Davies, the Clerk of the Parliaments and chief House of Lords official, would then indicate the sovereign’s assent in the language of royal administration ever since the Norman Conquest of 1066.

It was the last bill on the list, because its proceedings had concluded less than an hour before. It had gone that close to the wire.

“House of Lords Act,” Phillips intoned.

“La Reyne le veult,” responded Davies.

And that was it. The exchange represented 10 months of ferocious parliamentary debate over the House of Lords Bill introduced at the beginning of 1999. It was not wholesale reform of the upper house: the Leader of the House of Commons, Margaret Beckett, had been explicit in the bill’s first debate by MPs on 1 February.

“The most important thing about the Bill… is that it is all very simple. What our manifesto said is simple and this legislation is simple… The Bill removes the right presently enjoyed by some 750 people… to sit and vote in our Parliament solely on the basis of their birth.”

Simple, perhaps, but House of Lords reform had been a via dolorosa for unwary politicians, for 90 years, and a polite reminder lay on the statute book. The Parliament Act 1911 had for the first time significantly limited the powers of the Lords and removed their veto. Its preamble sounded arch:

“Whereas it is intended to substitute for the House of Lords as it at present exists a Second Chamber constituted on a popular instead of hereditary basis, but such substitution cannot be immediately brought into operation…”

“Immediately”. Prime Minister H.H. Asquith had introduced the Parliament Act, and was born a century before Tony Blair.

What did the House of Lords Act change?

There had been some changes, most significantly the Life Peerages Act 1958. That had allowed people to enter the Lords for their lifetime without then handing on their title. While life peers gradually dominated the active membership, existing hereditary peers were not affected nor were new creations prohibited: 59 new peers would receive hereditary titles after 1958, though within 10 years it was exceptionally rare.

A cross-party conference in 1917 and Harold Wilson’s Parliament (No. 2) Bill of 1968-69 had failed. Blair focused on one measure. The 1997 general election manifesto was pellucid: Labour would “end the hereditary principle in the House of Lords”, by “self-contained reform, not dependent on further reform in the future”. No arguments about the power of the Lords, or the membership of a new upper house, just remove the hereditaries.

The bill had been announced in the Queen’s Speech in November 1998. The Conservatives were opposing it absent any commitment to further reform, while some hereditaries saw themselves as Napoleon’s Old Guard at Waterloo: the old order was collapsing, but retreat was unthinkable and would not save them.

The Earl of Onslow, in Garrick Club bow tie and yellow socks, admitted his title was created for a politician “who got pissed with Pitt the Younger”. He was not against reform in principle but thought Blair’s bill inadequate; he announced that “if the government is going to play silly monkeys”, he would be as disruptive as possible. Threatening to force a vote on every clause of the Scotland Bill – there were more than 270 and each division took 20 minutes – he demonstrated the scale of that threat. “What fun to go out as a hooligan,” he mused.

The 92 exceptions

Before the bill was published, a deal was done to assuage some critics. The Conservative leader in the Lords, Viscount Cranborne, haggled with Blair to exempt 92 hereditary peers from the cull: they would remain until stage two of reform as a deposit to keep the government honest.

Cranborne was heir to the Marquess of Salisbury, and his family, the Cecils (“Siss-ills”, naturally), was descended from Lord Burleigh, Elizabeth I’s chief minister; his wiliness had four centuries of pedigree. He acted as a sacrificial lamb, keeping his party leader, William Hague, in the dark until after the deal was agreed. Blindsided and embarrassed by Tony Blair at Prime Minister’s Questions, Hague sacked Cranborne, who agreed he had “rushed in, like an ill-trained spaniel”.

But Hague honoured the deal. The reprieve for 92 hereditaries was inserted by an amendment formally in the name of the ex-Speaker of the Commons, Lord Weatherill. It took some of the fieriest heat out of proceedings; but, while the Commons passed the bill inside six weeks by majorities of more than 200, its scrutiny in the Lords occupied 15 days over eight months.

The debate: Courteous but grim

There were elements of an Ealing comedy. The Leader of the Lords, Baroness Jay of Paddington, stiff and didactic, was rhetorically vulnerable on the hereditary principle – she was the daughter of former Prime Minister Jim Callaghan. She was paired with the booming, grandiloquent Lord Chancellor, Lord Irvine of Lairg: he had compared himself to Cardinal Wolsey, and addressed the Prime Minister, once his pupil barrister, as “young Blair”.

Leading the Conservative peers was Cranborne’s replacement, Lord Strathclyde. Not quite 40, tall, heavyset and with an easy charm, he was another hereditary peer; although his title only dated from 1955, his full name was Thomas Galloway Dunlop du Roy de Blicquy Galbraith. He had already been around forever: succeeding his grandfather as 2nd Baron in 1986, he joined Thatcher’s government in 1988 and was Conservative chief whip from 1995 to 1998. Journalistic references to Billy Bunter were frequent.

It was courteously grim trench warfare. Fundamentally there were two separate arguments taking place: Labour found the hereditary peerage obnoxious on principle; most Conservatives, without defending it a priori, thought the Lords more or less worked, and, like Belloc, preferred to “keep a-hold of Nurse/For fear of finding something worse”.

The House ground through Committee and Report Stages of the bill in April, May and June – Cranborne called it “an extremely unhappy place” – and by Third Reading, on 26 October, the war was nearly over. Attendance for that last hurrah was 752, almost twice the daily average, and by one account 200 hereditary peers who had never taken their seats came to watch the death throes.

An objection from the floor

Charles, Earl of Burford, heir to the Duke of St Albans, did not recognise surrender. As the heir to a peerage, he was entitled to watch from the steps of the Throne. As the debate began at 3.24 pm, recorded in Hansard as “[Interruption.]”, Burford jumped on to the Woolsack and shouted his objections to the bill’s constitutional aspects.

“This bill drafted in Brussels is treason… before us lies the wasteland, no Queen, no culture, no sovereignty, no freedom! Stand up for your Queen and country – vote this treason down!”

To some gamey cries of “Get ’im out!”, Burford was swiftly removed.

So passed the old House of Lords. There was sadness, relief, grim satisfaction, anger but little joy. As Lord Irvine had warned earlier in the year, “the best compromises often do not give complete satisfaction to anyone. That is the nature of compromise.” Many felt this was not even the best compromise.

The 92 excepted hereditaries, replenished through by-elections, survived until last April, when the House of Lords (Hereditary Peers) Act 2026 wielded the axe. In Committee, Irvine had loftily dismissed the idea that the government might stop at expelling the hereditary peers and forget about “stage two” as “fanciful and without any foundation at all”.

Twenty-seven years on, we are still waiting for stage two.

Eliot Wilson is a writer and historian. He is a senior fellow for national security at the Coalition for Global Prosperity and a contributing editor at Defence on the Brink

Over 40 per cent of institutions face a deficit and first-class degrees have quadrupled since the mid-1990s, yet no party has a plan to match the problem, says Len Shackleton

UK governments value “soft power” over more traditional measures of economic and military strength. For a long time, the higher education system has been heralded as a key element in promoting British values.

Yet, as we argue in a The Higher Education Delusion, a new book from the Institute of Economic Affairs, our universities are in an economic, academic and cultural mess. Claims to be “world-leading” are out of date – and sometimes embarrassingly delusional.

Higher education is in chronic financial difficulties: Office for Students figures show that over 40 per cent of institutions are expected to have had an operating deficit in the last financial year.

Financial problems, a flawed funding system and excessive equality, diversity and inclusion (EDI) concern have led universities to maximise student recruitment with insufficient concern about applicants’ ability to cope with degree-level study and contribute to an academic community. This open-door policy includes an excessive dependence on almost 700,000 overseas students each year, sometimes inadequately screened and paying very high fees for often poor service.

Weaker students

Recruitment of weaker students – UCAS entry scores in seven major subjects fell nine points in the four years to 2023 – has led to slipping academic standards. This has driven grade inflation, the proportion of first-class degree awards rising from seven per cent in 1993–94 to 30 per cent in 2024–25, undermining the value of degrees as signals of ability and achievement to employers.

Higher education has expanded faster than demand for graduates, reducing the “graduate premium” and leaving 30 per cent of graduates in jobs that do not require a degree, or else unable to find jobs at all in a declining labour market. Many then resort to taking postgraduate qualifications in a bid to improve job prospects, despite evidence that many such qualifications add little to earning power.

Meanwhile, students are accumulating enormous paper debts which constrain aspirations and life choices, making it harder to secure decent housing and start families. Student “loans” are anyway misnamed: they are a bizarre form of redistributive tax which would fail to pass financial regulation of conventional loans. An increasing proportion of student “debt” will never be fully repaid. The way loans are treated in public accounts conceals the true cost to the taxpayer.

Student “loans” are anyway misnamed: they are a bizarre form of redistributive tax which would fail to pass financial regulation of conventional loans

Degree study has also moved away from the ideal of a liberal education; the rise of political correctness threatens free speech. Critical theory has come to dominate many areas of the social sciences. It underpins identity-based activism, or “wokeness”, which graduates spread beyond universities through EDI advocacy as they enter professions. Within the university sector there is a “greenhouse effect” – a self-reinforcing feedback process – which is making diversity of thought within institutions increasingly rare.

Research obsesses academics. It consumes too much of their time and energy, sometimes to the detriment of students. Unknown to most students, who think fees go to fund teaching, a substantial chunk goes to subsidise research which adds little to useful knowledge.

Most researchers will not find a cure for cancer or a new subatomic particle or even attempt such important work. In the last round of the Research Excellence Framework (the peer-reviewed assessment of university research), around half of all the research submitted was in the social sciences or the arts and humanities. Research funding should be reduced and probably concentrated in fewer universities and research institutes.

Universities are over-regulated, limiting competition and innovation. There should be room for new types of institution to develop, with the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) likely to help this process. AI is already undermining many traditional features of universities – such as classroom teaching and essay-based assessment – and this trend will only accelerate.

The higher education sector needs to be dragged out of its current malaise, but no political party has this on its agenda, or at least not in a way that matches the scale of the problem at all. It’s time they did.

Professor Len Shackleton is editorial and research fellow at the Institute of Economic Affairs

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. Villig’s own €5,000 loan covered exactly one prototype. Everything after that came from investors willing to bet that Bolt’s low-cost, fast-mover approach would eventually outlast better-funded rivals in the markets it entered. Operating profit told a similar story of a company just crossing the line, at €19.5 million, reversed from the prior year’s €87.7 million loss. A margin that thin is not really a statement about profitability so much as a statement about intent. Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. Neither programme produced a unicorn by itself. What they produced was a population that treated computers as ordinary tools a generation before most of Europe did, and a legal and administrative system built to let a small number of people start companies with very little friction.

The first of the ten billion-dollar companies was Skype, built in Tallinn in 2003. Skype itself has since been folded into Microsoft and no longer exists as a standalone business, but it left something behind in Tallinn that the other nine companies on the list arguably needed first: a generation of engineers and early employees who had already helped build something that scaled to hundreds of millions of users, and who knew, from direct experience, that it could be done from Estonia rather than London or Silicon Valley.

It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Annus died in 2020, but the firm he helped start is still one of the more active early-stage investors operating out of Tallinn, another channel through which Skype’s original payout kept funding whatever came next.

The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. Estonian startups collectively reported €3.9 billion in revenue in 2024, up 14.7 percent on the year before, according to Invest in Estonia’s own sector figures, and the sector now employs about 14,400 people directly, or roughly one in every 38 working Estonians, at an average monthly salary of €3,650, more than double the national average. A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Where the tiredness comes from

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.

]]> In a series of staged online sales, people selling a used gadget with a known flaw often owned up to it more than buyers predicted — the sellers reported caring more about honesty and fairness, and less about the price, than the buyers assumed https://siliconcanals.com/s-in-a-series-of-staged-online-sales-people-selling-a-used-gadget-with-a-known-flaw-often-owned-up-to-it-more-than-buyers-predicted-the-sellers-reported-caring-more-about-honesty-and-fairness-and/ Fri, 18 Sep 2026 02:00:00 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109366

Across five studies of secondhand-market haggling, sellers were often more candid than buyers expected. Three minutes of small talk before the haggling narrowed the gap, and so did asking buyers to think about the seller's conscience first.]]>

A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

Shira Garber and three colleagues staged a string of these secondhand sales online across five main studies and a pilot, added a second pilot that surveyed people about what drives negotiators, and reported the results in an open-access paper in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin this July. Buyers, they found, often underestimated how honest sellers would be. Sellers also reported more concern with being honest, fair and kind, and less concern with the money, than buyers credited them with.

How often did sellers come clean?

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

The way the question is asked

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

A few minutes of small talk

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Across the study, buyers rated their seller’s likely honesty at 6.56 on a ten-point scale, while coders scored the sellers’ actual replies at 7.51. Among pairs who chatted first, that difference was no longer statistically significant. Sellers’ scores did not differ significantly between the two conditions. The chat raised buyers’ expectations of honesty instead.

Study 4 tried a different nudge on 358 participants. Some buyers were asked about the seller’s moral concerns before predicting, others afterward. Thinking about the seller’s conscience first raised buyers’ expectations, and the gap was nearly halved.

It did not close. The authors suggest one reason: 85 percent of sellers in that study disclosed, a rate higher than in the matching condition of Study 3 for reasons they say are not readily apparent.

Where the suspicion comes from

Study 2 measured three motives, adding the pull of money to the two that Study 1 had tracked. The 214 management undergraduates who took part rated, on a seven-point scale, how much the seller had been weighing being decent, feeling guilty, and getting the best price. Sellers put their concern with being a decent person at 4.99, and buyers guessed 3.78. Buyers put the seller’s interest in money at 6.03; sellers reported 5.06.

The sellers still cared about the money. They cared about it less, and about their own decency more, than the buyers pictured.

The paper’s explanation leans on moral typecasting, the idea that people tend to see others as either doers or feelers, rarely both. A seller holds the object and the information, so, the authors argue, a buyer casts them as a doer, and the competitive setting makes that doer look like someone chasing an advantage rather than guarding a clean conscience. In the abstract’s words: “While sellers tended to be honest because of moral identity concerns, buyers expected them to be driven primarily by self-interest.”

Two duller explanations get a hearing too, and the authors say their own mechanism is not the only one. Poor forecasting in general, they point out, gives no reason to expect guesses to run low rather than high. Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

Small stakes, narrow scope

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.

]]> Quote of the day: “Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself” https://siliconcanals.com/d-quote-of-the-day-sometimes-you-find-yourself-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-and-sometimes-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-you-find-yourself/ Thu, 17 Sep 2026 10:45:39 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109380

What happens when your plans collapse, your phone dies, and you're stranded at a gas station thousands of miles from home—and it's the best thing that could've happened.]]>

The last time I was properly lost, I was standing at a petrol station somewhere north of Chiang Rai with a dead phone, a warm bottle of water and a dog who clearly ran the place. My bus had left without me. I had four hours to wait, nothing to do and no way to tell anyone about it.

It was the calmest I had been in about eighteen months.

Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself.

Yes, it is the sort of line that ends up engraved on a bracelet and screwed to somebody’s kitchen wall. Both of which have happened, it turns out. I went looking for whoever wrote it and found nothing, only evidence that it has been circulating since at least 2014 with no author attached. Anonymous, then. It holds up better than most things sold at a craft market.

Nowhere is mostly an absence of audience

Here is what I think the line is really about. Nowhere has very little to do with distance. It is any situation where nobody knows your job title.

In a city you are surrounded by people who already have a version of you loaded. The neighbour who thinks you are the loud one. The old colleague who still introduces you by the thing you did in 2019. You end up performing that version without noticing, because it is easier than correcting everybody.

Take the audience away and something odd happens. For a day or two you feel faintly useless, because nobody needs anything from you. Then the noise drops. You start hearing your own opinions, which are less impressive and a good deal more honest than the ones you say out loud.

That is the whole mechanism. No mysticism required.

The year my diary went blank

I lost my business, restaurants, during the pandemic. The deal was agreed over a phone call while I sat on a plastic chair in a dining room with the lights off, and it was the least bad option available to me at the time.

For years my day had been decided for me by suppliers, staff rotas and the seven o’clock rush. Then it was not. I woke up on a Tuesday with an empty calendar and genuinely no idea what a Tuesday was for.

I would love to tell you this was peaceful. I reorganised the same cupboard twice. I developed strong opinions about a neighbour’s parking. I rang people I had not spoken to in five years and could hear them wondering what I wanted.

The useful part arrived about three months in, once I had run out of things to tidy. With no restaurant to point at, I had to work out what I would actually do with a day if nobody was paying me for it. The answer was writing, which was inconvenient, as it pays considerably worse than a burger.

You can get lost for the price of a bus ticket

You do not need to sell a business or fly to Patagonia. Nowhere comes in small doses and most of them are free.

Pick a district of your own city you have no reason to visit and spend three hours there on foot. Not a famous one. A dull one, with hardware shops and a wet market and nothing on sale to anyone carrying a suitcase. I do this in Bangkok about once a month and I have never regretted it, though I have frequently regretted the shoes.

Go somewhere your phone cannot help you. Not switched off, just outgunned: the lanes are not on the map and the only language on offer is one you do not speak.

Be a beginner at something in public. Take a class where you are visibly the worst person in the room. It is physically uncomfortable for about twenty minutes. After that it stops mattering, and what is left is quite close to fun.

And if you do travel, leave one day entirely unplanned. No booking, no list, no reservation you have to walk fast to reach. Most people schedule a trip so tightly that they never get further than a warmer version of their normal week.

What actually turns up

Let me manage expectations. You do not come back from a petrol station with a revelation.

What you come back with is a shorter list. Two or three things you thought you cared about turn out to belong to somebody else. One or two things you have never mentioned to anyone are suddenly all you think about when there is nothing else to think about. That is it. It looks like very little on paper. It does not feel that way at thirty-eight, when you are still doing a job you picked at twenty-two to impress someone who stopped watching years ago.

There is a trap in this, though. Some people use the middle of nowhere as somewhere to hide, and the giveaway is that they keep having to go back. If every trip is an escape from the same unaddressed thing at home, the scenery is doing the work of a conversation you have been avoiding. Distance is excellent for seeing a problem clearly. It has never once solved one for me.

The dog at the petrol station, for the record, took no interest in any of this. He sat under the ice cabinet, moved twice in four hours, and had evidently worked something out about Wednesdays that I am still catching up on.
