]]> Calogena, a French nuclear startup developing a small modular reactor (SMR) designed to supply low-carbon heat to district heating networks, has secured €40 million.

The funding came in the form of a grant from the European Commission’s Innovation Fund ,and it marks the first time that European funding has been given to an SMR earmarked for the direct construction of a commercial facility.

“This funding marks a major milestone for Calogena. Having developed our technology and brought it to industrial scale, we are now entering the construction phase of our first commercial reactor,” said Julien Dereux, Executive Chairman of Calogena.

Calogena was founded in 2021 as a subsidiary of Groupe Gorgé, a Paris-based high-tech industrial group with approximately 3,500 employees and €600 million in revenue. The company is developing a 30-thermal-megawatt, water-cooled SMR specifically designed to decarbonise district heating networks.

Its reactor is based on pool-type research reactor technology, a design proven in hundreds of installations worldwide. It operates at low temperature (100°C) and low pressure (6 bar), less than a bicycle tyre, making it simpler and safer to operate than conventional power reactors.

Another strength of Calogena’s SMR is its compact footprint, requiring just 3,000 square metres of land and under 1,000 square metres of building. The design also does not require major water or electricity supply, and refuelling requires only one lorry delivery every two years. Each module can supply heat to around 20,000 households and produces less than 80ml of nuclear water over a lifetime of use.

The grant follows more than €50 million already secured under France’s national industrial strategy programme, France 2030, which helped the company develop its technology and bring it to industrial readiness. 

The €40 million grant will be used to fund the construction of Calogena’s first commercial reactor in Pierrelatte, which would serve as the company’s inaugural commercial reference project. The company says the town will receive locally produced, low-carbon heat, an alternative to the carbon-intensive and largely imported energy sources that currently account for nearly one-third of Europe’s total energy demand. 

“The European Commission’s support confirms the maturity of our project and its potential to address one of Europe’s major energy challenges: producing local, low-carbon, cost-competitive heat at scale while strengthening energy sovereignty. Pierrelatte would be our first commercial reference and should pave the way for wider deployment across Europe,” added Dereux.

In addition to the Pierrelatte project, the company is also pursuing projects across Europe and is in contention to supply more than fifteen reactors in Finland, where it opened a subsidiary in 2025. In June, Calogena signed a cooperation agreement with Veolia, a European leader in district heating, to explore the deployment of its SMRs across Central and Eastern Europe.

As the European district heating market is projected to reach around 1,000 TWh by 2050, Calogena argues that its technology can provide a price-stable, long-term solution for energy sovereignty. It is targeting initial deployments from 2030, with its first commercial reactor in Pierrelatte scheduled to go live in 2032.

]]> Marble Imaging, a Bremen-based big data Earth Observation (EO) company setting up Germany’s first commercial constellation of very-high-resolution (VHR) satellites, has raised an additional €6 million in a Seed extension round led by Cherry Ventures. 

In December 2025, the company announced it had closed an oversubscribed €5.3 million Seed round led by High-Tech Gründerfonds, bringing total funding to €11.3 million.

“To make better decisions, data access must be immediate and actionable. Europe and many of its global partners lack this capability today. We at Marble are determined to close this gap, and Cherry’s trust helps us achieve this faster,” said Robert Hook, co-founder and CEO of Marble Imaging. 

Founded in August 2023 by Hook, Dr. Gopika Suresh, Alexander Epp, and Dr. Raul Scarlat, Marble Imaging is building its constellation of VHR satellites to provide up to hourly EO data and analytics for time-critical insights of the planet.

According to the company, the data and derived EO-based analytics will be vital in supporting rapid decision-making for defence, climate security, crisis and disaster management, green and sustainable energy transitions, infrastructure and mobility, and more.

It already offers advanced data analysis services, including object detection for situational intelligence, terrain analysis and trafficability assessment, coastal asset monitoring and land cover classification.

Marble highlighted that although VHR imagery is a core input for security and commercial intelligence, Europe and many of its partners rely on non-European providers. “This makes them vulnerable to being cut off from coverage over key areas of interest, as materialised in Ukraine or the Strait of Hormuz, creating massive economic as well as security knowledge gaps,” it stated. 

Marble is therefore setting up Germany’s first commercial constellation of very-high-resolution (VHR) satellites. The German startup is also building an AI-powered analytics platform that converts multi-source data into insights. It also notes that as Marble’s constellation scales, the interplay of these segments will create a uniquely well-trained AI solution that delivers actionable decision support for users in the defence, civil security, and critical infrastructure sectors, and beyond.

“Europe needs its own eyes in space, and Marble Imaging is building them. They are using AI to turn pixels into answers, exactly what government and defence customers need. This team has spent their careers in the industry and knows what it takes to build something very big. The product Marble will deliver doesn’t exist in Europe yet, but we’re convinced it has to,” said Filip Dames, Founding Partner at Cherry Ventures.

Marble’s first satellite, Marble Sat-1, is fully funded, has completed pre-flight testing and is scheduled to launch in early 2027. It is designed to capture imagery at up to 0.7 m spatial resolution in the visible and near-infrared spectrum and will also gather data in the shortwave infrared spectrum. 

The company plans to use this capital to accelerate the scaling of its constellation, with a goal of 30 satellites by 2030. It will accelerate satellite and launch procurement for Germany’s first commercial very high-resolution constellation

“Scaling from here is a question of capital, not technology. The demand is proven, the hardware comes from experienced suppliers, and our software is already used by paying customers. We need to invest in more satellite capability in space, and this round accelerates our path to delivering sovereign intelligence with a European identity – stable access, transparency and democratic governance that partners around the world can count on,” said Hook.

AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ Aerospace Global News Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:57:10 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-AGN_Icon_Jet-32x32.png AGN https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/ 32 32 Slovakian ACMI carrier AirExplore shuts down after 16 years of operations https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/airexplore-shuts-down-ceases-operations/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 16:03:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56417 The carrier is the latest member of the Avia Solutions Group of airlines to shut down in recent years due to mounting losses.

The post Slovakian ACMI carrier AirExplore shuts down after 16 years of operations appeared first on AGN.

]]> Slovakian ACMI and charter operator AirExplore has ceased operations after 16 years, becoming the latest airline within Avia Solutions Group’s portfolio to disappear as the aviation services giant continues to restructure its international airline operations.

The carrier officially stopped flying on 10 November and has submitted a request to surrender its Air Operator Certificate (AOC), bringing an end to a business that developed from a small Slovakian operator into an internationally recognised provider of aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance (ACMI) services.

AirExplore ceases operations and grounds fleet

Founded in 2008, AirExplore began ACMI operations in 2010 with a Boeing 737-400 before expanding its fleet with Boeing 737-800s. It subsequently established partnerships with major European airlines and expanded into cargo operations, including the use of converted Boeing 737 freighters.

Avia Solutions Group acquired AirExplore in June 2023, adding another established European operator to its growing portfolio of ACMI businesses.

The shutdown comes despite efforts earlier this year to integrate AirExplore’s management and back-office functions with fellow group subsidiary KlasJet.

In February 2026, Avia Solutions Group announced that the two airlines would operate under a shared management structure, with AirExplore retaining its identity and focusing on ACMI operations while KlasJet continued concentrating on VIP and private charter services.

At the time of its grounding, Planespotters.net reported that AirExplore operated an all-Boeing fleet comprising three Boeing 737-800s, having gradually wound down the remainder of its fleet throughout 2026 following the integration with KlasJet.

These aircraft are now in storage awaiting disposal.   

A growing list of airline closures

AirExplore is not the first Avia Solutions Group airline to cease operations since 2023. Its closure follows several significant setbacks across the group’s international airline portfolio.

The Icelandic cargo operator Bluebird Nordic was the first major casualty. Acquired by Avia Solutions Group in 2020, the airline ceased operations on 30 April 2024 after struggling with excess capacity and weakening demand in the air freight market.

It subsequently surrendered its AOC and returned aircraft to lessors.

The group’s most high-profile collapse came in November 2025, when SmartLynx Airlines Latvia ceased commercial operations. The Latvian ACMI operator had been sold by Avia Solutions Group to Dutch investment vehicle Stichting Break Point Distressed Assets Management in October 2025, shortly before its demise.

Consequently, although its closure forms part of the group’s recent history, SmartLynx was no longer owned by Avia Solutions Group when it stopped flying. With the demise pf SmartLynx in Europe, SmartLynx Australia rebranded back to its original name of Skytrans Australia in mid 2025.

Lastly, Ascend Airways, the UK-based operator which was acquired through the purchase of Synergy Aviation in July 2023. Having commenced commercial operations in April 2024, the airline announced on 28 April 2026 that it would surrender its UK AOC and cease flying.

Ascend cited rising fuel costs, reduced aircraft availability and reliability problems affecting its CFM LEAP-1B engines.

It also highlighted the disadvantages of operating under a UK AOC, including higher costs and restrictions on reciprocal wet-leasing arrangements with European Union operators. Its six Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft were subsequently earmarked for return to lessors.

Together, these closures demonstrate the challenges facing the group’s airline businesses, particularly in the competitive and capital-intensive ACMI market.

What happens to the ASG Boeing 737 MAX order?

The latest developments also raise questions about Avia Solutions Group’s ambitious Boeing fleet expansion plans.

In November 2024, the group announced its first direct order with Boeing, comprising 40 firm Boeing 737-8 MAX aircraft, alongside purchase rights for another 40.

Deliveries are scheduled to begin in 2030. The agreement was announced as part of a strategy to expand capacity and meet growing demand from airlines seeking seasonal ACMI services.

The order was placed at group level rather than specifically for AirExplore or any individual subsidiary. Boeing’s announcement stated that the aircraft would enhance the fleets of Avia Solutions Group’s airlines, without identifying individual operators or allocating specific delivery numbers.

The closure of AirExplore, SmartLynx, SmartLynx Australia, and Ascend Airways therefore does not automatically mean the Boeing order will be cancelled.

However, the disappearance of several operating platforms raises questions about which remaining subsidiaries will ultimately receive the aircraft and how the group intends to deploy them.

With Avion Express, KlasJet and its international BBN Airlines operations continuing to provide ACMI and charter capacity, Avia Solutions Group still has established businesses through which it can pursue its expansion strategy.

In the meantime, the 737 MAX order remains a group-level commitment, with deliveries still several years away. Whether the group maintains its original expansion ambitions following this latest airline closure remains to be seen.

]]> NASA tests glowing paint to help design the next generation of flexible wings https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/nasa-tests-pressure-sensitive-paint-moving-wing/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 15:08:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56350 NASA has tested glowing unsteady pressure-sensitive paint on a moving aircraft wing model in a low-oxygen wind tunnel to measure real-time aerodynamic forces.

The post NASA tests glowing paint to help design the next generation of flexible wings appeared first on AGN.

]]> NASA has successfully tested a pressure-sensitive paint on a large, freely moving aircraft wing model for the first time in a low-oxygen wind tunnel, demonstrating a new way to measure the changing aerodynamic forces that can cause wings to bend and vibrate during flight.

The experiment, conducted at NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia, used a specialised coating that glows pink-purple under ultraviolet light. High-speed cameras recorded changes in the paint’s brightness as air flowed across the wing, allowing researchers to measure how pressure varied over its surface.

NASA announced the milestone on 2 October, saying the results could support future tests of flexible wings designed to bend and adapt during flight. Such designs are being studied as a means of improving aircraft efficiency, but engineers must understand how the movement of a wing interacts with the air flowing around it.

The latest experiment builds on several years of work by NASA to improve pressure-sensitive paint technology. It also follows separate research reported by Aerospace Global News in September, when scientists at the University of Manchester developed a formulation that reduced temperature-related errors in aerodynamic measurements.

How NASA’s glowing paint measures airflow

The Langley experiment used a standard research model known as the Benchmark Supercritical Wing inside NASA’s Transonic Dynamics Tunnel. The model is not a replica of a particular aircraft. Instead, it provides a common test subject that engineers can use to compare wind tunnel measurements with computer predictions.

The paint contains light-sensitive materials whose brightness changes in response to pressure. When the coated wing is illuminated, cameras capture those changes, and computer processing converts the images into measurements showing how aerodynamic pressure varies across the surface.

Traditional wind tunnel experiments often use small holes drilled into a model, connected to pressure sensors through tubes. These instruments provide accurate readings at selected points, but engineers must estimate what is happening between them.

Pressure-sensitive paint provides measurements across the coated area, revealing pressure patterns that individual sensors might miss.

NASA has used conventional pressure-sensitive paint for more than a decade. Its newer technique, called unsteady pressure-sensitive paint, or uPSP, can also capture rapid changes in pressure caused by turbulent airflow and other disturbances.

These fluctuations are important because air does not always pass smoothly over an aircraft. Changes in airflow can produce uneven forces, vibrations and movements that affect how the structure behaves.

The latest test was particularly demanding because the wing model was free to move rather than being held completely rigid, and the experiment took place in a low-oxygen environment.

NASA said this was the first time the technique had been demonstrated under that combination of conditions on a large-scale model.

Why moving wings matter

An aircraft wing must withstand changing forces throughout a flight. As it moves through the air, pressure differences generate lift, while turbulence and other disturbances can cause the structure to flex or vibrate.

Engineers refer to the interaction between aerodynamic forces and structural movement as aeroelasticity. Understanding it is particularly important when developing lightweight wings that may bend more than those on conventional aircraft.

If aerodynamic forces and structural movement reinforce each other under certain conditions, the resulting vibrations can become dangerous. Aircraft designers therefore need reliable measurements to predict how a wing will respond across its operating conditions.

NASA’s new experiment allows researchers to collect detailed pressure information while the test model is moving. The data can then be compared with computer simulations used to predict aerodynamic loads and structural behaviour.

The agency said the demonstration would help prepare for experiments involving flexible aircraft models intended to change shape during flight.

NASA makes wind tunnel data available much faster

The latest achievement follows a major improvement in NASA’s ability to collect and process pressure-sensitive paint measurements.

In July 2025, the agency reported that advances in high-speed cameras, more sensitive coatings and supercomputing had made its measurement process approximately 10,000 times faster, while producing engineering visualisations with 1,000 times greater resolution.

NASA said some datasets could be processed in as little as 20 minutes, allowing engineers to review the results and adjust their experiments while a wind tunnel test was still underway.

Previously, analysing measurements could take days or weeks. If researchers discovered that additional information was needed, arranging another wind tunnel session could introduce further delays.

“The result of these improvements provides a data product that is immediately useful to aerodynamic engineers, structural engineers, or engineers from other disciplines,” said E. Lara Lash, an aerospace engineer at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California.

The improvements emerged from a five-year NASA research effort that began in 2019 and concluded at the end of 2024. Much of the work was carried out at Ames, where researchers connected an 11-foot transonic wind tunnel to the NASA Advanced Supercomputing Facility.

A scale model of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket was used during the development programme. The agency has also used pressure-sensitive paint in earlier tests involving aircraft wing models.

Lash said the technology could help engineers identify structural problems that might otherwise be difficult to predict.

“Aerodynamic forces can vibrate different parts of the vehicle to different degrees,” she explained. “Vibrations could damage what the vehicle is carrying or can even lead to the vehicle tearing itself apart. The data we get through this process can help us prevent that.”

From research models to future aircraft

NASA is developing the technology for use in aircraft and spacecraft testing, with the longer-term aim of making the improved capability available across its wind tunnel facilities.

The agency has also indicated that researchers from industry, universities and other government organisations could use the system.

Robert Pearce, NASA’s associate administrator for aeronautics, who recently saw a demonstration of uPSP-generated data displayed at Ames, hailed the new tool as a national asset that will be available to researchers all over the country.

“It’s a unique NASA innovation that isn’t offered anywhere else,” Pearce said. “It will help us maintain NASA’s world leadership in wind tunnel capabilities.”

Here’s what you get https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/frontier-first-class-bookings-march-2027/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 14:11:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56392 The ultra-low-cost carrier's new first class cabin debuts on 5 March 2027, with introductory fares from $129 and Starlink WiFi set to follow.

The post Frontier is selling first class seats for the first time. Here’s what you get appeared first on AGN.

]]> Frontier Airlines has opened bookings for its new first class seats, which will be available on flights beginning 5 March 2027. The US low-cost carrier is expanding its premium seating and preparing to introduce in-seat power and Starlink WiFi.

The airline announced that installation of its first class and additional extra-legroom seats has begun. It expects to complete installation by the March launch date. USB-C power and Starlink connectivity will follow a separate rollout during 2027.

The new first class gives Frontier more cabin products to sell alongside its low fares. Its first class offers more seating space and baggage allowances, but food and drinks remain available for purchase.

Eight first class seats at the front

The first two rows will have a 2-2 layout, creating eight first class seats without middle seats. 

Frontier says first class offers up to 37” of seat pitch. While wider and offering more legroom, the seats are pre-reclined, which means they don’t recline further. 

Behind first class, rows three through eight will offer Premium extra-legroom seating with up to 34” pitch. Selected rows will also offer UpFront Plus, which guarantees an empty adjacent middle seat.

That leaves Frontier with three different ways to sell additional personal space: a wider 2-2 seat in first class, extra-legroom rows and a blocked middle seat.

“We’re transforming what customers can expect when they fly Frontier,” said Bobby Schroeter, the airline’s chief marketing officer. “First Class seating, more room to stretch out, in-seat power and fast, reliable Starlink WiFi will bring a new level of comfort and convenience to flying with us. We’re continuing to deliver the great value our customers count on, combining more comfort and choice with Frontier’s low fares.”

Introductory bundles start at $129

Frontier is advertising introductory First bundles from $129 one way, including a first class seat, two checked bags, a carry-on bag and Board First priority boarding.

Premium bundles start at $90 one way and include an extra-legroom seat, a carry-on bag and priority boarding. The Premium offer does not include the two checked bags included in the First bundle.

The promotional prices are subject to availability and apply to new bookings made through Frontier’s website or app by 23:59 Eastern time on 16 November 2026. 

They cover selected nonstop domestic flights between 5 March and 5 April 2027. Customers must buy the flight and bundle together to qualify. 

Power and Starlink follow in 2027

Frontier has also announced it will install USB-C power at every seat in the first eight rows. Work to add power outlets will begin in 2027 and progress throughout the year, alongside the rollout of Starlink WiFi.

As AGN reported in July, Frontier initially planned to introduce its first Starlink-equipped aircraft in early 2027. 

“Together, these enhancements will give customers more ways to relax, stay productive, and enjoy their time onboard – with the same low fares they expect from Frontier,” Schroeter said.

The separate installation schedules mean passengers booking the new seats for March may not find charging or connectivity on their aircraft.

]]> Watch: Real-life Iron Man flies jet-powered suit at NASA’s Kennedy Space Centre https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/gravity-jet-suit-nasa-max-power-expo/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 13:13:59 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56396 Gravity Industries founder Richard Browning demonstrated his turbine-powered jet suit at NASA's MAX POWER Expo at Kennedy Space Center, Florida.

The post Watch: Real-life Iron Man flies jet-powered suit at NASA’s Kennedy Space Centre appeared first on AGN.

]]> A turbine-powered jet suit developed by UK company Gravity Industries was demonstrated at NASA’s MAX POWER aerospace expo in Florida on 7 November. The NASA event showcased aircraft, spacecraft and new transport systems.

Footage from the demonstrations shows Gravity Industries founder and chief executive Richard Browning lifting off the ground at Kennedy Space Centre in the company’s latest jet suit.

Pretty cool things at @NASA today! @takeonGravity @capeweek_us https://t.co/pns6AGy1VV

— Collin Craig (@CollinCraigAI) November 7, 2026

The display gave visitors a close-up look at one of the world’s most advanced examples of personal flight technology, a concept Gravity has been developing for almost a decade.

How does Gravity’s jet suit fly?

Gravity’s system uses small gas turbines to generate thrust, with engines carried on the arms and back. It allows a pilot to leave the ground without the wings or rotor system of a conventional aircraft.

Jetpack Dude from @takeonGravity going ham at Up.Summit today. @UPSummitVC https://t.co/sG1Lez9uCv

— GoatGains (@TheGoatGains) November 8, 2026

The company’s current technology description says its latest Mk4 suits combine arm-mounted microjet engines with three additional turbines on the back. 

Gravity says it uses polymer, aluminium and titanium 3D-printing processes to manufacture its latest suits. 

Reporting on Gravity’s work with manufacturing specialist EOS in 2018 described printed cable guides, electronics and battery housings, arm brackets and thrust-control components. The collaboration reduced the number of parts in an assembly from eight to three, simplifying assembly.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Gravity Industries (@takeongravity)

Gravity dates its first prototypes to March 2016 and Browning’s first off-ground flight to November that year. The company launched publicly in April 2017.

Who is Richard Browning?

Richard Browning is the founder and chief executive of UK-based Gravity Industries, a company known for developing turbine-powered personal flight systems.

Browning first achieved sustained jet suit flight in 2016 and publicly launched Gravity Industries in 2017. His demonstrations have attracted global attention and earned comparisons with the fictional Iron Man suit.

How fast can the Gravity jet suit fly?

Gravity Industries has previously reported speeds in excess of 80mph during testing. The wearable aviation technology combines multiple micro gas turbines to provide lift and directional control, with movement controlled largely through the pilot’s arm position and body balance.

From public displays to rescue trials

The potential applications extend beyond eye-catching demonstrations at events. Gravity markets its technology for medical response, maritime operations and access to difficult terrain, aiming to move an individual quickly past obstacles.

The Great North Air Ambulance Service explored jet suit paramedic response in the Lake District. In 2022, it announced work with Gravity and offshore wind developer Ørsted to trial jet suit paramedics for the wind industry.

The Royal Navy also documented a 2021 trial involving HMS Tamar and Royal Marines from 42 and 47 Commando. Gravity personnel operated the equipment throughout the exercises.

At the time, trial sponsor Lieutenant Colonel Will Clarke said: “Whilst the technology may not be ready for military adoption just now, it shows significant promise”.

Aerospace technology on show at Kennedy

NASA’s MAX POWER event brought together air shows, technology displays and space exhibits at Kennedy Space Centre on 7–8 November. 

The programme included NASA and external partners, with aircraft, rovers and autonomous vehicles among the technologies displayed. AGN also reported on NASA’s X-70 Fractal announcement at UP.Summit at Kennedy that week.

For Gravity, which also markets its jet suit for various brand-building and corporate events, the expo provided another venue to demonstrate personal turbine-powered flight.

]]> Pentagon cannot account for $85m in F-35 parts, new report finds https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/f35-parts-accounting-failures/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 12:59:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56343 Why the watchdog says the US needs a new systems to better track F-35 parts to reduce risks including theft, fraud, and negligence.

The post Pentagon cannot account for $85m in F-35 parts, new report finds appeared first on AGN.

]]> The government watchdog has once again shone a spotlight on deficiencies in tracking the vast, geographically dispersed US-stockpiled F-35 components. At least $85 million of parts remain lost, with the true tally unknowable under the current system.

These lost components are not necessarily stolen. Many may be secure but misplaced in warehouses; others may be double-counted; some may have been scrapped without proper records. By virtue of being unaccounted for, it is impossible to know.

$85 million in F-35 components remains lost

A new Government Accountability Office (GAO) report published this week finds that the US DoD is struggling to account for the parts of the F-35 programme. It says the records of the F-35 parts are “outdated, inaccurate, and incomplete.”

As of March 2026, the F-35 Joint Program Office (JPO) still did not know the status of lost F-35 parts worth over $85 million. These parts were highlighted by the GAO in a 2023 report.

For context, $85 million is comparable to the flyaway cost of a new F-35A.

Without implementing procedures for monitoring losses, the JPO will not be able to know the full extent of lost F-35 components. This risks reducing its ability to mitigate concerns such as waste, theft, and fraud.

Earlier this year, a UPS freighter carrying some Australian F-35 components, including a canopy, was diverted to Hong Kong, where the parts disappeared. This would appear to be stemming from a separate set of issues than the GAO is highlighting with the JPO.

JPO needs a new management system for tracking F-35 parts

The watchdog found that the DoD is not maintaining complete records of some government-owned 26 million parts. These are valued at around $31 billion and held by over 700 contractor- and government-managed facilities around the world.

A warning is: “Without accurate data in its APSR and properly executed inventory procedures for F-35 parts, DOD management will not have the information it needs to support warfighter readiness and reliable financial reporting.”

A mature, fully functioning property accountability programme needs to be established by the JPO to ensure its oversight of asset accountability.

The GAO does acknowledge that the DoD is taking some steps, including F-35 parts on its financial statements and developing procedures to value parts with missing cost information.

US Air Force reverse-engineers and 3D prints F-35 parts to beat supplier delays US Air Force reverse-engineers and 3D prints F-35 parts to beat supplier delays

Far from unique among fighter jets

It should be stressed that the F-35 is far from unique when it comes to missing parts, or other headline-grabbing issues like delays and cost overruns.

As the world’s premier fighter programme and one expected to cost the DoD more than $1.9 trillion over its life cycle, the effort attracts an extraordinary amount of popular attention and reporting.

One area where the programme is reasonably unique is in its vast scale and its massive geographical footprint. The DoD has to station and maintain its fleet in numerous bases and aircraft carriers around the world.

Discussion of F-35 issues is partially enabled by the considerable openness in the programme, with the type of information contained in the GAO report likely classified for equivalent programmes in countries like China and Russia.

Components almost certainly get lost for programmes like the Eurofighter, Rafale, Gripen, and others, but the data is lacking, which frustrates any meaningful comparison.

]]> Cathay orders 14 more Airbus jets as fleet investment tops $19 billion https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/cathay-group-order-14-airbus-aircraft/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 11:26:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56369 The additional aircraft form part of a wider investment programme that will see Cathay spend more than HK$150 billion between 2026 and 2035.

The post Cathay orders 14 more Airbus jets as fleet investment tops $19 billion appeared first on AGN.

]]> Hong Kong’s Cathay Group has placed a further order for 14 Airbus aircraft, strengthening its commitment to fleet modernisation and expansion as it looks to increase capacity across its regional and short-haul networks.

Announced on 11 November, the latest firm order includes 11 Airbus A330-900s and three A321neos. The deal brings Cathay’s total firm orders for the A330-900 to 41 aircraft and adds to its existing commitment for 32 A320neo Family aircraft, including the A321neo, announced in 2023.

The additional aircraft form part of a wider investment programme that will see Cathay spend more than HK$150 billion (approximately US$19 billion) between 2026 and 2035, supporting its ambition to strengthen Hong Kong’s position as a leading international aviation hub.

Cathay’s A330neo order grows to 41 aircraft

The largest element of the latest agreement is the purchase of 11 additional Airbus A330-900 widebody aircraft, bringing Cathay Group’s total firm commitment for the type to 41.

The airline originally ordered 30 A330-900s in 2024, with the latest aircraft building on that agreement. The additional 11 aircraft are expected to be delivered between 2031 and 2035, although Cathay and Airbus have not announced a specific entry-into-service date for the individual aircraft.

The A330-900 will play an important role in Cathay Pacific’s regional fleet, providing additional passenger and cargo capacity across its extensive Asia-Pacific network.

The aircraft will also give the airline greater flexibility to operate longer routes as demand and network requirements evolve.

The new aircraft are expected to contribute to the gradual renewal of Cathay Pacific’s existing A330 widebody fleet, while supporting further growth from its Hong Kong hub.

Powered by Rolls-Royce Trent 7000 engines, the A330-900 offers a range of up to 8,100 nautical miles (15,000 kilometres).

Airbus says the aircraft can deliver a 25% reduction in fuel consumption, CO₂ emissions and operating costs compared with previous-generation competitor aircraft, such as the Boeing 777.

The type also features Airbus’ Airspace cabin, designed to improve the passenger experience through a more modern interior and enhanced comfort.

A321neo aircraft destined for HK Express

The remaining three aircraft in the agreement are Airbus A321neos, which will be operated by Cathay Group’s low-cost subsidiary, HK Express.

The additional purchase builds on the Group’s 2023 commitment for 32 A320neo Family aircraft, comprising a combination of A320neos and A321neos.

The latest announcement does not specify the breakdown of the original 32-aircraft order, so the Group’s total A321neo order cannot be established from the published figures alone.

Unlike the A330-900s, which will primarily support Cathay Pacific, the additional A321neos will help HK Express expand its network, particularly to destinations in mainland China and other short-haul markets.

The aircraft’s single-aisle configuration makes it well suited to the airline’s low-cost operating model, allowing it to increase capacity on popular regional routes while benefiting from improved fuel efficiency.

Airbus has not disclosed a delivery schedule or specific entry-into-service date for the three additional A321neos. Their introduction will form part of Cathay Group’s wider programme of aircraft deliveries from 2026 onwards.

The A321neo is the largest member of the A320neo Family and offers improved range, efficiency and passenger capacity compared with previous-generation aircraft.

According to Airbus, the A320neo Family delivers at least 20% fuel savings and CO₂ emissions reductions compared with its predecessor generation.

Cathay Group targets 150 new aircraft deliveries

The latest Airbus order is part of a much wider fleet investment programme at Cathay Group, which is seeking to expand its operations while improving the efficiency of its aircraft fleet.

Following the announcement, the Group’s planned aircraft deliveries from 2026 onwards have increased to 120. Its longer-term ambition is to take delivery of 150 new aircraft over the next decade and expand its network to serve 150 destinations, subject to favourable market conditions.

The investment programme extends beyond Airbus passenger aircraft. Cathay’s future fleet additions will also include Boeing 777-9 long-haul aircraft, alongside Airbus A350F and A330 freighters for its cargo operations.

Cathay Group Chief Executive Officer Ronald Lam said the latest orders would strengthen the airline’s fleet and improve connectivity through its Hong Kong hub.

He added that the Group’s total committed investment between 2026 and 2035 has now exceeded HK$150 billion, underlining its confidence in the long-term prospects of Hong Kong’s aviation sector.

The investment is also intended to support the city’s position as an international connecting hub, with Cathay looking to increase capacity and improve its competitiveness across the Asia-Pacific region and beyond.

A significant commitment to Airbus

The latest agreement reinforces Cathay Group’s relationship with Airbus and highlights the importance of both the A330neo and A320neo families to its future fleet strategy.

With 41 A330-900s now on firm order and three additional A321neos joining its existing A320neo Family commitments, Cathay is making a substantial investment in next-generation aircraft.

For Airbus, the deal represents another significant endorsement of its latest-generation aircraft, while for Cathay it provides the capacity and operational flexibility needed to support its ambitions over the coming decade.

]]> Boeing’s bumper October orders overshadowed by falling 737 MAX deliveries https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/boeing-aircraft-deliveries-down-october-2026/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 10:50:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56364 The decline highlights the continuing difficulties facing the US manufacturer as it attempts to stabilise production and increase manufacturing rates.

The post Boeing’s bumper October orders overshadowed by falling 737 MAX deliveries appeared first on AGN.

]]> Boeing has recorded a 14% month-on-month decline in aircraft deliveries in October, handing over 49 aircraft compared with 57 in September. The figure was also lower than the 53 aircraft delivered during October 2025.

The decline comes amid continuing difficulties for the US aerospace manufacturer as it attempts to stabilise production, increase manufacturing rates and rebuild confidence following years of operational and production-related challenges.

As reported by Reuters, despite the weaker delivery performance, Boeing achieved a significant milestone on the orders front, recording its strongest October for net orders (new orders minus cancellations) since 1997. The company secured 165 new aircraft orders during the month and reported no cancellations.

Avolon order provides major boost to Boeing

The majority of Boeing’s October orders came from aircraft leasing company Avolon. As reported by Aerospace Global News, on 4 November, Avolon placed an order for 140 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft, accounting for most of the month’s new business.

Of the 165 orders recorded in October, 140 were Boeing 737 MAX aircraft ordered by Avolon, six were 737 MAX aircraft ordered by Allegiant Air, plus four additional 737 MAX orders coming from unidentified customers. The remaining 15 orders were for Boeing 787 Dreamliners, with the customers not publicly identified.

The order performance provides an encouraging sign of continued demand for Boeing aircraft, even as the manufacturer faces difficulties converting its production capacity into aircraft deliveries.

737 MAX deliveries fall as production challenges continue

The Boeing 737 MAX remained the company’s largest contributor to October deliveries, although handovers declined significantly. Boeing delivered 32 737 MAX aircraft during the month, compared with 43 in September.

The reduction comes as the manufacturer continues to experience difficulties increasing production of its best-selling single-aisle aircraft. Chief Executive Kelly Ortberg told investors in October that Boeing would fall short of its target of delivering approximately 500 737 aircraft during 2026.

The company is working towards a production rate of 47 aircraft per month; a milestone Ortberg now expects Boeing to reach in early 2027.

One of the principal obstacles remains the production of aircraft wings, with Boeing struggling to manufacture them quickly enough to support its planned increase in 737 output.

In addition to the 32 737 MAX aircraft, Boeing’s October deliveries included 11 787 Dreamliners, two 777 Freighters, and three 767s. One of the three 767 aircraft was delivered for Boeing Defence’s KC-46 aerial refuelling tanker programme.

Supplier dispute creates further production issues

Boeing is also dealing with supply-chain difficulties affecting its wide-body aircraft programmes. While wing production remains a bottleneck for the 737 MAX, a dispute with a supplier has brought wing production for the 777 freighter and 767 programmes to a halt.

These difficulties threaten to complicate Boeing’s efforts to increase aircraft output across several production lines. Resolving supplier-related problems and improving manufacturing consistency will be important if the company is to meet its longer-term production ambitions.

Boeing remains behind Airbus in annual deliveries

Despite its October slowdown, Boeing’s cumulative delivery performance for 2026 remains ahead of last year’s level. By the end of October, Boeing had delivered 524 aircraft, about 6% more than the 493 delivered in the same period in 2025.

However, the company continues to trail its European competitor, Airbus. Airbus delivered 621 aircraft during the first ten months of 2026, giving it a lead of 97 aircraft over Boeing.

The comparison highlights the challenge Boeing faces in closing the delivery gap with Airbus, despite its improvement against the previous year’s figures.

Boeing’s wider recovery programme

Boeing’s October delivery figures come against the backdrop of a concerted effort to restore manufacturing stability and improve production performance.

The 737 MAX programme is particularly important because it is central to the company’s commercial aircraft business and its financial recovery.

The delayed move towards producing 47 aircraft monthly illustrates the difficulties Boeing continues to face in bringing together its manufacturing operations and supplier network.

The company’s recent workforce plans also underline the pressure to align staffing levels with actual production requirements.

Reuters separately reported on November 10 that Boeing planned to reduce employment in its commercial aircraft division by approximately 5%, reflecting slower-than-expected production increases.

The combination of production delays, supplier difficulties and workforce adjustments suggests that Boeing’s recovery remains a work in progress.

Strong orders but deliveries remain the key challenge

Boeing’s October performance presents two contrasting pictures. On the one hand, the manufacturer secured 165 new aircraft orders without a single cancellation, its strongest October net-order performance since 1997.

The Avolon order for 140 737 MAX aircraft provided a particularly significant boost to its order book.

On the other hand, the 14% monthly decline in deliveries demonstrates that strong customer demand does not automatically translate into higher aircraft handovers.

Boeing must now address its wing-production bottlenecks, resolve supplier disputes and achieve more consistent manufacturing output.

Its target of reaching 47 737 aircraft per month in early 2027 will be an important test of whether the company can turn its substantial order backlog into sustained delivery growth.

In the meantime, Boeing’s order performance is encouraging, but its ability to increase production and close the delivery gap with Airbus remains the bigger challenge.

]]> KLM and British Airways report highest SAF shares as study exposes reporting gaps https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/airlines-using-most-saf-2026-study/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 10:14:24 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56359 A new comparison of 30 airlines' climate reports reveals which carriers are using the highest shares of sustainable aviation fuel. KLM Group and British Airways lead.

The post KLM and British Airways report highest SAF shares as study exposes reporting gaps appeared first on AGN.

]]> KLM Group (including KLM Cityhopper, Martinair and Transavia) and British Airways reported the highest sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) shares in a new comparison of 30 airlines. British Airways’ parent company, IAG, reported the largest voluntary SAF volume.

The C Level study found that SAF accounted for 4.6% of KLM’s fuel consumption in 2025, compared with 4.5% for British Airways. 

IAG, which owns British Airways, Iberia, Aer Lingus and other airlines, reported approximately 175,000 tonnes of voluntary SAF in 2025, up from about 156,000 tonnes in 2024. That represented around 60% of its total reported SAF use of 291,100 tonnes.

The study reveals significant differences in how airlines report SAF purchases, particularly whether fuel was required by law, purchased voluntarily or financed through customer contributions.

SAF shares reported by airlines

KLM Group and British Airways reported the highest SAF shares. IAG separately reported a 3.3% share across its airline portfolio, including British Airways. The remaining published figures in C Level’s comparison were below 2%.

Which airlines reported the highest SAF share?

Selected figures from C Level’s November 2026 airline comparison, primarily based on 2025 disclosures. Approximate and group-wide figures are identified.

Airline / group SAF share of fuel Key finding
KLM Group 4.6% Highest reported SAF share in the comparison.
British Airways 4.5% Second-highest reported SAF share.
IAG (group-wide) 3.3% Group figure; not specific to Iberia or Aer Lingus.
SAS 1.73% SAF growth reflected customer purchases and legal requirements.
Air France 1.71% About three-quarters of SAF was legally required.
Finnair About 1.6% Discloses mandated and voluntary SAF separately.
Lufthansa Group About 1.5% Group-wide figure, not Lufthansa Airlines alone.
Air Canada About 1.5% C Level calculation; SAF funding was not fully disclosed.
TAP Air Portugal About 1.28% A ticket surcharge helps fund legally required SAF.
Qantas 1.1% Carbon-credit activity includes regulatory and customer programmes.
Virgin Atlantic About 1% Its 2025 SAF use matched UK legal requirements.
SWISS 0.9% Customers funded all voluntary SAF, according to C Level.
United Airlines About 0.7% Customers and public incentives funded some SAF.
Cathay Pacific 0.68% SAF grew; customers paid for much of its carbon credits.
American Airlines 0.33% SAF use rose without a US federal blending mandate.
Singapore Airlines About 0.09% C Level calculation; SAF remains a small fuel share.

Note: Figures cover 2025 consumption. They measure SAF as a share of fuel consumption, not absolute SAF volumes or overall environmental performance. Group-wide results overlap with some individual airline figures.

Source: C Level, Which airlines are greenest? (November 2026) .

IAG leads the study’s voluntary SAF comparison

Voluntary SAF is not necessarily financed entirely by airlines. IAG says corporate customers support part of its programme, including a Microsoft agreement announced in April 2025 to co-fund 39,000 tonnes over five years.

The agreement involves emissions-reduction certificates associated with the SAF, which Microsoft can use in accounting for business-travel emissions. Such arrangements complicate comparisons of airlines’ own spending.

C Level said it could not identify a single airline among the 30 that published a complete figure showing how much voluntary SAF it financed itself, after excluding dedicated contributions from corporate and individual customers.

Without a consistent split, it is not possible to rank carriers by how much of their own money they spend on additional SAF.

United and American increase SAF volumes in the US

The US does not have a federal SAF blending mandate equivalent to the EU and UK requirements.

United Airlines said it used approximately 27.7 million US gallons of SAF in 2025, up 104% from 13.6 million gallons in 2024. The airline said SAF represented only about 0.7% of its more than 4.1 billion gallons of annual jet fuel consumption.

United expanded SAF use to three additional hubs in 2025: Houston Intercontinental, Newark Liberty and Washington Dulles, bringing its SAF operations to six hubs.

American Airlines reported an increase from 2.91 million US gallons in 2024 to 14.07 million in 2025, according to C Level.

Mandates are changing the European numbers

The EU’s ReFuelEU Aviation regulation introduced a minimum 2% SAF share for fuel supplied at EU airports from 2025. The UK introduced its own 2% mandate that year.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) reported in September 2026 that fuel suppliers delivered approximately 1.1 million tonnes of SAF at EU airports in 2025. That’s equivalent to 2.8% of the 39.3 million tonnes of aviation fuel supplied.

EASA also found that approximately 80% of the SAF supplied was aviation biofuel, overwhelmingly produced from used cooking oil. Around 85% of feedstocks were imported, the agency said.

The regulation has changed what year-on-year airline comparisons mean. A carrier can report a large rise in SAF use because suppliers are legally required to blend more into the fuel it purchases, even if the airline has not increased its voluntary commitment.

C Level found Finnair used 16,360 tonnes of SAF in 2025, more than triple its 2024 figure of 4,685 tonnes. Of the 2025 amount, approximately 14,100 tonnes came through the mandate and 2,259 tonnes were voluntary, funded jointly by Finnair and its customers. The airline’s voluntary volume actually declined from 2,657 tonnes in 2024 despite the sharp increase in total SAF use.

Does using more SAF make an airline greener?

The study deliberately avoided producing a single overall ranking of the ‘greenest’ airlines because its measures are not interchangeable.

Wizz Air reported the lowest carbon emissions per passenger-kilometre among the 17 airlines C Level considered sufficiently comparable, at 50.6 grams of CO2. TUI Airways followed at 60.7 grams of CO2, although differences in methodology limit direct comparisons.

That does not mean Wizz Air used the most SAF. Low-cost and leisure carriers can achieve lower emissions per passenger because they operate relatively dense cabins and carry more passengers per unit of fuel.

The emissions figures also differ in how they treat flight distances, cargo and greenhouse gases, limiting precise comparisons.

Carbon credits are also distinct from SAF: paying for emissions reductions elsewhere does not replace the fossil fuel burned by an aircraft.

What the latest SAF figures tell us

The C Level findings show that SAF consumption is increasing, particularly where government mandates require its use. However, airlines’ disclosures make it difficult to establish how much additional SAF they purchase at their own expense.

Until airlines consistently separate mandated fuel, voluntary purchases and customer contributions, comparing their independent investments in SAF will remain difficult.

US Air Force explores new defences https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/usaf-f35-netting-tyndall-drone-protection/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:13:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56267 The US Air Force is looking for contractors to install anti-drone netting to help protect F-35 Joint Strike Fighters amid growing concerns over drone threats.

The post Could netting protect F-35s from drones? US Air Force explores new defences appeared first on AGN.

]]> The US Air Force is looking to protect its F-35A fighter jets at Tyndall Air Force Base in Florida with netting, according to reports.

Netting remains one of the most affordable, quickest, and reliable layers of protection for parked aircraft from small UAS threats.

The Air Force’s 325th Contracting Squadron at Tyndall has issued a request for information entitled “Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) Netting Installation for Aircraft Sunshade Structures.”

It explained that the USAF is conducting market research for the installation of netting on existing aircraft sunshade structures. The contract is particularly focused on small businesses.

The Air Force stated, “The Government is also interested in unique and innovative solutions, including any proof-of-concept or operational C-UAS netting installations already fielded or under evaluation at other Department of Defense installations.”

Protecting USAF’s F-35A stealth fighters

While a number of defence-tech companies are currently working on developing an array of effective counter-UAS solutions, one of the most effective solutions remains an old-fashioned net or other physical barrier.

In the procurement notice, the requirements are for a contractor to install counter-UAV netting on all four sides of six existing aircraft sunshade structures. Each structure is around 630 feet long, 65 feet wide, and 30 feet high.

The War Zone identifies that these shelters are designed to accommodate up to six F-35A stealth fighters at a time. Tyndall is a major hub for the United States Air Force’s F-35 operations and is located in Florida’s Panhandle.

The topic of netting over US fighter jets is not new. Plans have been floated to erect netting around sunshade-type shelters for F-22 Raptors stationed at Langley after mysterious late 2023 drone incursions.

Across the United States and Europe, there have been numerous reports of unexplained drones flying over air force bases and airports.

Realistically, these small drones likely present the biggest aerial threat to Allied parked aircraft in their mainland home bases in peacetime.

Notably, in 2026, saboteurs attempted to destroy Ukrainian Antonov An-124 Ruslan transports parked at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport. At least one explosive-laden drone is reported to have found its mark but failed to explode.

Drones or birds? The detection challenge behind NATO’s false alarm Drones or birds? The detection challenge behind NATO’s false alarm

An effective solution against small FPV-type drones

Netting may be ineffective against heavier one-way attack drones, missiles, and certain types of warheads, but they are very effective against many types of lower-end FPV-type drones.

The Air Force explicitly identifies the purpose as blocking Group 1 “small” drones from striking the aircraft.

— Thomas van Linge (@ThomasVLinge) September 10, 2026

Netting may have been enough to block Ukrainian FPV strikes on Russian bombers during Operation Spider Web.

More recently, opposition fighters in Myanmar (Burma) struck junta Yak-130 light combat aircraft in their hangars at Mandalay for the first time with small drones. The outcome was unclear, but released footage appears to show the drones struggling to bypass the protective netting.

In Ukraine, roads and entire neighbourhoods near the frontline are now often encased in netting.

]]> China highlights GJ-11 combat drone ahead of air force anniversary https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/china-gj11-stealth-drone-new-footage/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 16:03:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=56206 New images and state reporting reveals more of China's new higher-end stealth strike and loyal wingman drone that appears to be entering service.

The post China highlights GJ-11 combat drone ahead of air force anniversary appeared first on AGN.

]]> Chinese state media has released new images of its GJ-11 stealth combat drone, which publicly flew for the first time in a November 2025 PLAAF video. The GJ-11 is believed to have entered service.

The stealthy drone is a flying wing and is known in China as the Xuanlong, or Dark Dragon. It was first unveiled in China’s 2019 National Day military parade in Beijing

China’s CCTV unveils detailed pictures of its GJ-11 drone

The video of the drone appeared in a report by China’s CCTV state broadcaster in a countdown to tomorrow’s 77th anniversary of the PLA Air Force.

Images provide a good look at the drone, including its large internal weapon bay, which has been designed to carry relatively large missiles. The GJ-11 has a shielded jet nozzle, low-visibility coating, and a faceted optical window mounted beneath the nose.

According to reporting by the South China Morning Post, this appears similar to the electro-optical targeting system found on China’s leading J-20 fighter.

Like various US designs, including the upcoming Lockheed Martin Vectis, the GJ-11 has its air intake on top of its fuselage. It also bears a flattened tail section.

The state-run English-language outlet, Global Times, reported that CCTV also revealed: “Two post-95s drone operators Shi Xiaoran and Fu Ting, are among the first batch of female drone operators trained independently by the PLA Air Force.”

Role of the GJ-11 stealth combat drone

Chinese state TV characterized the GJ-11 as a pioneer and a pathfinder. Core future missions include ground strikes and serving as a loyal wingman drone for fighter jets.

A video shows it flying in formation with a J-20 stealth fighter and J-16D electronic warfare aircraft, although it is unclear if they are teaming.

China released a video a year ago showing it firing a live PL-15 air-to-air missile.

The CCTV report stated that the GJ-11, operating in coordination with another drone, “can serve as the eyes of crewed fighter jets, conducting forward reconnaissance to identify enemy air defence systems.”

It added, “They can also act as decoys to draw enemy fire and expose hostile positions, or even function as airborne weapons platforms, launching guided munitions under the direction of manned aircraft.”

Its internal weapons bay is capable of accommodating a variety of air-to-surface munitions. The design is reported to provide strong stealth and endurance, while also being able to carry out suppression of enemy air defence (SEAD) missions.

China’s B-2-sized stealth drones spotted at Malan test base in satellite imagery China’s B-2-sized stealth drones spotted at Malan test base in satellite imagery

The GJ-11’s development & naval variant

Cloud cover has been an issue for targeting. The state report featured operator Shi Xiaoran saying the GJ-11 almost failed to locate its target during its first live-fire test on account of thick cloud cover.

Circling back for another pass, the drone is reported to have targeted and hit the target. The CCTV did not elaborate on the circumstances.

China has shown for the first time how operators work the Gongji-11 (GJ-11) strike drone, which it describes as a “door-kicking tool” meant to break through enemy air defenses first. The drone is meant to destroy key targets and open the way for crewed aircraft. Operator Shi Xiaoran said a single combat sortie usually lasts more than six hours, and some operations can run for several days.

— Clash Report (@clashreport) November 9, 2026

China’s new stealth drone is believed to have been developed and tested at the PLA AF base in Malan, Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region.

It also has a carrier-based naval variant, the GJ-21. That drone is reported to have successfully carried out a take-off and landing operation on the PLAN’s Type 076 Sichuan amphibious assault ship last week.

.sie-field-hero{position: relative; 
 left: 50%;
 right: 50%;
 margin-left: -50vw;
 margin-right: -50vw;
 width: 100vw; 
 min-height: 480px;
 max-height: 560px;
 background-size: cover;
 background-position: center 40%;
 background-repeat: no-repeat; 
 background-color: #003B73;
 overflow: hidden;
 margin-bottom: 0;}
.sie-field-hero--no-image{background: linear-gradient(
 135deg,
 var(--field-color, #003B73) 0%,
 color-mix(in srgb, var(--field-color, #003B73) 65%, #000) 100%
 );}
.sie-field-hero__bg-img{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center 40%;
 z-index: 0;
 display: block;}
.sie-field-hero__overlay{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 1;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.90) 0%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.60) 38%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.25) 65%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.12) 100%
 );
 display: flex;
 align-items: flex-end;
 padding-bottom: 52px;}
.sie-field-hero__inner{width: 100%;
 max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-field-hero__label{display: block;
 font-size: 13px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}
.sie-field-category-badge{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 7px;
 padding: 6px 14px;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.18);
 border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.35);
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 12px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 20px;
 margin-bottom: 14px;
 backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-category-badge i{font-size: 11px;
 opacity: 0.9;}
.sie-field-hero__title{font-size: clamp(30px, 5vw, 54px);
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #ffffff;
 margin: 0 0 14px;
 line-height: 1.1;
 letter-spacing: -0.02em;
 max-width: auto;}
.sie-field-hero__tagline{font-size: clamp(15px, 2vw, 18px);
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 margin: 0 0 28px;
 max-width: auto;
 line-height: 1.55;
 font-weight: 400;}
.sie-field-hero__actions{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 12px;
 margin-top: 4px;}
.sie-field-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 8px;
 padding: 12px 24px;
 background: #1E56B0;
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 6px;
 text-decoration: none;
 transition: background 0.2s;
 white-space: nowrap;}
.sie-field-hero__cta:hover{background: #163e82;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary{background: transparent;
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);}
.sie-field-hero__cta--secondary:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border-color: #fff;}
.sie-field-body{max-width: 1200px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px 80px;}
.sie-field-highlights{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 0;
 background: #f0f4fb;
 border: 1px solid #d4e0f5;
 border-radius: 12px;
 margin: 32px 0 40px;
 overflow: hidden;}
.sie-field-intro-block{margin: 0 0 48px;}
.sie-field-intro-block p{font-size: 17px;
 line-height: 1.78;
 color: #374151;
 margin: 0;
 margin-top:40px;}
.sie-field-section{padding: 64px 0;
 border-bottom: 1px solid #E5E7EB;}
.sie-field-section:last-child{border-bottom: none;}
.sie-field-section-header{margin-bottom: 40px;}
.sie-field-section-header h2{font-size: 32px;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #003B73;
 margin: 0 0 8px;}
.sie-field-section-header p{font-size: 17px;
 color: #003B73;
 margin: 0;}
.sie-breadcrumb{padding: 16px 0 0;}
.sie-breadcrumb__list{display: flex; gap: 8px; list-style: none;
 margin: 0; padding: 0; font-size: 0.85rem; color: #6B7280;
 flex-wrap: wrap;}
.sie-breadcrumb__list li:not(:last-child)::after{content: '/'; margin-left: 8px;}

 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list > .program-card{width:auto;max-width:none;margin:0}
 /* The flow view (AI matching on) groups results into one .sie-flow__branch
 per country. Each branch carries max-width:560px inside a 798px rail, so
 two never fit and they stack — the "single strip". Releasing the cap and
 tiling the branches gives two country panels per row at this width, and
 more on a wider screen, without touching the cards inside.
 ⚠️ Scoped to .lh-herosearch: Leonardo renders the same flow markup. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branches{display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(360px,1fr));gap:18px;align-items:start}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branch{max-width:none;width:100%}
 /* ── The figures strip ────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Serif numerals, monospaced labels, hairline rules, no card, no shadow,
 no colour fill behind each figure. The register of a register. */
 .lh-stats.lh-stats--figures{background:#F4F2ED;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-bottom:1px solid #E4E0D8;padding:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stats-grid{max-width:1200px;margin:0 auto;padding:0 clamp(16px,4vw,48px);display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(4,minmax(0,1fr));gap:0}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat{padding:clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) clamp(14px,2vw,28px) clamp(20px,2.4vw,32px) 0;border-right:1px solid #E4E0D8;text-align:left;background:none;border-radius:0;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat:last-child{border-right:0}
 /* Every cell except the first gets inner space on its left, so each rule
 sits with equal air on both sides instead of crowding the next figure.
 The first keeps padding-left:0 so its numeral lines up with the margin
 the hero headline uses. */
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat + .lh-stat{padding-left:clamp(18px,2.4vw,34px)}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat-num{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-size:clamp(27px,2.9vw,40px);font-weight:600;letter-spacing:-.5px;line-height:1.05;color:#12233D;background:none;-webkit-text-fill-color:currentColor}
 /* #6B7A8D measured 3.92:1 against the warm band — under the 4.5:1 that
 11.5px text needs. The cool grey was fine on the old cold background and
 quietly failed when the palette warmed up; #4F5967 measures 6.2:1.
 Worth remembering when warming any other background. */
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat-label{margin-top:8px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.3px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#4F5967}
 @media(max-width:700px){
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stats-grid{grid-template-columns:repeat(2,minmax(0,1fr))}
 .lh-stats--figures .lh-stat:nth-child(2){border-right:0}
 }
 /* Monogram instead of a repeated building glyph. Hairline tile, serif
 letters — it reads as a placeholder somebody chose, not as missing data. */
 .lh-uni-logo-placeholder{display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;background:#F4F2ED;border:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-radius:5px;color:#8A8578}
 .lh-uni-monogram{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-size:22px;font-weight:600;letter-spacing:1px;color:#12233D}
 /* ── For institutions ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
 The one full navy band on the page. It is dark on purpose: it marks a
 change of audience, so a student scrolling past knows at a glance that
 this part is not addressed to them. */
 .lh-inst{background:#12233D;color:#fff}
 .lh-inst-wrap *,.lh-inst-wrap *::before,.lh-inst-wrap *::after{box-sizing:border-box}
 .lh-inst-inner{max-width:1200px;margin:0 auto;padding:clamp(48px,6vw,88px) clamp(16px,4vw,48px);display:grid;grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1.35fr) minmax(0,1fr);gap:clamp(28px,4vw,64px);align-items:start}
 .lh-inst-badge{margin:0 0 16px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;letter-spacing:1.8px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#D7A83F}
 .lh-inst-h{margin:0 0 16px;font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-size:clamp(26px,3.1vw,40px);line-height:1.16;font-weight:600;letter-spacing:-.5px;color:#fff;max-width:20ch}
 .lh-inst-body{margin:0 0 26px;font-size:clamp(15.5px,1.4vw,17px);line-height:1.65;color:#C6D2E0;max-width:54ch}
 .lh-inst-actions{margin:0;display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:12px}
 .lh-inst-btn{display:inline-block;text-decoration:none;background:#fff;color:#12233D;font-size:15.5px;font-weight:600;padding:14px 26px;border:1px solid #fff;border-radius:4px;min-height:44px}
 .lh-inst-btn:hover{background:#F4F2ED;color:#12233D}
 .lh-inst-btn--ghost{background:none;color:#fff;border-color:#44597A;font-weight:500}
 .lh-inst-btn--ghost:hover{background:none;color:#fff;border-color:#D7A83F}
 .lh-inst-terms{margin:0;padding:0;list-style:none}
 .lh-inst-terms li{border-top:1px solid #28405F;padding:20px 0}
 .lh-inst-terms li:first-child{border-top:0;padding-top:0}
 .lh-inst-k{margin:0 0 6px;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:19px;color:#D7A83F}
 .lh-inst-v{margin:0;font-size:15px;line-height:1.6;color:#C6D2E0}
 @media(max-width:860px){
 .lh-inst-inner{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 }
 @media(max-width:900px){
 .lh-hero .lh-portals--search{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-res-list{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 .lh-herosearch .sie-flow__branches{grid-template-columns:1fr}
 .lh-heroalt{flex-direction:row;flex-wrap:wrap}
 .lh-heroalt-card{flex:1 1 220px}
 .lh-hero-scrim{background:linear-gradient(180deg,rgba(250,248,244,.97) 0%,rgba(250,248,244,.93) 62%,rgba(250,248,244,.72) 100%)}
 }
 /* ── Institutional pass, part 2 (2026-11-08, evening) ──────────────────
 Brings the sections below the hero onto the palette and type the hero
 already uses, so the page reads as one document instead of two designs
 stacked on top of each other. Everything here is homepage-only (it lives
 in this template) and is pure CSS: delete this block to revert. */
 /* The page itself: the site-wide body is cold pale blue (#E8F1FA), which
 showed through every transparent section (the institutions carousel and
 the study fields block) as a blue band between warm ones. */
 body.page-id-150{background:#FAF8F4}
 /* ⚠️ THE HEADLINE NEVER WAS SERIF. leonardo-homepage-css.min.css carries
 `.lh-wrap .lh-title{font-family:system-ui !important; font-size:44px
 !important; font-weight:800 !important; color:#003b73 !important}`, so
 the Source Serif rule earlier in this block lost on every device. Only
 !important with equal-or-higher specificity can beat it. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title,.lh-wrap .lh-hero h2.lh-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:clamp(34px,4.4vw,58px) !important;line-height:1.08 !important;letter-spacing:-.6px !important;color:#12233D !important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D !important}
 /* The accent word: italic navy reads editorial; bright orange read promo. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-gradient-text{color:#12233D;-webkit-text-fill-color:#12233D;font-style:italic;font-weight:600}
 /* One label above the headline is enough. The H1 eyebrow ("STUDY IN
 EUROPE") already does that job; the extra pill only added noise. */
 .lh-hero .lh-badge{display:none}
 /* Phones: the hero had no side gutter, so the eyebrow sat flush against
 the screen edge while the centred text did not. Left-aligned, with the
 same 20px gutter as the rest of the page, it matches the desktop. */
 @media(max-width:900px){
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-center{padding-left:20px;padding-right:20px;box-sizing:border-box;text-align:left}
 .lh-hero .lh-hero-text,.lh-hero .lh-subtitle{text-align:left}
 .lh-wrap .lh-hero .lh-title{text-align:left}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{justify-content:flex-start}
 }
 /* ── Section headers: same voice as the institutions band ─────────────
 Serif headings and a small monospaced label instead of the rounded blue
 pills, which were the last "app" element on the page. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-header h2{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif !important;font-weight:600 !important;font-size:clamp(28px,3vw,40px) !important;letter-spacing:-.4px;line-height:1.15;color:#12233D !important}
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-badge{display:inline-block;margin-bottom:14px;padding:0;background:none;border-radius:0;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:11.5px;font-weight:500;letter-spacing:1.8px;text-transform:uppercase;color:#8C5A23}
 .lh-wrap .lh-section-sub{color:#4A525C}
 /* Section rhythm: paper / white / paper, so each block has an edge. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-how{background:#FAF8F4}
 .lh-wrap .lh-unis{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins{background:#fff;border-top:1px solid #E4E0D8}
 /* How it works: the three steps were top-aligned, so the middle card
 (longer text) hung lower than its neighbours. Stretch evens them. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-steps{align-items:stretch}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step{background:#fff;border:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-radius:6px;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step-num{background:#12233D;font-family:"IBM Plex Mono",ui-monospace,monospace;font-weight:500}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step-icon{background:#F4F2ED;color:#12233D;border-radius:6px}
 .lh-wrap .lh-step-arrow{color:#B7B1A5}
 /* Cards: tighter corners and hairlines everywhere. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-card{border-radius:6px;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins a[class*="card"],.lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--origins [class*="card"]{border-radius:6px;border-color:#E4E0D8;box-shadow:none}
 .lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--countries a[class*="card"],.lh-wrap .lh-dest-section--countries [class*="card"]{border-radius:6px}
 /* ── Study fields block (rendered by [sie_study_fields] after .lh-wrap) ─
 Six bright category colours, gradient pills and a gradient CTA made it
 the loudest part of the page. Same content, one navy, warm neutrals.
 The branch colours arrive as INLINE custom properties and inline
 backgrounds, so these overrides need !important to apply. Scoped to the
 homepage: the study-field pages keep their colour coding. */
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-title{font-family:"Source Serif 4",Georgia,serif;font-weight:600;font-size:clamp(28px,3vw,40px);letter-spacing:-.4px;color:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-subtitle{color:#4A525C}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__source-pill{background:#12233D !important;background-image:none !important;box-shadow:none !important;border-radius:4px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__junction-dot{background:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch{--branch-color:#12233D !important;--branch-bg:#F4F2ED !important;border:1px solid #E4E0D8;border-radius:6px;box-shadow:none}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-accent{display:none}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-icon{background:#12233D !important;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__branch-count{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-card{background:#FAF8F4;border:1px solid #EDEAE3;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-card:hover{border-color:#12233D}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__field-icon{background:#F4F2ED !important;color:#12233D !important;border-radius:5px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-flow__leo-link{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leonardo{background:#12233D !important;background-image:none !important;border-radius:6px}
 body.page-id-150 .sie-fields-leo-btn{background:#fff !important;color:#12233D !important;border-color:#fff !important;border-radius:4px}
 /* Alignment: the search widget carries its own 24px side padding, so the
 bar sat indented from the headline above it; and the trust row was
 centred under a left-aligned column. Both now share the text's edge.
 Only the LEFT padding goes: removing the right one too pushed the
 "AI-enhanced matching" toggle across the seam into the navy side. */
 .lh-herosearch .sie-sps-wrap{padding-left:0 !important}
 .lh-hero .lh-trust-row{justify-content:flex-start}
 /* Institution cards: the stylesheet tints each card top a different pastel

 monogram or logo is the only thing that differs between cards. */
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-card:nth-child(n) .lh-uni-card-top{background:#F4F2ED !important;background-image:none !important;border-bottom:1px solid #EDEAE3}
 .lh-wrap .lh-uni-cta{color:#0B5FA5 !important}
 .lh-wrap .sie-dest-hub__name{color:#12233D}

<h1 class="title-h1 eac-page-title">Conference on the Future of Europe : the future is in your hands</h1>
<span><span>sandoel</span></span>

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>
