]]> https://tech.eu/2026/10/29/former-uk-government-minister-afolami-raises-ps5m-for-ai-insurance-broker-startup/ Thu, 29 Oct 2026 10:21:54 +0000 https://tech.eu/2026/10/29/former-uk-government-minister-afolami-raises-ps5m-for-ai-insurance-broker-startup/feed 0 true <![CDATA[MuRay raises €7.1M to inspect rocket engines and turbines beyond X-ray limits]]> https://tech.eu/2026/10/29/muray-raises-eur71m-to-inspect-rocket-engines-and-turbines-beyond-x-ray-limits/ https://tech.eu/2026/10/29/muray-raises-eur71m-to-inspect-rocket-engines-and-turbines-beyond-x-ray-limits/#comments Hamburg-based deeptech company MuRay has raised €7.1 million in funding to further develop its Active Muon Imaging technology and bring it to industrial customers.

The financing includes a €3.5 million private investment round led by First Momentum Ventures and co-led by Caelora, a wholly owned subsidiary of Marvel Fusion. Other participants include Superangel, Mätch VC, Arcas VC and Tiny VC, alongside existing investor Nordic Science Investments. The company also received €3.6 million in non-dilutive public funding, including a grant from the EU's Horizon Europe programme.

Founded by Dr Andi Hektor and Dr Kristjan Põder, who serve as co-CEOs, MuRay is developing imaging technology that uses controlled muon beams to examine the internal structure of dense materials and components.

Quality assurance is the company’s initial focus, particularly for complex, safety-critical components such as 3D-printed rocket engines and gas turbine parts, where detecting internal defects remains a challenge.

Conventional X-rays struggle to penetrate dense materials, while MuRay's technology uses muons to produce high-resolution 3D images of components made from metals, ceramics and composites. The system can identify differences in material composition and density, enabling inspections within minutes rather than hours.

According to the company, the technology could allow manufacturers to detect defects directly on production lines while operating at a significantly lower radiation dose than conventional X-ray methods.

Dr Andi Hektor, co-founder and co-CEO of MuRay, said:

X-rays reach their limit at a few centimetres of steel, yet much of modern industry, from reusable rockets to gas turbines, is built from metal far thicker than that. Active muon imaging lets manufacturers see inside those large, dense components.

Beyond manufacturing quality assurance, MuRay is exploring applications across the space, aerospace, defence and energy industries, where more detailed inspections could help shorten maintenance cycles for components such as reusable rocket engines and jet engines.

In collaboration with the German Space Agency at DLR, MuRay has modelled the inspection of a rocket engine and plans its first real-world assessment in 2027. The project aims to demonstrate the technology's ability to detect internal defects in safety-critical components.

Dr Kristjan Põder, co-founder and co-CEO, added:

Defects that manufacturers can't see keep parts out of service for longer than they should be. Our technology helps them find those defects and get components back into service faster.

MuRay is also exploring applications in cargo and border security, where its technology could detect nuclear materials such as uranium within dense cargo. Longer-term possibilities include radioactive waste monitoring, the inspection of large structures such as bridges and buildings, and clinical diagnostics.

The new funding will support further technology development and MuRay's commercialisation plans, including a mobile imaging system approximately the size of a shipping container, designed to enable inspections directly at industrial sites.

The company plans to launch its first imaging service for industrial customers in 2027, combining DESY's existing electron beam in Hamburg with its own imaging system, followed by its first full-scale system incorporating a laser-driven accelerator in 2029.

The app lets shoppers scan a product in the supermarket and instantly see whether it is an ultra-processed food (UPF), along with healthier alternatives.  More than 70 per cent of products on supermarket shelves are ultra-processed.

A growing body of evidence on UPF’s

UPFs are designed to tempt, backed by clever marketing and often on special offer. In November 2025, an international team of researchers published a series in The Lancet linking the growing share of UPFs in diets worldwide to the rise in chronic disease.

Brussels has taken notice. In July, the European Commission asked its scientific advisers how the EU should define ultra-processed food. Their advice is expected in March 2027.

The Commission has also approached FLTRD co-founder Anke Kuik for her expertise.

“The fact that UPFs are now on the European agenda is an important step,” says Kuik. “It shows this isn’t a passing trend, but a problem that calls for a structural response.”

How does the PureScore work?

The PureScore rates products on three components that together determine the score:

Ingredients: the type and amount of added sugars, fats, salt and additives. Refined ingredients stripped of their nutrients also lower the score.

Processing techniques: processes such as heating, hydrogenation and extrusion that alter the natural structure of food. The more intensive the processing, the lower the score.

Organic certification: organic products score higher because they contain fewer pesticide residues. This structure reflects the three main ways UPFs are thought to affect health: loss of nutrients, the addition of harmful substances and a higher risk of overconsumption.

The FLTRD app now covers more than 150,000 products from seven supermarkets, all of which have a PureScore. This independent, science-based score rates a product’s degree of processing based on its ingredients and processing techniques, so people can easily make healthier choices. 

In the Netherlands, more than 35,000 people already use the app on iPhone and Android.

The goal is for 100 million people to use the PureScore to guide their grocery shopping within five years.

“In France, one in three people already uses a similar app. That’s a clear sign people want more insight and guidance,” says Kuik.

“This investment allows us to bring in the people we need to accelerate.

We’re expanding to Belgium before the end of the year, and we’ll be licensing the PureScore to food producers and retailers. We believe everyone has the right to understand the impact of what they eat.”

A structural shift in the market 

Victor Straatman, partner at 4impact capital, shared:

“The European debate on ultra-processed food signals a structural shift in the market. As the European Commission explores which policy frameworks are needed, transparency is becoming a commercial priority for the food sector.

Our investment is directly tied to that shift. FLTRD has the data and the methodology to objectively measure a product’s degree of processing, at exactly the moment verifiable product information is becoming a firm market requirement.”

Alongside 4impact, several angel investors from the FMCG industry have participated in the round. One of them is Jeroen Lubbers, who now invests in healthy food initiatives after many years in the sector. 

“Consumers have the right to see at a glance what’s really in a product and what healthier alternatives are available.

Clear information is essential, especially for people with food intolerances. Food producers also need a quick, objective way to assess their products and identify opportunities for improvement. FLTRD makes that information accessible and easy to use for consumers and producers alike.”

Founded by Marius Blaker Høgevold (CEO) and Hans Nyvold Kjellby (Chairman and CCO), Fronted aims to address these challenges through an integrated platform combining cross-border recruitment, Employer of Record (EOR) services and company entity setup and management. By incorporating local labour regulations into its software, Fronted aims to reduce manual processes, improve pricing transparency and simplify compliance across different jurisdictions.

Marius Blaker Høgevold, co-founder and CEO of Fronted, highlighted the challenges businesses face when expanding internationally, particularly the costs and complexities associated with existing service providers.

We are building the invisible software layer that takes away the headache of cross-border administration, giving ambitious companies a trusted Nordic partner to scale globally with total transparency and ease,

said Høgevold.

Founded by Axel Löwenhoff and Allan Zimmermann, KineDB is developing a general-purpose database designed to operate across different environments, from cloud infrastructure to local devices without an internet connection. Axel Löwenhoff, co-founder of KineDB, explained how the growing use of AI in software development is changing the requirements for database infrastructure:

The way AI has opened the gates for developers of all levels to experiment and launch new software is a wonderful thing. A consequence, however, is a lot of software where creators haven’t necessarily considered the underlying databases essential to functionality.
With KineDB, we want to remove that as a layer of complication for engineers, by providing a database that works within this new environment.
